the rapporteur. mr president, it is on the initiative of the committee on constitutional affairs that the european parliament is tackling for the first time, with a specific report and a draft resolution, the issue of the role of regional and local authorities in european integration. it is not difficult to understand the reasons and aims of this initiative. in fact, especially in the last decade, there has been a widespread phenomenon of decentralisation, regionalisation and the growth of local autonomy in the member states of the union, a phenomenon which should be appreciated and taken seriously into account when reflecting and discussing the state of the european union and its future. regional and local authorities have acquired a significant weight in the transposition of community legislation and the management of community programmes within the individual states. they must therefore also feel involved in the preparation of union policies and acts. in this connection, the draft resolution which is now before parliament for a vote in plenary contains significant proposals: to incorporate into the new constitutional framework the principles of respect for regional and local identities, and thus the application of subsidiarity, not only in relations between the union and the member states but also towards regional and local authorities; to commit the commission, also on the basis of its white paper on governance, to involve representatives of regional and local authorities in the preparation of its proposals; urge the member states to promote and enhance each of them according to the characteristics of its constitutional order the participation of regional and local authorities in the decision-making process of the union. with the resolution we have prepared, which, if supported by a broad consensus in the vote, will represent an important point of reference for the next debate, at the beginning of february, in the brussels convention, the cause of the recognition of the role of regional and local authorities in the construction of europe will take a significant step forward. i hope that, even through amendments which correct or clarify the text adopted by the committee on constitutional affairs, some of the concerns expressed by myself and other colleagues in committee will be taken into account and that we will avoid coercion and unilateralism which would harm the cause in which we believe. i would like to reiterate the criteria i used as rapporteur: first, it is necessary to refer to all the autonomous territorial entities operating within the member states. as we all know, they vary greatly in size and nature, but all of them, from the largest to the smallest, whatever their role and weight, represent certain common values: the value of closeness, of the closest adherence to the feelings, opinions and needs of citizens, the value of the most immediate and widespread democratic participation possible, and all of them must therefore be recognised in the european constitution as playing a decisive role in achieving the objective assigned to the convention on the future of europe: the objective of a stronger union closer to its citizens, of a union that grows not only more efficiently but also more democratically. i therefore did not propose in my draft report any division of the regions or local authorities into different categories. the granting of special status and rights to a part of the autonomous territorial entities would give rise to difficult and counterproductive disputes, including the very definition and delimitation of one or the other category, for example that of regions with legislative powers, and would obscure the value of the recognition of the whole reality, the whole universe, of regional and local powers. secondly, care must be taken not to burden an institutional system and procedures which, by all accounts, must be simplified. and when i say 'institutional system' i also mean the court of justice and its functioning. in general, care must be taken not to aggravate a decision-making process which is already subject to many influences by means of a complex of filters and more or less rigid brakes. in conclusion, i trust that my colleagues will reflect on my remarks and facilitate a broad convergence in the votes tomorrow. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that mr napolitano's report, to which we owe our thanks for the difficult and complicated work he has done, should be an opportunity to stress, with all the institutional strength of the european parliament, the need for the new europe, the one which will be based on the constitutional treaty which the convention is drawing up, to give full meaning to the application of the principle of subsidiarity, without any distortion. this means that the result will only be achieved if subsidiarity is not limited to relations between the union and the national states, but extends to territorial collectivities, regions and municipalities, while strictly respecting the constitutional order of each country. it is only the territorial collectivities - the regions and the municipalities - that give substance to democracy of proximity; it is they who make it possible to strengthen the very roots of democracy and to bring citizens closer to the institutions, including the european institutions. the convention is the place to untie this knot. it started by concentrating its attention only on the first level of subsidiarity, that between the union and the states. we must get out of this trap because if we sanction this double level of subsidiarity - between the union and the states and between the states and the territorial collectivities - we prevent - i believe this is the knot around which we are all getting a little tangled - the recognition of the direct link between the european institutions and the territorial collectivities that already exists and is bearing promising fruit, if it is not misinterpreted or, on the contrary, if it is not killed in its birth. it is a trap that we must avoid. to do so, i hope that the convention will draw on the debate that has been taking place in europe on this subject for a long time, especially in the council of europe. i hope that the convention will succeed in recognizing and enshrining the right to local and regional autonomy, a right which will be regulated in the laws of the individual countries but which must be such, the uniqueness of subsidiarity, the equal dignity of the levels of government, the right of local authorities to have their own financial resources and the right to bring cases to court, which can find ways of balancing the technical requirements to prevent this from becoming a boomerang against the needs of the territorial collectivities, but which cannot prevent this from happening. perhaps the idea of strengthening the channel through the committee of the regions can be the solution we all need.
mr president, i too would like to thank president napolitano for the excellent work he has done and to concentrate on what has been the most controversial point in his report, namely paragraph 8. it seems to me that the obvious and normal consequence of the european union's transition from a system based on an international treaty, negotiated by diplomats, to a federal political union, based on a constitution, is that of organisation, of strengthening the instruments of constitutional control. the argument that direct access by certain regions with constitutional, and therefore legislative, powers would result in a deadlock in the court of justice seems to me to be a very weak argument indeed, because if that were the case, then we would have to find a way of strengthening the court of justice, making the system stronger and better able to accommodate these appeals. it seems to me, moreover, that there is a need to make these constitutional remedies - as mr duff has already said - more immediately recognizable and accessible to the citizens, and this not only in the case of the regions but also in the case of violations of the fundamental rights of citizens. i think this is an important aspect of the future european constitution, and that is why i think it is frankly exaggerated to over-dramatize the possibility offered by this report, which is also the most innovative and original part of it, and to consider it a kind of drama that we would not be able to handle. it seems to me, moreover, that the proposed compromise has two fundamental limitations, because it proposes two filters, two filters which are themselves insufficient: the state cannot be the filter of the region because it is very often in conflict with the region itself and its powers, and the committee of the regions, which was created deliberately weak, cannot be an additional filter for the powers of the legally recognized regions, also because it introduces, maintains the idea of a false neutrality, as commissioner barnier said, and a false equality between the regions: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the regions are not treated in the same way.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the napolitano report deals with one of the most controversial issues facing the convention: the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption by the end of the year. i think it is right that the proposal on the union's powers should not interfere with the national laws. we cannot, however, ignore the fact that some national constitutions confer important legislative powers on the regions, and the convention will have to recognise this, without, however, creating privileges, without disturbing the internal market, without dissolving the need for a political europe. in the light of all these considerations, i think it is right to give the regions with legislative powers the possibility of appealing directly to the court of justice when their prerogatives are affected by european decisions. i think it would be a mistake to ignore that some regions or länder in germany, italy and spain represent territorial collectivities of a much larger size than many of the realities that have been consolidated into national states. the search for a broad consensus on this report, which president napolitano rightly urged, is a requirement of a constituent process which must encourage the participation of the regions and local authorities in the future of community europe.

use of the internet might be a more appropriate way forward.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in financial markets, where market liquidity is closely linked to the confidence of traders in the reliability of payment and securities settlement systems, the inefficient operation of these systems can be a source of risk for the markets themselves. reliable payment and settlement systems require a clear legal framework, rules and procedures governing the holding, transfer, lending of securities and related payments, and the setting of securities-related encumbrances. clearing and settlement, which are essential elements of all securities transactions, are therefore of fundamental importance for the smooth functioning of integrated financial markets. it should be noted, however, that despite the growing foreign securities market, there is still not only a high degree of fragmentation in the eu clearing and settlement infrastructure, but also excessive and certainly uncontrolled crossborder cost incidence. however, to achieve concrete objectives, it is necessary to know the operational situation of the sector in order to make appropriate adjustments. the two largest markets are the united states and europe. the us has chosen the depository trust and clearing corporation, which includes both clearing and settlement systems and is traceable to a single management body, whose proven functionality has resulted in significant cost containment. the european model, with as many as 20 csds, is a fragmented reality, the advantage of which is that competition is limited only to the acquisition of new areas of influence. no price war has ever occurred, as market liquidity is channelled through a single operational player. the examination of the existing framework and the in-depth investigation carried out by the giovannini working group have revealed that a multiplicity of technical, legal and fiscal obstacles are at the origin of the high costs and inefficiency. the removal of technical obstacles should be the first objective to be pursued and can be considered easily achievable. the standardization of computer language, like the standardization of paper documentation, does not require any particular operational effort. the harmonization of legal and fiscal rules is certainly more difficult. the ambitious objective to be achieved would be the establishment of a single securities code, which would provide a real guarantee for traders; but reaching agreement between member states on this is certainly difficult because of the delicate and sensitive issues linked to the diversity of rules in property law and in company and bankruptcy law. the establishment of this code must therefore be seen as a long-term objective. a fact sheet should be drawn up in the near future to inform market participants of the differences between the laws in force in the member states. as regards tax obstacles, the difficulties arise not only from the diversity of systems but also from strong resistance to change and harmonisation on the part of some member states. given the need for a post-trading re-ordering aimed at eliminating the confusion between infrastructure and functions and to cancel out existing natural monopoly positions, a formula for core settlement services operated on the legal basis of a service owned by the user and regulated by a non-profit-making, non-profit-making statute is necessary. this choice would ensure market integrity, easy access for users to services, effective surveillance against operational risk. there could be no distortion of competition, because the guarantee is provided by the fact that the service provider participates in the management of the institution. innovation and technical progress could also be achieved as the formula in paragraph 11 of the report states that non-profit comes after the necessary investment needs have been met. the separation between essential and value-added functions is also considered essential. the latter could in any case be carried out by the csds, but with separate structures, including logistically, through subsidiaries or joint ventures. the clearing and settlement service includes guarantee, margin, clearing, settlement and liquidation activities. a simple reading of the text shows that these are all public utility activities. the value-added services offered by banks or separate depository structures are: securities lending, collateral management, cash management, corporate actions, income management and tax services: all activities of a purely commercial nature. finally, strong cooperation between states is also considered essential for proper surveillance.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are dealing with a subject of great importance to all european citizens. we are talking about health, about the elderly, and i would say that the health systems of all the member states of the european union are experiencing similar situations, although with different intensities. they are already facing major challenges, particularly in the area of health expenditure containment and coverage. the ageing of the population, advances in medical technology and the growing demand for healthcare services have led to a significant increase in the costs of the healthcare system, sometimes unsustainable for current economies, and of care for the elderly across europe. some figures to illustrate: in the european union, the share of the population aged over 65 will increase from 16.1% in 2000 to 22% in 2025 and 27% in 2050, a third of the population. at the same time, the proportion of the elderly over 80 years, which was 3.6 percent in 2000, is expected to reach 6 percent in 2025 and 10 percent in 2050. although the provision of healthcare and care for the elderly remains essentially a matter for the member states, we realise that such a trend, with its considerable and complex implications, cannot be effectively and comprehensively addressed at national level alone. these issues need to be integrated into the framework of wider european cooperation in order to achieve effective results, as expressed in the principles and objectives of the community action programme on public health and the specific objectives set out in the un action plan. to achieve these objectives, the cooperation of all health care professionals is needed. there is a need for better cooperation in the exchange of information, good practice, research, the creation of a database for the social and health sector, with statistical analysis and projections, the development of common qualitative and quantitative standards, thus defining health indicators and developing common standards for the monitoring of health services. the barcelona european council of march 2002 also stressed the need to establish and develop cooperation between member states in this field, by exchanging good practice and information and by addressing common challenges at european level. the european union has already stressed on several occasions the need to develop a comprehensive strategy that embraces the economic, employment and social implications of demographic ageing, mobilising the full potential of people of all ages and strengthening solidarity between generations. in line with the principle of solidarity and access to care for all, both social protection and the provision of quality health services in the member states will need to be maintained and improved in order to fully achieve the objectives of financial sustainability, accessibility and quality. this should eventually lead to the creation of a single market for health services and products: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. another important aspect to consider is the risk that the objective of financial sustainability is overvalued in relation to the costs of accessibility and quality. solutions should be indicated as soon as possible: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. finally, greater attention should be paid to certain aspects of the development of health and social services for the elderly, in particular those which are not self-sufficient and which represent the major and most important problem, such as the treatment of mental illnesses linked to senility, the maintenance of the autonomy of the person, integration, access to rehabilitation and rehabilitation services, prevention, care and support for families taking care of the elderly, the fight against maltreatment and neglect. the commission yesterday issued its eighth warning to become the world's most competitive economy by 2010: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. well, the aging population knot is a very important knot in this regard. therefore, in the hope of seeing the european parliament soon more actively involved in the elaboration of the broad economic and health policy guidelines, i invite the commission and the council to take account of the decisions contained in this report in preparing the joint summary report for the 2003 spring european council and the european convention, which i believe should include, as a general objective, a high level of health protection. only in this way, with the social europe, will we, i believe, move from the europe of banks and coins to the europe of people and nations. mr president, mr president of the ebrd, mr commissioner, this first decade of the european bank for reconstruction and development has been a time of lights and shadows. mr markov's report tends to paint a very positive picture, especially as regards the last few years, which is understandable in many respects, but in the past, including the recent russian crisis, problems have emerged which have led to unsatisfactory or even bankruptcy results, as in the case of the russian crisis, which involved the ebrd together with many other international financial institutions. this probably stems from one of the main points of contradiction in the institutional activities of the ebrd, which is to promote the market economy through a non-market instrument, i.e. a loan guaranteed by public funds, with the possibility - as the markov report also says - of taking risks that other institutions would not take. this brings us to a very sensitive point in the activities of the ebrd, which i am well aware is well known to the heads of the institutions, namely the risk of the private venture capital being displaced by the ebrd's financing of the development of endogenous credit in these countries. it is a difficult balance to strike, but one which i believe must be carefully managed. the eib's intervention must not end up undermining the growth of a private credit sector. two more points to close: i believe that in future the focus will shift more and more to the neighbouring countries and less and less to the countries which will be joining the european union, precisely because in these countries the risk of displacing the emergence of a private market economy is greater. finally, i address the european union as the majority shareholder of the ebrd: we invest, for example, in ukraine through the ebrd. it is a worthy undertaking, but with one hand we give and with the other we remove the trade restrictions which are very heavy on a country like ukraine: it would be good if both hands agreed on the action.
mr president, commissioner, president of the ebrd, ladies and gentlemen, first of all let me congratulate the rapporteur on his careful analysis of the ebrd's activities. the choice of economic activities must be able to combine the local and international dimensions and require the provision of credit to encourage not only the emergence of well-established initiatives in the territory but also their spread to other markets. the task of the ebrd is certainly to strengthen this aspect, but it is more important to seek it out and to strengthen it in the countries with low industrial development which are in greatest need of support and revival. if this objective involves risks and, in some cases, unforeseen losses, it is not necessary to abandon planned initiatives and investments, but to draw on new experience in order to manage credit more carefully and to interpret risks more thoroughly. the bank also takes an ethical approach to its credit management. the institutional commitment is to invest in all countries that are inspired by democratic principles and are committed to promoting the market economy. the first time, the bank asks customers for valid projects at current market prices; it also requires that there are no conflicts of interest or dominant positions in the operational area to be financed and that, in any event, the interests of the community are respected. in the public sector, the ebrd calls for maximum transparency to ensure competition and equal treatment of market participants. the rapporteur's view is commendable and acceptable when he encourages the commission to support small local banks which, in turn, must deal with the management of small loans. at this point, mr president, i would like to sound a warning. the credit system of small banks is disappearing or is shrinking considerably. this is a worrying fact because no economic or financial manoeuvre, however good, can replace the support that small banks have always offered to small and mediumsized enterprises. we must also note that small loans are totally neglected in many member states, particularly in those which are in the process of enlargement, and this is increasing day by day the financial exclusion, which is understood as the existence of serious gaps in the provision of financial services in the form of microcredit in the economically weaker areas, where a form of discrimination based on geographical criteria, red-lining, is taking place. the ebrd, which has already chosen to operate from albania to ukraine, from kazakhstan to moldova, is to help ensure that these marginalised economies are fully integrated into the international economy.
mr president, commissioner, i think we really all have to be grateful to mr martin, not just for the good work he has done, as has been acknowledged by everyone, but because he actually enables all of us to make a stand on this subject of aquaculture. it has been said before: i would like to say that the commission has been very careful in its approach to the problem of the fisheries sector, and that it has been very careful in its approach to the problem of the fisheries sector. as other colleagues have said, it is the numbers that speak: this is a sector where employment is growing; it is a sector that meets a growing demand. it is a sector which alleviates the difficulties of many coastal areas which otherwise would have no alternative. it is also a sector that helps us to fight the battle we face with the decline in the stocks of extractive fisheries. moreover, unlike the fisheries reform, this is an area where the commission and parliament are quite in agreement. i am glad to have heard today from commissioner solbes the appreciation he has for this report, and we can all see that there is a convergence on the issues of food safety, research, the environmental compatibility of this sector. so we are at a good meeting point. i would just like to ask the commissioner to pay more attention to the two points which parliament is making: one, as regards the amendment of the fifg regulation, of the financial regulation, in particular as regards the admission of young people and the conversion of installations; the other, as regards the natural disaster fund. it is not possible, mr commissioner, to affirm the value and usefulness of an economic sector without being consistent in the measures to support it.
mr president, i too am grateful to the rapporteur because i believe that this report will enable us to make a few definitive points: the commission has also been active in the development of aquaculture as a substantial source of supplementary income, especially for fishermen living and working in marginal areas, but also in its capacity to reduce fishing activity and preserve our resources. however, some problems remain, especially for small-scale and artisanal fisheries. conversion to aquaculture needs help because it is expensive: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. the financial instrument for fisheries guidance should provide for specific and timely concessional credit measures, otherwise aquaculture will remain a choice for the privileged. the commission's target of 8 000-10 000 additional jobs is an ambitious challenge, but it requires a concrete commitment to promote the economic viability of aquaculture. another objective - one to which this parliament is particularly attentive - is food safety, environmental impact and animal health. this requires a code of conduct with well-defined rules and parameters, and above all, it requires that all products from third countries be subject to our standards of hygiene, food safety and animal welfare. this is not only, as it seems, to avoid unfair competition, but above all to make a real contribution to the quality of our sustainable development.

the commissioner, i am sure that the subject under discussion tonight is one of the great themes of world and european politics. for example, the first is that world agricultural trade and the negotiations which define and will define its aspects and procedures represent the moment of confrontation between the liberalization of markets and the will of governments to pursue the objectives of protectionist agricultural policies which go beyond mere production and which also invest the so-called non-trade aspects, such as environmental protection, food security, the protection and promotion of quality, the safeguarding of rural areas. we have listened to you carefully tonight, commissioner, and it is clear from your words that the european union has expressed a strong desire to negotiate an agreement for further liberalisation of trade in agricultural products. but we believe that the agreement must be balanced and that it must be a win-win agreement. i think this is also the position repeatedly supported by commissioner fischler for community agricultural policies, who, not more than a week ago, in the committee on agriculture stressed that the rules which will emerge from the new negotiating rounds next autumn must be equal and fair for all. the idea that emerges of reducing export subsidies is certainly an attractive one, and one that can certainly be supported, but only if other subsidies that distort international trade are also regulated in the same way. and then we have another big political theme that runs through tonight's theme: we need a holistic view of the system. the current economic context, which will involve and capture future scenarios in the agricultural sector, cannot be limited to international trade, because international trade is directly involved in the proposal for a revision of the community's agricultural policy. what was supposed to be a mid-term review of the analysis has become a real form in which european agriculture is given a new look. the community's policy guidelines in this area, in addition to looking at the market as an instrument of economic development, are directed at consumer protection in europe: the european food safety authority has recently introduced a new approach to food safety. this principle of food safety has been brought up and acquired at the wto level as well, but it has been acquired as an idea; the commission has already taken a number of steps to ensure that the quality of our products is protected. production costs in the european agricultural economy differ significantly from those in developing countries, as standards of quality, safety and hygiene are different. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a good one. in a globalised world, european farmers must invest in the quality of their products in order to win over particular market segments that are sensitive to new consumer demands. production standards have now been refined towards traceability of production from the stable to the table. in this sense, the possibility of marketing european agri-food production on a world scale must go hand in hand with the economic development of the less wealthy countries, with mutual respect for local agri-food production, in a global context of balanced growth, regulated both by the economy and by certain rules, but above all by the common sense of growth that benefits everyone at the expense of no one. the basic theme, therefore, which we have to deal with at this moment is that in the proposal which you, commissioner, have presented to us tonight, there is a principle: we need a common agricultural policy which continues the forms we have known. in his words and in the documents before us there is a principle which we accept with great difficulty: the commission's proposal for a mid-term review, which includes the decoupling and abolition of the blue box, takes precedence over the negotiating procedures in the wto, which instead provide for an attempt to defend the aid in the blue box introduced by the mcsharry reform. this implies the need to reconsider the negotiating procedures, effectively tearing up the blue box chapter and thus definitively renouncing the possibility of defending direct payments in a multilateral context. if this were to happen, we believe that it would be the beginning of a demobilization of the european agricultural sector, which is strategic not only for the sector as such but for the whole european economy.
the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i thank commissioner vitorino for this opening statement, which paves the way for my report. the directive we are discussing represents a real leap forward in the debate on citizenship of the union and the free movement of persons. for the first time, citizens are being recognized as having rights, not as subjects of economic interest but as persons, as holders of subjective rights which, together with objective rights, constitute european citizenship. the rights of free movement and residence are directly derived from the european treaty, come from a long way back, as the commissioner has said, and confer on citizens new and very important fundamental rights. it can be said that this directive lays the foundations for the dual citizenship - national and european - enshrined in the draft treaty, which is also discussed in the convention. the right of permanent residence which is being pursued is a concrete example of this. before examining the directive in more detail, it is appropriate to clarify its scope. it is addressed to community citizens and their family members, whatever their nationality. the principle of equal treatment of third-country nationals who are members of a community family has been enshrined in clear terms since the 1960s and this directive makes it even more effective and efficient. this is a right derived from that of the community citizen whose family they are members of. it should be made clear at the outset that this directive does not apply to third-country nationals, and in any event not to those who are not related to community nationals, even if they reside in a member state or exercise freedom of movement within the union. the great merit of this directive is that it contains all the previous provisions on this subject in a single text. another advantage is clarity, and i believe that some of the rapporteur's amendments have also helped to simplify the overly bureaucratic procedures as much as possible. the commissioner also stressed that the european parliament had a duty to ensure that the european parliament's powers were not undermined by the council's decision to suspend the application of the schengen acquis. the registration procedure should be simple and straightforward and, in any case, the principle of self-certification should be applied, as is already the case in some member states. this must also apply to means of proof, such as income guarantee and health cover. for thirdcountry nationals, proof of the relationship must be provided by an identity document, the sole purpose being to avoid possible abuse. another innovative principle carried forward by the directive concerns the expulsion of third-country nationals who have a right of residence in the community. the directive provides that expulsion may not be carried out under any circumstances. this approach applies the amsterdam principle of creating an area of freedom, security and justice without frontiers, but some member states will probably want to intervene with their own rules on this issue. i have left the most pressing issue for last, as is always the case when a debate is held in this house: the family, its composition, the definition of a couple and a spouse. in order to prevent such a large number of innovative regulations from becoming hostages to the usual iron fist, i have made a very open effort as rapporteur, pushing myself to the extreme limits of my principles and those of the political group i represent, in order to bring the directive as a whole to fruition. moreover, the definition of spouse is not open to question under community law, and the court of justice has repeatedly stated this. in this area, and also in relation to civil partnerships, the rapporteur takes up a number of amendments tabled and then withdrawn by the socialist group, which call for the laws of the various member states to redress the differences which still exist at community level. this democratic call for subsidiarity, for national sovereignty, i believe, respects all sensitivities and should avoid the usual crusades which risk devaluing the content of the report and undermining the scope of the directive. in short, each member state regulates family matters on the basis of national legislation and national sensibilities. it would be a real pity if we were not able to deliver a serious and agreed text to the council, given the tremendous opportunity we have to take part in the codecision on this matter. it is not possible to impose on 13 states a model shared by only two of them, or to give priority to symbols and dogmas over the serious rules which millions of citizens expect to regulate their lives. in conclusion, the rapporteur's line - it must be said - largely coincides with that of the commission, which has been able to provide a coherent and objective text interpreting, as we know, also the council's position. we have the opportunity to deliver new, modern and more secure rules to citizens. i hope that the vote in this house will enable us to approve them and i thank the rapporteurs for their opinions and all the colleagues who have made my work easier with their amendments and have certainly improved the content of the directive. madam president, the proposal for a directive on the right of free movement and residence of european citizens and their families within the territory of the member states marks a fundamental step the rapporteur. mr president, madam vice-president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, we are faced with a european question, even if the list of speakers is dominated by italians and austrians. let me say, however, at the outset that i understand the austrians' concerns as a mountaineer. the austrian case and the alpine question as a whole are the direct consequence of a transport policy which must be radically changed, as clearly indicated in the white paper, which, by a completely coincidental circumstance, we shall be discussing this afternoon. there are two requirements: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the free movement of goods and the single market, and on the protection of the environment, road safety and human health. in essence, what is called, in a somewhat fashionable term, sustainable development. what should be the transport logic? less lorries, more trains, less transport monoculture, more intermodality, fewer roads and road switches, more rail switches, an overall rebalancing of the situation which takes account of the freedom of the market but also of the need for guidelines, including clarity on the real costs of transport, consequent charging, the release of resources for railway investment, the european railway system package, safety with the appropriate tunnel directive and with common rules to make road transport safer; finally, there is a growing push for less polluting vehicles and, in conclusion, the use of systems such as the galileo satellite system for monitoring truck fleets. the austrian case: the same applies to other mountain ranges, such as the pyrenees. we are facing an explosion in freight traffic, and this phenomenon will increase even more with enlargement. historically, austria has had this eco-points system, which was about to expire, and we have seen a strangely undulating european council since laeken until midnight last year, when what the committee called a virtual solution was found, i.e. one that did not really exist in the real world of numbers. that is why the european parliament, by a large majority in the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, has chosen its own path, starting from the premise that a legal basis must be in view, namely the transport protocol to the alpine convention, which will be the only instrument that will also oblige the european union to regulate the flows of truck traffic in the alpine area. a new policy is needed which sees the swiss model as an example that must be copied in some way. the committee i chair has done its best to find a balanced solution: we have invited the ministers, we have also made sure that the date of the brenner basic railway is moved permanently from 2021 to 2012; we have tried, in the amendments we are putting to the house, to find a solution that goes beyond the logic of the ecopoints, but we found a solution, up to 2006, that was based on the need, as i said, to take account of the guidelines of the alpine convention, but i would say, more generally, of the sensitive areas of the alps: it is not by chance that amendment no 15 refers to other areas, such as the fréjus area in the north-western alps, the mont blanc area and the austrian alps, in short, the alps as a whole, because i believe that this is the overall picture we have to face today. we have tried very carefully, especially in article 13, to find this modulation of tir, this logic of the 2004-2005-2006 quotas, the logic of which in 2005-2006 will lead to the prohibition of euro 0 and euro 1, a quotas for euro 2 and a free passage for euro 3. finally, as regards the amendments: i do not think that the swoboda and simpson amendments, which substantially amend the proposal which was adopted by a large majority in the committee, are acceptable, nor is the rack amendment acceptable because it changes the cards in the deck profoundly, even in this case. i think the green amendment no 19 is interesting, because it is based on the future debate. finally, i think we should say 'no' to amendments nos 20 and 21, because they also change the whole of the proposal. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that as chairman of the committee, as rapporteur, i had the duty to strike a balance. i would perhaps, as a mountaineer, have gone further, but i think it would be appropriate for parliament to take note of the current state of the debate.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me return to the subject of the spring summit. the ultimate lisbon objective of making the european economy the most competitive knowledge-based economy in ten years has been seen by many as an optimistic and comforting slogan from the outset. in fact, it is becoming less and less so, as, three years later, little has been done to achieve this goal. the european economy is still at a standstill, the necessary reforms are being postponed or watered down from top to top, and the hopes of europe's unemployed to find jobs through growth are still tied to the relaunch of the us locomotive economy. the spring summit is likely to see the heads of state or government reaffirm - though in the present climate it is not certain - their commitment to the lisbon objectives. a letter has already been circulated to the greek presidency reaffirming the need and the will to re-energize the european economy through ambitious structural reforms. well very well, we would say but we radicals believe however that, instead of setting or re-proposing big goals, we must do right away good and right things: urgently reform social security systems, which for many states represent not only a serious injustice towards future generations but also a real time bomb for the sustainability of public finances; the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the reforms and will continue to monitor the implementation of the reforms. a genuinely integrated european financial market needs to be created; it is necessary to reduce drastically the burdens that are particularly on small and medium-sized enterprises in europe - fiscal, bureaucratic, in terms of labour regulation - and which are one of the reasons why a substantial part of european entrepreneurship and micro-entrepreneurship - i think of italy but not only - is pushed into the underground economy, an economy that escapes regulation, that escapes legality precisely because of the excessive burdens that are imposed. these are the things that should be done if we are to avoid being deceived by slogans, by magic words - words which are used a lot in this house - such as the european social model or the social market economy. i think we do well to ask ourselves whether these models are, today, really capable of protecting the weaker bands, the outsider bands.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i congratulate mrs stihler on her report. as a surgeon oncologist and university researcher, i have read the report very carefully and i agree with many of the proposals contained in it. i think, however, that the argument was made in an overly alarmist tone, and i will explain why. for nearly 50 years, silicones have been widely used in consumer products - soft drinks, puddings, cakes, pharmaceuticals, paediatric materials, pacemakers, heart valves, lipsticks, creams, fabrics - and have been shown not to cause cancer in humans. for 40 years, silicone breast implants have been used around the world for both aesthetic reasons, for example in the case of serious psychological problems, and for reconstructive reasons, for example in the case of a mastectomy for breast cancer where no age limit can be indicated. in 1986 the university of los angeles examined three thousand women who had been wearing prosthetics for at least six years and found no increased risk of neoplasia or mobility. in 1992, the university of calgary, in examining eleven thousand women, came to the same conclusions. the american association of rheumatologists also sponsored two studies on the risk of autoimmune disease in women wearing silicone prostheses, always demonstrating good tolerance. the average life of prostheses is therefore between 15 and 25 years and spontaneous rupture is often asymptomatic. there are therefore no serious reasons to prevent its use, except for young women under the age of 18. i would point out that the report makes no reference to breast implants for preventive therapeutic purposes, when the results of predictive genetic tests, which are increasingly used in the field of cancer, have shown a high risk of carcinogenesis in patients, especially in the case of children of mothers who have cancer, and this is a practice which will become more and more widespread. as regards paragraph 10a, i would point out that in all the member states of the union the informed consent of the patient is already in use, a mandatory instrument signed by patients after receiving all the relevant information, before any therapeutic act, including implantation of prostheses. i therefore think it is superfluous to talk about a passport. i also think it is useful to set up a european register and a national register for the collection of data on breast implants, which are implanted for both aesthetic and therapeutic reasons. in addition, an annual check by a senologist with a free ultrasound is important, without the need for invasive examinations such as mammography and ct scans, which still subject the patient to radiation and prove to be more expensive practices for national health services. the collection of data on implanted prostheses and the regulated follow-up would facilitate the collection of case data for a more precise assessment, which would certainly give all women a sense of security.

qualifications. that preference must, of course, be given considerable consideration in advance in the context of competitions, but it cannot be a practical constraint on the actual result. in other words, to give absolute and unconditional preference to the under-represented sex in the event of appointment or promotion is, according to what the court has established, tantamount not only to going beyond the objective of promoting equal opportunities, but also to substituting for that objective an outcome of equal representation which can only be achieved by implementing the same objective. now, this philosophy of the court and this fundamental principle that, with a certain degree of restraint, determines a substantial balance of decisions, i think it is appropriate that they should be adopted as the appropriate instruments which parliament must provide in order to achieve a more mature equality, which is an achievement in the process of social and cultural life.

with all the levels of jurisdiction, which can guarantee the full right of defence. in the absence of this context, the creation of a european public prosecutor is illogical and unjustified, and i would like to stress this and also say this to the commissioner, who has somewhat hastily shelved the problem. we must think carefully, because the creation of such a body is premature, given that the objectives of judicial cooperation - which prevails here - have not been achieved and that it is necessary to harmonize the rules on criminal matters of the bodies of the member states. the court of justice cannot simply be given jurisdiction in criminal matters: the court of justice and the court of first instance were set up for different purposes and therefore there is no need to create a european public prosecutor when it is enough to strengthen judicial cooperation, based on the principle of subsidiarity, which is the criterion we must bear in mind. we must therefore proceed to deepening the competences of eurojust and to strengthening and coordinating these powers at european level. the amendments tabled are therefore intended to clarify matters. the rest of the relationship can be fine. we are very concerned that, with the sole exception of italy, where the judicial system is being changed at the very moment we are speaking, in no other european country do prosecutors enjoy the same status and powers as we would like to give to the european prosecutor, which is a cause for alarm in terms of legal consistency and the european legal area. these are the concerns we will express about the european public prosecutor, but since the question is actually raised in this measure, we must raise them in this parliament now and remedy them by means of amendments.
mr president, the reports by mr patrie, mr thyssen and mr whitehead, although different, show a common thread of disappointment which, if it exists, is shared by them and by the content of their own work. the commission's assertions that the functioning of the internal market is being compromised by the fragmentation of european and national rules are undeniable. the commission has also been very active in the fight against fraud, and i am sure that the commission will be very active in this area. the need for a simple and homogeneous legal framework, consisting only of essential rules, applicable irrespective of the nature of the commercial transaction, which explicitly provide for protection throughout its entire course, including post-contractual and post-sales relations, is therefore equally indisputable. we therefore welcomed the commission's approach to the need for a global approach to the problem, on the one hand aimed at defining obligations, starting with fair commercial behaviour, and on the other, based on objective criteria, to avoid different interpretations by the member states. but if all this makes sense, it is impossible not to notice that the commission itself sometimes behaves in a heterogeneous way: firstly, there is an excessive dilution of the time with which the problem is being tackled, but not only that. the 2001 green paper on consumer protection, for example, has, as is well known, launched a season of wide consultation and valuable debate on the future of community consumer law. however, without any result, we have seen in the meantime the proposal for a regulation on the promotion of sales in the internal market, which, on the one hand, shows a lack of attention to the european parliament's own view of the global approach and, on the other, gives the paradoxical impression that it prefers to continue to follow sectoral paths. again , please . the different approaches to similar issues, such as, for example, labelling, where the presence of similar substances is regulated in a different way after a few months, are not well-suited to the desired outcome. it is considered that it is not worthwhile to object to the different use of preparations, taking as a final reference that of human health: this is the case with cosmetics and detergents. the idea is that, in order to remain in this field for a while, consumers need to know the products used, but also that, in order to do so, they need useful information, which can enable them to make choices, including political ones, directly. this is without prejudice to, and with the greatest appreciation for, the important work of the consumer protection organisation. however, if the principle is to pursue a high level of protection, while aiming at an acceptable harmonisation of the rules in the internal market, two ways appear to be possible, one consequential to the other: the first is the one mentioned by mr whitehead in considering that a case-by-case analysis is more appropriate to determine whether, in amending existing legislation or drawing up new legislation, minimum or maximum harmonisation measures are more appropriate. once this has been established, the other way is to ensure that the member states correctly transpose and apply community legislation in practice. and here again the commission has a decisive role to play, although it is true that, in general, only five states have so far met the targets set by the barcelona european council on implementation rates.
president, i am not entirely convinced by the whitehead report on certain points, because i cannot agree with some of the priorities set out in the consumer action, while others are, in my view, not sufficiently emphasized or even not found in the documents before us. i would like to make a number of proposals in this connection which i consider urgent and necessary for an effective policy to protect the widespread interests of consumers: first, the need to set up a european observatory on the development of consumer prices and public services in the various member states, in order to monitor the extent and nature of increases, especially since the adoption of the euro. secondly, as regards the sensitive issue of public services and banking and insurance services, i believe that it is absolutely necessary to adopt a policy aimed at opening up the boards of directors of public companies operating these services - credit agencies, insurance companies and public service companies - to adequate representation of the widespread interests of users. the european union should take the necessary measures to ensure that consumer users are involved in the management of this activity if true economic democracy is to be achieved. i also think that the proposals for protecting young people in particular from the serious dangers of smoking are neither adequate nor sufficient. the spread of the phenomenon, especially among young people, is accompanied by increasing, truly frightening, data on the geometrical extent of lung cancer cases, which requires europe to make a much greater effort in the actions already planned. it is time for europe to declare war on the dangers of smoking, by means of more appropriate awareness campaigns and by bringing the legislation of the member states up to the highest level in preventing the dangers of smoking.
mr president, three reports on consumer affairs combined in one analysis is a rare and precious opportunity after the years of lukewarm attention that this parliament and the commission have devoted to the consumer category. the first report is, as we have heard, on the green paper on consumer protection in the union; the second on the consumer policy strategy 2002-06; the third, a very robust text, is on the legal protection of consumers themselves. the strategy proposed by the commission sets out these three medium-term objectives, to be achieved through a programme of immediate application but to be periodically reviewed with commission documents certifying the progress made. the achievement of a common level of consumer protection means harmonizing not only the security of goods and services but above all the different legal aspects through which consumers exercise their role as guarantors in commercial transactions in the internal market. the effective application of consumer policy presupposes that consumers are accorded the same importance by an identical guarantee of coverage throughout the territory of the union. the programme also sets out a plan of priority actions through which consumers can agree with the member states on control procedures and, where appropriate, on appeals, thanks to a system of genuine administrative cooperation. consumers and their various supply chains must have the capacity and resources to promote their actions on a level playing field and full participation with other players in the internal market; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the principle of minimum harmonisation of consumer protection policy is also enshrined in the treaty. it is now important that the minimum becomes a more incisive, comprehensive and complete policy, shared by all. to achieve this, new rules are needed which are shared and, above all, which repeal the previous ones.

mr president, for too many years now, the military regime has been systematically violating human rights in burma. parliament should live and there is no parliament, although there have undoubtedly of shan state is subjected to forced labour. these people have no choice: or forced labor or prison. their work, for which they receive no pay, consists of constructing military infrastructure, roads, buildings, military camps and also performing military services. they work nonstop from morning to night, receiving no food, except a small amount of toasted rice. although the burmese penal code has i am the rapporteur's substitute. mr president, i am unworthily replacing mr nistico, the rapporteur, who cannot be present, and i assure the commissioner that i will convey to him his thanks and congratulations. for the information of my colleagues, i shall therefore briefly describe the measure which we shall be voting on tomorrow, and which, as the commissioner anticipated, constitutes a meeting point which the parliamentary delegation to the conciliation committee supported, shared and recommends to the house for a positive vote tomorrow. as the commissioner has already said, this is an amendment to the 23rd amendment to directive 76/769 on the restriction of the placing on the market and use of certain dangerous substances and preparations, i.e. substances classified as carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction. the proposal is based on article 95 of the treaty and has two main objectives: on the one hand, to protect the internal market by introducing harmonised provisions on the placing on the market and use of the abovementioned substances; on the other hand, a high level of protection of public health and the environment must be achieved. it is worth remembering that we are dealing with 25 substances in particular, 14 of which are classified as category 2 carcinogens, such as certain cobalt salts, cadmium, benzopyrene, azo dyes, etc. three of these are classified as mutagenic and eight as toxic to the reproductive system. for example, cobalt is known to induce carcinogenic effects in laboratory animals and humans, in particular lung cancer and cancer of myocardial tissue; cadmium powders, on the other hand, in addition to lung cancer, can cause testicular cancer. as can be seen from these brief examples, these are very dangerous substances. during this year and a half, two years of work, parliament adopted two amendments at first reading in february 2002, which the council accepted in part in june 2003 by adopting its common position. at its second reading in 2002, parliament approved an amendment to the recitals. we are therefore at the final stage of this conciliation, of this trilogy, and, as has already been mentioned, the problem that remained to be defined was that concerning not substances but products in which these substances may be present. the agreement on the only point which was under discussion at the conciliation provides that the commission should submit as soon as possible a legislative proposal to ban the use of products - this time products - containing substances classified as carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction, whereas - and this is an underlining point which the rapporteur is keen to make - there is scientific evidence that these substances are released from these products and in fact expose the general public to the risks described above. the delegation therefore considers the result achieved satisfactory to parliament and recommends that the house approve it.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the uen group i would like to make a few comments. a year and a half ago i sent a question to the commission, stressing the possibility of such incidents, because viruses, bacteria and toxic substances are being used and manipulated all over the world, and we are not aware of it. the current viral infection, known as sars, is causing a real wave of panic around the world about the possibility of rapid spread. the fears arise mainly from the fact that little is known about its characteristics, which are insufficient at the moment, so that we can all consider ourselves to be free from contagion. the outbreak appears to have originated in guadalong province, china, from where the infection spread to major cities in the east: hong kong, singapore, bangkok, shanghai, beijing, and then spread worldwide, causing infections and deaths. these areas - as you all know - are not closely monitored, either for hygiene or for the possibility of administering medicines suitable to fight these diseases. the etiological agent of the current viral infection remains unknown, probably originating from a mutation of an animal virus, corona virus; it's thought that a scientist who was manipulating a virus to create a vaccine or modify it, this virus escaped and it appears that the scientist himself died from it. what we know about this syndrome is that it is transmitted by direct and environmental transmission. the diagnosis possibilities for the syndrome at this time are only semiological, as no clinical diagnostic kits are yet available. the applicable therapy is none. the only treatment available to those infected is supportive therapy, since the active antiviral agents that can combat it are not yet known to medicine. it is clear that the fact that the etiological agent cannot yet be identified raises some important issues for the people of the european union and the rest of the world, even taking into account some of the main aspects that are at the basis of its spread. the virus seems to have spread from one of the major economic centers in the east, through which a large number of things and people pass: china, a country that only today has given its willingness to exchange information; the cuban-chinese internet is impossible to connect to. for all these reasons, the commission is called upon to: first, to set up a task force of experts not a number or a committee to monitor the spread of the disease within the eu; when i go into the operating room, i choose a helper and an assistant, i don't want a school; secondly, to establish, in agreement with the who, a standard isolation procedure for suspected cases in eu citizens, to be applied to all member states, and thus not leaving each state with its own procedure; thirdly, to invite all member states to have a database of persons who have been in or travelled through the areas at risk in the last three months, with monitoring of their health conditions in order to respond promptly in the event of the disease; fourthly, to indicate, in agreement with the who, the methods and timing of quarantine and disinfection of persons, animals and objects coming from the risk areas, thus avoiding different alert levels from one state to another; fifthly, to set up an emergency health fund, as was done in the past in the case of natural disasters, so that each member state can equip itself to deal with this potential epidemic. these organisational and information strategies are crucial to responding quickly and effectively when the vaccine becomes available.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, before i turn to some specific points, i should like to thank the european commission in the person of mrs reding and her colleagues, and the greek will be to launch the calls for proposals in a short time. since the lisbon council in march 2000, much progress has been made in relation to e-learning, and the proposal for an action for the application of new technologies in education has led today to a legislative resolution which will give birth to a genuine multiannual programme. as i have already argued in the course of the work on the commission's first communication, i have focused in particular on the importance of the role that teachers will have as a channel for the development of digital literacy in our schools. it is in this sense that the issue of teacher training, or at any rate the possibility of equipping teachers to be ready to use the new technologies, is a matter of absolute priority, and the efforts which are seen in the commission's text are certainly to be rewarded and supported. i have nevertheless considered it appropriate to make some amendments to the commission's proposal, first of all on the subject of the multiannual budget. the question i asked myself at the beginning of my work was: what budget can be said to be adequate for such an ambitious multiannual programme? it is not easy to answer this question because resources for culture and education always seem to be particularly scarce. what encouraged me and pushed me in this direction was the proposal made by the european commission itself in the 2003 budget: in fact, eur 18 million was allocated there as a preparatory action from expenditure commitments under budget line b3-1000. the reason why i am amending the proposal for eur 36 million, which has been put forward by the commission itself, is that: is it not at least unusual to decide to spend less each year on a multiannual programme than the estimated expenditure for the preparatory action? in this respect, i would like to congratulate the commission for having reminded it that eur 18 million, multiplied by 3, amounts to eur 54 million, which seems to me to be the most appropriate figure. the second point to be stressed is the issue of the redistribution of the budget. the budget initially included 25% in the commission's proposal to tackle the digital divide. i want to make it clear why i asked for a reduction in this amount in my amendment. i am absolutely convinced that it is useful to combat the digital divide in social terms. i also believe that funds should be sought in other community instruments - the structural funds, the european social fund, the leonardo da vinci programme - because if e-learning funds were to be used to meet the need to bridge the digital divide, essentially to provide minimally adequate responses, almost the entire budget of the e-learning action itself would be absorbed. as regards the electronic twinning of european schools, in line with the objectives adopted in the previous resolution of the european parliament, i wanted to stress that teacher training remains a priority. i would like you to reflect on the fact that in 2002, on average, 90% of primary schools, 98% of secondary schools, 99% of vocational and technical schools in the member states were connected to the internet, but only 39% of teachers, only 50% of secondary school teachers and 58% of teachers in vocational and technical schools used the internet as a teaching tool. in reality, these averages conceal dramatic differences between member states: the average for denmark is about 75%, as opposed to greece's 9%. these figures, which are already very clear, suggest two conclusions: the first concerns the use of the internet as a tool to facilitate teaching. it is not just a question of the availability of infrastructure or school equipment, but also a problem of teacher training and school organisation. the second concerns the use of technological resources. the aim can really be to exchange good practice in this respect at the methodological and didactic level between teachers in different member states, i.e. to set up virtual classrooms. for these reasons i would like to stress that the commission's proposal should give greater importance to finding the most effective ways for teachers to integrate the use of the internet into their teaching and to encourage the dissemination of good practice in this area.

body. i am simply quoting the reports by mr nassauer, mr karamanou and mr deprez: in these reports we are still calling for greater involvement of parliament in the budgetary procedure and for europol party. according to the group's minutes, during a hearing europol director jürgen storbeck stated that parliamentary scrutiny of europol is currently unclear. he points to the difficulties of being mr president, recent international events have once again demonstrated the need for a european union capable of joint action, both when it comes to defending its security and when it is necessary to defend the right of all peoples to aspire to a democratic and pluralist system which therefore respects human and civil rights; mr president, the morillon report puts european defence in a realistic and responsible context of solidarity and complementarity with the united states, and therefore represents a challenging step forward, made up of forecasts, economic sacrifices and military investment. a necessary and urgent step from not underestimating the new terrorist and state threats; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european research area. the report excludes dangerous illusions which would not make the world safer or more democratic, much less make europe more united. among these dangerous illusions is the rebirth of a one-sided pacifism, which renews yesterday's "better red than dead" one, and there is also the illusion of an independent, strong and authoritative europe because it is divorced from the united states: the european parliament has been a party to the treaty of rome since the beginning of the century, and it is not the council that is responsible for the decisions taken by the european parliament. it is an illusion that has deep roots in european nationalism and outdated ideologies, an illusion that explains the strange right-left alliance in the face of the war in iraq and that exalts, conversely, the value of democratic interventionism. a political illusion more dangerous than imperial unilateralism and blind pacifism: claiming to lead europe, he divided it; the european union has divided the fifteen, it has offended the countries of eastern europe while reunification is in progress, it has widened the distance with the united states and, by anticipating the use of the right of veto, it has helped to paralyse the security council, providing justifications for military intervention outside the un. the union must clarify its political vision before it can rely on institutional engineering; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. mr president, commissioner, this proposal for a directive aims to regulate, with safety and quality standards, the therapeutic activities based on the use of tissues and cells of human origin, which take place annually in europe and which now affect hundreds of thousands of patients. the sector is also set to expand not only into the traditional field of transplants - for example, of cornea, skin and heart valves - but also, thanks to advances in biotechnology, into reconstructive surgery, reproductive medicine and the treatment of diseases such as cancer, diabetes and parkinson's disease. it is therefore a field of particular interest to european research centres and businesses, which must be able to develop. however, respect for ethical imperatives is fundamental to the use of tissues and cells of human origin. the proposal for a directive therefore imposes high standards of quality and safety for substances of human origin in order to protect health. however, these ethical imperatives need to be further defined: first, by ensuring full health safety, to prevent or reduce the risk of disease transmission, including in the case of human tissues and cells from third countries; secondly, by ensuring that the human body is respected when it is taken from a living or deceased donor. in this respect, the obligation to give informed consent in a specific form by the donor or by the donor's family members and the prohibition on the taking of cells and tissues from foetuses resulting from voluntary termination of pregnancy and from cloned human cells are particularly important. thirdly, by respecting the privacy and confidentiality of the information collected during the collection of tissues: donation must be anonymous, both to the donor and to the recipient, without prejudice to traceability requirements. personal and family data may not be disclosed to third parties such as employers, insurance companies also to avoid the risk of unjustified discrimination. fourthly, considering the principle of the gravity of donations: the donation is a voluntary act of human solidarity, but it can be adequately encouraged by specific action and by proper information from the states. this requirement should also be maintained with regard to imports from third countries. with these considerations, i believe that the directive as a whole can represent a step forward in the harmonization of legislation between the member states, which is moving in the direction of greater protection of the health of european citizens.
mr president, commissioner, i sincerely hope that this report, on which our friend peter liese has devoted so much energy, will be able to have a physiological, euthotic birth, without the use of force, as was the case with the report on blood, a report which has been controversial for many years but for which we have succeeded, with effective, intelligent and motivated cooperation between parliament, the commission and the council, in finding a solution after so many years. i shall make only a few remarks tonight, four in particular: firstly, i think it is right - as peter liese said - that the donation of cells and tissues should be voluntary and not paid, a principle already endorsed in the blood report. however, where industries have contributed to improving the quality and preservation of cells and tissues, for example by genetically engineering tissues to make them histocompatible, it is also right to recognise appropriate compensation. secondly, i hope that amendment no 83 proposed by the undersigned and by mr liese will be adopted, which calls on the commission to draw up, as soon as possible, new rules on the back-differentiation of adult cells into stem cells. the retrodifferentiation of adult cells obtained by transferring their nucleus, rather than into a nucleus-free oocyte, into a medium rich in nutrients and other growth factors, could overcome the current ethical problems concerning the therapeutic use of human embryonic stem cells. thirdly, as regards the use of stem cells for research purposes, i hope that the rules laid down in the sixth framework programme will always remain valid and that today we cannot let in through the window what has not entered through the door. fourthly, and finally, i agree with the commission's proposal that the directive should cover the use of cells and tissues for research when it is carried out on humans, but not when it is experimental research in vitro or on animal models. i would therefore ask the rapporteur, mr peter liese, if amendments nos 7 and 19 are adopted, to find greater flexibility during the second reading to avoid burdensome administrative procedures slowing down research in europe in areas of fundamental importance, such as pharmacogenetics and pharmacogenomics, aimed at designing new drugs which are much more effective and free from toxic effects.

proposed rules, two further objectives were pursued: the first concerns the implementation of a practical sensitivity towards small and medium-sized enterprises, especially as manifested in the beginning of my speech - was the ratio of approach to the problem, the choice of which by the commission was characterised by the gradualness of the implementation of the legislation. the second, which almost justifies the first, is the need to call on the work of a third body, in the specific case a scientific committee, to carry out the implementation itself. the work to amend the regulation this is also a task that is underpinned by the joint commitment of the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteurs. if, therefore, the two last-mentioned aspects are true as they are and if it is true that the work in the committee on the environment was fruitful and widely shared, it is puzzling that some colleagues, without taking anything away from the subjective right of each, have tabled further amendments for the plenary. however, i must say that i agree with the points made by nos 47, 52, 53 and 60, which undoubtedly add important additional aspects in a complementary way. i must also say
