- the next item is the report (a5-0145/2003) by mr manders, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on environmental liability with a view to the prevention and remedying of environmental damage (com (2002) 17 - c5-0088/2002 - 2002/0021 (cod)).
mr president, first of all i would like to express my sincere thanks - not by chance - for the enormous work done by both the rapporteur, mr manders, and by my colleague mrs niebler. i would like to make two comments: the first is of a particular nature, the second is of a general nature. the commission's proposal is also in line with some of the previous speeches. i understand that the agricultural world has welcomed the proposal for a directive on environmental liability, particularly because the commission has opted for a horizontal approach. in the course of the parliamentary work, other sensitivities have emerged in committee, so that it is very difficult at the moment to accept the idea of farmers being held responsible for environmental damage whose causes are to be sought outside their sphere of influence. in that regard, any extension of the scope of the directive - the obligation to provide a financial guarantee, the inversion of the burden of proof and, above all, the exclusion of certain exemption measures - would place farmers in a situation of great difficulty in the management of their business. in concrete terms, a farmer could be required to pay compensation for environmental damage caused by an activity for which he has been granted a permit, even though he has complied with all the legal provisions governing that activity. i am sure that farmers are prepared to take responsibility, but not when they have no influence on the cause of the damage. for this reason and in this spirit we have worked in the legal affairs committee, producing a guideline which avoids serious repercussions on the agricultural world and the rural environment in general. i hope that the rapporteur will agree with this position and that the european parliament will ratify it. as regards the general consideration, it also reflects a fear. the extension of the scope of the directive to the original commission proposal risks, in my view, rendering the proposed regulatory framework and the resulting insurance guarantees uncertain, thus making it difficult to apply an idea which is useful to european society at large.
mr president, the directive we are about to vote on can and must represent a breakthrough which will be clearly perceptible to all european citizens. from seveso to the infamous disasters of the doñana nature park, the sinking of the prestige oil tanker and the most recent, in chronological order, the discovery of the devastating effects on the health of unborn children caused by the environmental degradation of the chemical pole at priolo, all these are cases which require the adoption of a european civil liability regime for environmental damage. a strong political signal is needed, which can also be useful in stopping some of the regressive trends that are emerging here and there. mrs wallström, for example, is well aware that the italian government is about to embark on a revision of the penal code which, among other things, provides for the decriminalisation of environmental offences. all the more reason, therefore, for a system which strictly applies the 'polluter pays' principle and thus creates strong incentives to prevent and avoid such situations in the future. the ultimate aim is prevention, not compensation for damage. in the light of this objective, we have worked within the committee on the environment to remove certain dangerous derogations which allow for broad and generic means of defence and which, in reality, equate environmental authorizations with a kind of licence to pollute, with the serious risk of rendering the proposed regulatory system ineffective. we have worked to ensure that the responsible operator, not the taxpayer, bears the costs of environmental remediation. it is also necessary that all economic activities which may result in damage to the environment be taken into account and covered by the liability regime. such a system should, as a general rule, provide for objective liability for environmental damage, whether or not it is caused by an activity considered to be dangerous. this directive is of the utmost importance. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment is a long-awaited one and is a fundamental element of european environmental legislation, provided that the reinforcing amendments we have worked on with the 16 compromise amendments, which i warmly invite to be put to the vote and which restate the substance of what was voted on in the committee on the environment and then deleted by the committee on legal affairs, are accepted. if this is not the case, as mrs gebhardt has already said, and in particular if amendments nos 99, 103 and 107 are not adopted, our group will not be able to approve the manders report.
mr president, a framework regulation on environmental liability is necessary because it is right that the polluter should pay. however, this regulation must be balanced and also take into account the needs expressed by the european industry. the position taken by the committee on legal affairs, summed up in the report by mr manders, whom i thank for the important work he has done, is an acceptable compromise, even if it requires some sacrifices. some of the amendments now proposed are particularly dangerous, as they would make it impossible for operators to quantify insurance cover. the definition of environmental damage plays a central role in the structure of the directive, as does the definition of biodiversity and damage to biodiversity. in my view, amendments nos 23, 84 and 98 are not acceptable: if the event does not produce any negative effects, it is not harm but risk. amendment no 95 is also unacceptable, because it betrays the polluter-pays principle. the concept of liability is independent of the relationship of the law of the place of residence. the definition of contamination of soil by gmos is inappropriate, as it is part of a general definition which does not list the sources of contamination exhaustively. it is necessary to refer to proportional, not joint and several liability, which would create a regime based on suspicion. prevention must remain the priority objective of activities that may have an impact on the environment. finally, the financial guarantees: in order to allow the consolidation of the insurance market, maximum flexibility should be allowed beyond the first five years of application of the new legislation. in conclusion, i would ask my colleagues to support the compromise reached by the committee on legal affairs, which at the same time is a clear and strong signal in favour of protecting the environment but is not a penalty for european industry.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for a directive on liability for environmental damage takes a balanced approach, putting pressure on operators to prevent pollution and to repair damage, and suggests only a few regulatory provisions to achieve these objectives. any fundamental change to this proposal for a directive would have led to an unworkable and impractical solution to an already complex issue, and i believe that the work done by mr manders and other colleagues in the committee is the best possible summary of this need. the committee on legal affairs did not change the substance of the commission's approach, but it did clarify some of its basic principles. the directive shall not have retroactive effect. exceptions based on compliance with a permit according to the state of knowledge must be maintained; if liability is compulsory, insurance need not be. the guiding principle of the directive is that the polluter must bear the cost of repairing the environmental damage caused by his action. awareness of the financial implications of such damage will lead to greater efforts to prevent it from occurring. the polluter pays principle therefore aims to regulate the issue of remediation and to encourage prevention. a mandatory financial security scheme could disrupt that relationship, as operators would have less incentive to prevent damage if they knew that their financial liabilities are covered by a policy, a tax or a fund. a compulsory financial security system could certainly be described as a 'pay-by-insurer' principle, with the risk of the transfer of responsibility from the operator to the person providing the financial security. we all have a social responsibility to protect the environment, which is by its nature a finite resource. operators must recognise that their activities may have repercussions and that they will have to compensate for any damage that is caused intentionally or through negligence. in these terms, the 'polluter pays' principle is acceptable. the reasoned approach of the committee on legal affairs will lead to a directive which will reflect the interests of both industrial development and the environment.
the rapporteur. mr president, the commission's communication on environmental agreements is part of the process of simplifying and improving the regulatory framework, which we all want. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment and the environment from the adverse effects of ionising radiation is a step in the right direction. the ultimate aim is to maintain legal certainty in the territory of the union by encouraging greater dynamism among economic and social actors. the environmental agreements are part of this. while i share the commission's approach of distinguishing between two types of agreement, and with the amendments i have subsequently made, i fully recognise the usefulness of such instruments as a complement to regulatory measures, to be used only in anticipation of environmental improvements of equal or greater scope than those achieved by traditional legislative procedures. the treaty contains no specific provision on environmental agreements. the use of these instruments must therefore be made in full compliance with and in conformity with all the provisions of the treaty and the community's international commitments. the backbone of community environmental policy is and remains the legislative provision, which can only be supplemented by voluntary agreements in certain specific cases. in drawing up the opinion we are about to vote on, and taking account of the debate on this subject and the positions adopted by parliament, i thought it appropriate to introduce some clarification and guarantee in order to make the instruments indicated in the communication acceptable and actually practicable. i refer in particular to the binding conditions which must be met in advance and which i shall briefly summarize: firstly, i have worked to make the concept of voluntary agreement more explicit as a means of integrating community legislation. secondly, i called for the definition, upstream, of the areas which could be the subject of voluntary agreements, through both co-regulatory and self-regulatory instruments. the use of such instruments should be based on a common framework of reference which indicates, at the preliminary stage, the intention to use voluntary agreements in that particular area. this intention should be reflected in the commission's annual programming documents, in a broader document such as a white paper or a thematic strategy; thirdly, i proposed that the criteria for evaluating the proper use of environmental agreements be developed. i believe that, in order to ensure the transparency and effectiveness of the voluntary instruments, it is necessary to define the conditions for their application and to verify the procedures for their implementation. as stated above, the objectives of the agreement, defined within a legislative framework of reference, must nevertheless be translated into obligations for the parties. failure to meet or achieve the objectives set will trigger the use of legislative mechanisms, either to supplement or to replace the agreement. in the final analysis, the distinction between co-regulation and self-regulation is appreciated here: in the first case, these instruments must be embedded in a binding legal framework, which gives the council and the european parliament the right to participate and adopt objectives, ensures public access and participation and includes effective monitoring and sanctioning mechanisms. in the second, the commission's role may be to stimulate or encourage by means of a recommendation, or to give recognition by means of an exchange of letters with the representatives of the sectors concerned. whatever the instrument chosen, parliament's power of scrutiny of the results achieved is not affected, nor is the use of typical legislative instruments at any time. on this basis, which the committee on the environment has improved and approved, we give the commission the go-ahead to start experimenting with this mix of legislation and voluntary commitments in the areas it has indicated, and in particular with pvc. we've enriched and rearranged the toolbox; now, let's make the most of them all!

commission. – firstly, as regards drinking water in developing countries, the commission proposed in its communication on water management in developing countries that priority should be given to ensuring a supply to every human being – especially the poorest – of sufficient drinking water of good quality and of adequate means of waste disposal, with the general objective of reducing poverty and improving people's health and quality of life. this focus on access to safe water and sanitation was further reinforced in the context of the world summit on sustainable development with the launch of the eu water initiative and the signature of the eu-africa strategic partnership on water affairs and sanitation. after johannesburg we started to concentrate on a long-term effort to translate these political commitments into action on the ground and, for sewerage, action under the ground. we are engaged in a dialogue to anchor the process at country level. the core of this action is to catalyse and support the engagement of all partners at the local, national and regional levels, from central and local governments to civil society users and private professional actors, reflecting the multi-stakeholder partnership approach under the water initiative. a key objective is to focus on the millennium development goals and the targets for access to water and sanitation for the poor. we negotiated this in johannesburg and we are now trying to tackle the problem. the commission is also exploring the opportunities to increase financial support for these objectives, including the possible creation of a specific water fund using development aid as a catalyst to attract other financial resources in response to the countries' prioritisation of water in their poverty reduction and sustainable development strategies. this proposal by the commission is presented in the recent communication on the establishment of an eu water fund. secondly, concerning drinking water in industrialised countries, the european union started more than 20 years ago to take steps to secure drinking water quality. the drinking water directive of 1980 established quality standards for drinking water as well as regular monitoring obligations, thus ensuring a high level of protection throughout the union. in 1998 the drinking water directive was amended to check the parameters and related values and, where necessary, tighten them up and ensure greater transparency and more information to citizens. in order to comprehensively protect water resources, the european union has recently thoroughly restructured its water protection policy by adopting the water framework directive: protection of all waters, rivers, lakes, ground waters and coastal waters, establishing a binding obligation to achieve or maintain good quality for all those waters by 2015 at the latest; ensuring a broad participation of citizens, stake-holders, ngos when developing the necessary protection measures; and underpinning the environmental objective by economic instruments such as economic analysis and water pricing, reflecting cost recovery and thus promoting the wise use of water and the protection of our water resources. environmental policy in the field of water is complicated and supported by targeted efforts in research policy, where the sixth framework programme is devoting considerable effort and budget to the issue of water resources and their protection, and in regional policy both for the existing member states by instruments such as the structural and cohesion funds and in candidate countries by instruments like ispa and phare.

mr president, i would like to draw attention to a region on the edge of the continent, the caucasus, which the minister has already mentioned and which the rapporteur, mrs napoletano, has mentioned. europe is interested, and the caucasus has been a part of europe for many historical periods. armenia and georgia are among the oldest christian countries. in the middle ages, armenia was considered a great european power. at the end of the 19th century, no one could deny the role of baku, the capital of azerbaijan, as a powerful centre, including a european one, among the pioneers of the oil industry. today, among other things, azerbaijan is the main supplier of crude oil to the european union. after the first world war and before the collapse of the soviet union, local governments in the three countries, despite their differences, referred to european values. the versailles conference had given certain european powers the task of helping to bring about the birth of new democracies. the three republics took part in the pan-european conference in helsinki from 1972 to 1975 as part of the soviet delegation; all three are members of the council of europe. so it's not about strangers. the eu-south caucasus parliamentary cooperation committee has made several visits to these countries, and the solution suggested by the three governments to get out of the crisis has always been to get as close as possible to europe. even potentially very dangerous crises, such as in nagorno-karabakh, can hopefully be resolved within the european framework. for economic reasons, the united states and russia are present in the region. local governments, of course with different nuances, therefore have to make balancing exercises, and yet they would prefer a greater presence of another leading actor, such as the european union. our cooperation committee, for which i am the spokesman, was impressed by the basic feeling expressed by the three countries - armenia, georgia and azerbaijan - of being historically part of the european community.

first time, we have also made specific reference to the euro area. the economic strategy contained in the economic policy guidelines is, of course, based primarily on lisbon. in the report by mr garcía-margallo y marfil there is a certain criticism, he says, of the lack of ambition in the broad guidelines. i think that criticism is unwarranted. the broad guidelines are a good way of translating the lisbon decisions into our commitments, and it is true that we want to set out obligations in a much more concrete way, so that they can be better assessed. i agree with him and will come back to his idea of a specific plan of action, but the fundamental problem is not to make new plans but to put into practice what has been agreed. from our point of view - and this is a fundamental point which mr garcía-margallo y marfil has stressed - we must also take account of the time in which we find ourselves: cyclical conditions, which are not the easiest. but i also agree that it is not because we are in a difficult time that we have to abandon the fundamental elements of our strategy. our strategy is based on three fundamental ideas: sound macroeconomic policies, structural reforms and sustainability of processes. in sound macroeconomic policies, i think we agree that budgetary balance is fundamental and i also share your view of the particular importance of not repeating the mistakes we have made in the past, with procyclical policy behaviour, which can ultimately create problems in the future. that was one of the concerns of the commission in its communication last november, when we stressed the need to use the stability and growth pact not only in the bad times of the cycle but also in the good times, which is, in the end, essential to avoid future difficulties. in the end, what we want is to let the automatic stabilizers play and have a correct policy. as regards growth potential, i think we fully share the view that the necessary structural reforms, which are essential to make the union's economy more resilient to external shocks, must be put in place, but these reforms must be comprehensive and applied jointly if they are to be effective. we share the need to increase employment. the fundamental question we are faced with, however, is whether we should put in place specific incentives for employment or rather devise a general economic policy, which takes employment as its objective, and this seems to us to be the best option. the honourable member said that one of his concerns was to put in place an action plan for structural reform. the honourable member raises two problems: why we do not have a list of structural reforms, and why, in that list of structural reforms, mechanisms are not put in place to enable us to monitor them more efficiently. i think the list of structural reforms is included in lisbon, we look at where we are in the synthesis reports every year, and it is true that it is up to the member states to put them into practice. the establishment of a new supplementary plan would not solve the problems. we believe that the plans already exist, what needs to be done we know. i think the key is how we put these plans into action. we therefore believe that two fundamental aspects must be considered. firstly, the reports which the commission publishes each year on the implementation of the broad economic policy guidelines. the idea behind the move from one year to three years is to pay more attention to implementation and less to the definition of annual principles. secondly, and this is where we come to an important aspect of economic policy coordination, to pay more attention to the system of peer pressure that we have established in the union. the honourable member raises an important question: is it enough, yes or no? i think it is enough if there is a political commitment from the member states to implement what we have decided together. we must not forget that the model of economic policy coordination is a coordination of national economic policy, based on a community system which allows us only to act under peer pressure, with the exception of the recommendations which help us to highlight certain elements of non-compliance and, of course, the stability pact. as regards strengthening sustainability, it is only worth highlighting the importance of public debt, to which we pay particular attention, because i agree with the honourable member that action is needed on this point, and the idea of offsetting future liabilities with current assets to cope with these difficulties, which seems to us to be a fundamental idea. we also consider that everything that involves a greater and better use of natural resources is essential, and in this sense any element of sectoral subsidies, which ultimately leads to a less environmentally efficient system, must be considered, just as sustainability and social cohesion must be considered as objectives of economic policy. in conclusion, and also briefly referring to another proposal in your draft for a lisbon implementation plan, i think we share your concern in this respect. the commission has clearly expressed its concern about the lack of implementation of lisbon. it is certainly behind schedule, but i do not think that the solution is to go back to drawing up new plans. i think the solution is to move more quickly on what we have already decided. the political will is essential here and, in this sense too, parliament's support and the positions adopted by it will be crucial for the implementation of all these elements.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, mr garcía-margallo's report, which i consider to be an important contribution to the definition of effective coordination of the economic and social policies of the union, also brings into sharp focus the limitations which have characterized the formulation of the broad economic and social policy guidelines in recent years: on the one hand, there has been too long a lack of willingness to define a proactive policy capable of countering the stagnation and recession trends still prevailing in many of the union's economies; on the other hand, the principle of streamlining and coordinating employment policies with the broad economic policy guidelines has been recognised, at least belatedly. in addition, the objective of implementing the strategy defined in lisbon in 2000 by 2010 with the structural reforms resulting from it has been taken up, perhaps still vaguely. we should not underestimate this progress, but we must stress that we must now overcome delays and ambiguities by providing for effective coordination between the economic, employment and environmental policies of the member states through the definition of a real timetable setting intermediate milestones for the achievement, by 2010, of the objectives set in lisbon and gothenburg, in particular as regards public investment in the fields of research, education, lifelong learning and participation in a european network of basic services, starting with transport and telecommunications. it is also necessary to set up an institutional coordination structure in the euro area which will allow, as stated in the report by mr garcía-margallo, a single representation of the euro area in all the economic and financial institutions operating on a world scale. finally, the stages of an economic, social and environmental policy compatible with the lisbon strategy and the flexible management of the stability and growth pact should also be defined for the euro area. these choices should become, from 2004, the core of the broad economic policy guidelines and the new objectives with which to enrich the flexible management of the stability and growth pact. in this connection, i would like to emphasize that it is necessary to dispense with generic formulations and many ambiguities: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the financial interests of the european communities against fraud is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. in short, the commission cannot be indifferent to the fact that a deviation from the 3% or the minimum 60% target for public debt is due to an increase in current expenditure, or perhaps to a general reduction in taxes, or to a policy of boosting public and private investment - for example in research, training and retraining for older workers who choose to prolong their working life - especially if these investments are formally recognised by the commission itself as objectives of common interest. the same priorities should be pursued, as commissioner solbes has said, also in periods of growth, when the conditions are created for greater compatibility between the broad guidelines of economic and employment policy and the parameters set out in the stability pact, which is also - the central bank itself must not forget this - a pact for income and employment growth and, after lisbon, for full employment and social cohesion.

mr president, a committee chairman can only feel great satisfaction in seeing colleagues congratulate each other, like mr rothley and mr lehne, on work done under my direction. i'm really satisfied mr president, without wishing to detract from the great work done by my colleagues, this is a subject on which there is no end to analysis and reflection. i should like to dwell briefly on the electricity market. the european scenario shows structural differences which, in my view, are difficult to overcome by merely starting the process of liberalization. with reference to the european context, the electricity market has been concerned with linking markets, but not with creating uniform conditions regarding access to generation, institutional set-ups and fuel choice symmetries, etc., such as to create symmetrical competitive conditions in the generation segment. cross-border regulation through market mechanisms - for example, through outright auctions - in countries which are handicapped by domestic production conditions, undermines the economic advantage for final consumers which is derived from the availability of imported energy. in view of the cost differentials and congestion resulting from a demand for imported energy which is significantly higher than the supply, the ultimate effect will be to bring the external and internal price closer together. the nuclear issue is a further complication of this situation, which would create the particular situation of those who are called upon to contribute to the cost of decommissioning other countries when in reality they are not able to benefit, given the market mechanism provided for by the cross-border, from the energy produced by nuclear plants. while we believe that the proposed rent efficiency mechanisms for cross-border are acceptable in the long run, we believe that their application in the short term is highly detrimental. the package of directives is therefore acceptable and could only be agreed if it were to be achieved through a gradual application of market mechanisms, because cross-border regulation cannot produce the same positive effects for the final consumers of the member states in the presence of discrepancies in trade flows.

the commission. the european commission has of course analysed the prospects and the specific problems of youth unemployment in enlarged europe. the first concerns the fear of migration flows. the youngest workers are usually the ones who move. studies we have done show that mobility from the 10 future member states to the present european union of 15 will be relatively limited. it is estimated that there will be a surge in the first few years, reaching 250 000 people per year, of which half will be labour, but this labour mobility will begin to decline towards the end of the decade to less than 100 000 people. of course, these studies always have a considerable degree of predictability. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption, and the council will be consulted on it. in addition, past enlargement experiences in europe, as well as the study of the phenomenon of migration, suggest that new migrant workers from the new member states will move more towards the prosperous regions of their own countries, in large cities, where unemployment rates are relatively lower and job opportunities are relatively good. the first choice of young people in these countries is their own centres and their own regions with the greatest development, not the choice of going to another country. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. the second point concerns the transitional arrangements for the free movement of workers which have been decided at european level. as you know, there is an agreement on the free movement of workers during the first two years. after accession, each member state may decide on free movement, but may also postpone it for five years. it's the 5+2 rule. the third issue concerns the employment strategy, the implementation of policies where the european union has an added value. it is important to note that the european commission has been working with each of the applicant countries for three years now, where we are basically trying to support the creation of individual action plans to tackle unemployment. - the next item is the joint debate on the following reports, tabled on behalf of the committee on fisheries:- a5-0168/2003 by mr hudghton, on the proposal for a council regulation on the conservation of fishery resources through technical measures for the protection of juveniles of marine organisms (com (2002) 672 - c5-0026/2003 - 2002/0275 (cns)) - a5-0165/2003 by mr stevenson, on the proposal for a council regulation on the management of the fishing effort relating to certain community fishing areas and resources and amending regulation (eec) no 2847/93 (com (2002) 739 - c5-0030/2003 - 2002/0295 (cns)) - a5-0162/2003 by mr fava, on the communication from the commission to the european parliament and the council on the action plan to address the social, economic and regional consequences of the restructuring of the eu fisheries sector (com (2002) 600 - c5-0073/2003 - 2003/2039 (ini))
the rapporteur. mr commissioner, like many colleagues, i believe in the social, cultural and not just economic role of fishing, especially small-scale fishing, because of the role it can play in the processes of economic and social cohesion, especially in the most isolated and peripheral regions. we therefore welcome the commission's action plan to deal with the social consequences of the fisheries reform and we agree with the way in which these consequences should be dealt with by means of a compensation plan. in this context, there are many points in the commission's proposal which raise questions, for example because the reference data proposed are not up to date and relate to the year 2000. three years have passed since then and the commission itself admits that the assessment is rather theoretical. there has not yet been a serious and thorough debate on the model to be chosen: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing fleet is not disrupted by the introduction of new fishing vessels. finally, an updated version of the commission's action plan is missing, which would have been useful in some respects in the light of the conclusions of the fisheries council in december last year. that being said, commissioner, certain points in the proposal are not very convincing. let me give you an example. the mediterranean is completely ignored. the commission does not take account of its specific nature, but only considers certain areas of the north sea, the baltic sea; the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. our europe continues to look only north. this was the case during the many years of the construction of a community agricultural policy and it is the same today with regard to the community fisheries policy. but this is a risk, especially on the eve of the opening of the mediterranean free trade area in 2010, which will make this sea a great area of social, economic, human and political exchanges, and we must be prepared for this. another important point concerns the loss of jobs. the commission is apparently expecting the loss of 12 000 jobs to be recovered within four years. we think this forecast is optimistic because it underestimates the effects of the reform, and does not take account of the industry or related sectors, the shipyards and the processing industries. the european processing industry alone employs as many as 100 000 people. the commission's forecast fails to take account in particular of the fact that conversion is very unlikely for workers, such as those in the fisheries sector, who, especially in some parts of europe, have a low level of education and work in areas with very high unemployment rates. the idea that they can be recovered and converted back to other labour markets is an illusion, especially in the case of spain, greece, italy and portugal. in many countries, there is a lack of social protection and fishermen risk becoming waste workers, superfluous citizens. the european union is also facing an implicit risk of social, cultural and economic desertification in many parts of the union. aid should be concentrated on small-scale fisheries, given that half of fishermen are now engaged in small-scale fishing and that 75% of vessels are small-scale; it is true that the catch is very small, but small-scale fishing plays a key role in employment. the commission recognizes that the financial incentives for small-scale fishing have not done much, it recognizes that other measures are needed, but they will not be quick, and it speaks only of long-term prospects. these considerations lead us to ask: what resources should be invested to absorb the economic and social consequences of this reform? we do not agree with the restructuring of the structural funds. we think that these funds should be tied to other priorities. the fact that 80% of the regions concerned are objective 1 and 2 regions means that the structural funds are now necessary and strategic to tackle priorities which cannot be confused with the draft of this resolution. we believe that an ad hoc fund should be set up, a temporary measure to implement recovery plans. the commission has already done so. the fact that 22% of the workforce is female is not reflected in the commission's action plan. in essence, the long-term conclusions are approved. we believe, however, that it would be useful to re-propose some parts of the action plan and to analyse more closely the economic and social consequences of this reform.

mr president, i too welcome the work of the greek presidency in recent months and express my satisfaction with the work we did last night to conclude the agreement on better regulation. i am particularly grateful to the president of the commission for reminding us of the origins of the convention and of our objectives, which we sometimes forget when we see that some members of the praesidium, and especially its president, aspire to dress more like members of the intergovernmental conference than as founding fathers of europe. i believe that the convention, mr president, must remain the owner of the process of reforming the european union. if it fails to complete its work by 20 june, it must be allowed to continue working towards an agreement, which is perfectly possible provided that the convention plays its full role as a constituent or para-constituent assembly, does not accept blackmail from a few eurosceptics who have no interest in its success - this must be said and repeated - and claims the value of an open and parliamentary working method which is very different from the intergovernmental method, based solely on the balance of power. it is true that the president and the praesidium clearly miscalculated by deliberately prolonging the time of the final discussion without ever stating clearly on which points a broad consensus had been reached, thus deluding themselves that they could control the game of the convention at their will and giving the wrong impression that the convention was divided on everything; but today the governments which care about the success of this constitutional reform - and there are some, i am sure, and i am also sure that your government, mr president, is one of them - cannot simply turn off the lights on the convention if it does not complete its work to the satisfaction of the majority of its members. we believe that if the convention were to come to thessaloniki with options, that would be proof that the work is not finished. i believe that there are at least three areas where we need to give a signal of progress, democracy and clarity, which is directly visible to all citizens: direct access to justice for citizens in cases of breach of the charter of rights; the council's co-decision and majority powers are extended simultaneously, in particular for taxation and external relations. we cannot act as a global actor, committed to the values of multilateralism and democracy, if we are stuck at every step, driven by vetoes and controversies, and if this whole sector remains, as it is today, totally excluded from any form of parliamentary control. thirdly and lastly, we believe that the revision process cannot maintain unanimity and cannot see once again - and this is a very surprising thing in 2003 - the european parliament excluded from the ratification process. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. we have repeatedly denounced the strong imbalance, compared with the strategy decided in tampere, between the repressive aspects of the fight against illegal immigration and the policy of forced returns and the positive aspects, such as the establishment of legal and controlled channels of immigration, the relaxation of visa policy, measures for the integration of third countries based on the principle of non-discrimination. we hope, mr president, that the council will heed the loud and clear message that this parliament gave yesterday: no extradition treaty between the european union and the united states will be signed without clarification of the situation of eu citizens in guantanamo. we speak of citizens of the union not because we are not concerned or interested in others, but because we believe that through this key we can legitimately intervene on the whole question of the existence of a zone in the world where there is no law.

mr president, commissioner, i congratulate the rapporteur, karin jöns, on her report, which is rich in content and promising results, and i have the honour to do so because i am the director of a senology centre in italy. i fully share all the calls on the member states to achieve a voluntary participation rate of women in breast screening of over 70%, a rate that no nation has achieved today. i consider it of great importance to encourage and disseminate in the member states initiatives for technical and healthcare training, psychological support for breast cancer patients and the promotion, at community level, of training and specialization courses which - i would add - are provided by university institutions, university masters of the second level. these courses could also be funded with the resources we use for training. the call for the creation of european cancer registries as soon as possible is welcome, so that reliable and comparable data on the evolution of neoplastic disease as a whole are finally available in the european union. it is right to urge the member states to use the resources of the structural funds to finance the creation of health infrastructure. i fully share the rapporteur's call for, among other things, cosmetic interventions such as the implantation of prostheses, the supply of wigs and whatever else a patient needs to regain a body identity as close as possible to that which she had before the illness. in many countries these interventions are not paid for. however, there are some points that puzzle me. i would first like to point out that the report produced by a committee on women's rights and equal opportunities lacks an essential reference for this committee to be able to call itself 'an equal opportunities committee'. the rapporteur never mentioned male cancer patients. this type of cancer, unfortunately, also affects men: basically, one male in every 100,000 people, ages 58 to 63, gets breast cancer. i can add that their prognosis is worse than that of women precisely because, as they are not screened, their cancer is diagnosed late. i wonder if this committee should not at least give men the same right to information as women. male breast cancer accounts for 1% of all breast cancers and i understand that its incidence is not economically significant enough to be considered for screening. i would, however, like to see an awareness campaign aimed at the male population so that, like women, men too can find in early diagnosis the possibility of increasing their quantity and quality of life. the risk of developing breast cancer is particularly high among young people because of the widespread use of female hormones and metabolizers, which often cause untreated gynecomastia. the second point i would like to make is that concerning paragraph 7 (g) of the report. it seems to me that reminding patients of the possibility of exercising their right to sue a doctor for malpractice is a useless act, as already provided for in the charter of the rights of the patient, and also harmful, as it could undermine the relationship of trust between doctors and patients on which, as shown by studies and research, 50 per cent of the therapeutic result depends. i think it is more legitimate for this kind of control of the adequacy of the quality of treatment to be carried out by the institutions which are responsible for this, for example the european commission for the control of centres of excellence, the specialist breast unit.

commission. - mr president, i would like to divide my speech into two parts: the first part on aceh and the second on papua. as regards asean, the commission is one of the four co-chairs of the tokyo conference (japan, the united states, the european union and the world bank), together with the presidency. this conference encouraged the signing of a ceasefire agreement between the indonesian government and the aceh rebels, based - and i stress this - on the territorial integrity of indonesia. the agreement to cease hostilities is the most comprehensive attempt to settle a conflict that has lasted 26 years and claimed the lives of some 12 000 people, the vast majority of them innocent civilians. the commission, through its rapid response mechanism, contributed eur 2.3 million to the deployment of 50 international observers in aceh province. unfortunately, the situation on the ground has since changed. on 17 and 18 may, the commission and other co-chairs took part in eleven-hour talks in tokyo between the indonesian government and the free asia movement (gam) to try to save the faltering ceasefire. unfortunately, the talks failed, leading the indonesian president to impose martial law and launch a very large military operation. the commission has since been able to confirm what the honourable members have said. the situation is very serious, the information we are receiving is more than worrying, the human rights violations are serious. we are also very concerned about the demands made to international and non-governmental relief organizations to leave the province and the military censorship of media outlets covering the situation on the ground or events in the province. mr president, the commission believes that a military operation will not bring lasting peace to aceh, even if it is supposedly carried out with the best of intentions. this is why we firmly believe that the keys to peace continue to lie in good governance, justice, respect for human rights, the democratic process and development. we note the statement by the coordinating minister for political and security affairs, mr yudhoyono, that his government will respect the geneva convention and humanitarian law in aceh province. but the international community should call on the indonesian government to ensure that ngos and international humanitarian agencies have access to the province and are safe, because this is a prerequisite for the rapid and transparent delivery of the assistance that the citizens, the most affected populations, desperately need. we are convinced that there is no other option than to resume the dialogue around a negotiating table. the declaration by the indonesian government that it remains open to negotiations confirms this view. we therefore encourage the government and the gam to propose as soon as possible a framework for the resumption of these negotiations. the commission, like the other promoters of this initiative, will remain prepared to facilitate this process by any means possible. mr president, i now come to the second item on the agenda, the situation in papua. you are probably aware that the special act on the autonomy of papua was passed by the indonesian parliament in 2001. in 2002, following the conclusions of a study conducted jointly by indonesian and european experts, the commission mobilised funds from its rapid reaction mechanism to support the implementation of the law by the indonesian authorities, by placing an expert on decentralisation and indonesia at their disposal. and i strongly believe that this initiative was in strict respect of the territorial integrity of indonesia by the european union and that it had the full agreement and cooperation of the indonesian authorities. in mid-2003, the commission proposed technical assistance to the provincial government of papua and the implementation of the special autonomy law. the launch of this programme has not yet been approved by the indonesian government. the commission hopes that only technical reasons explain this delay. the commission took note of the presidential decree of 27 january 2003 establishing three new provinces in papua and that the indonesian parliament, which is required to confirm the creation of these provinces, has not yet taken a decision. we are nevertheless very concerned about the consequences that the application of this decree could have on the implementation of the special law on the autonomy of the province of papua. we remain convinced that the path opened up by the special law remains the one the indonesian authorities must follow. the commission calls on the indonesian government to implement the special law and maintains its offer of assistance in this respect. at the same time, the commission reaffirms its support for the territorial integrity of indonesia and remains attentive to the respect of human rights in this province, as in all other provinces of indonesia.

madam president, i too welcomed the communication by commissioner lamy, who is well aware that the future of the textile and clothing industries, which are already in difficulty because of the appreciation of the dollar, will depend on the choices made in the wto. the removal of quantitative barriers should also offer a growth opportunity to small and medium-sized enterprises operating in europe's textile districts. these firms must be able to expand their interests into new markets and to imagine new synergies with countries entering the international market. the expiry of the multifibre arrangement, however, sets out a scenario of more intense and concentrated competition in mature markets. it is not, of course, a question of calling for protectionist measures but, on the contrary, for more open and transparent markets, as mr ferrer has argued. the globalisation of markets will inevitably lead to the decentralisation of many traditional activities to developing countries with lower production costs. the fight against poverty and the spread of prosperity must be promoted by the abolition of customs barriers, but it cannot ignore the fact that employment in many european industries is threatened by social and environmental dumping rather than by economic competition. i would therefore like to recall some of the points raised by the commissioner. there is a need to improve access for community products, generally of higher quality, to third markets, which are in many cases protected by high duties and non-tariff barriers; the liberalization process must be accompanied by a guarantee of reciprocity, as the commissioner rightly said. the textile and clothing industry must be protected from unfair competition: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is not damaged. finally, also on the basis of experience gained in other fields, consideration should be given to the possibility of introducing a quality label for textiles and clothing, both to guarantee consumers and to curb illegal import flows that threaten the growth of the economy and the fairness of international trade.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this recommendation for the second reading on the council's common position on the proposal to amend the seveso directive deserves a brief flashback. in a delicate context of dramatic accidents affecting the chemical industry, but above all the people living around these sites, and the environment, the commission has presented to parliament and the council its proposal to amend directive 96/82 of 9 december 1996 laying down rules on the control of the risks of accidents caused by dangerous substances: the commission has proposed a proposal which has the merit of being based on very thorough scientific work and of looking at this delicate issue in a constructive way. in the first reading i explained, together with other colleagues, the reasons why the european parliament should send a strong signal. my approach, which i confirm today, is to ensure that accidents never happen again, as far as possible, while ensuring the safety of citizens and workers in these plants and, of course, protecting the environment. the council reached a common position which took up substantially many of parliament's concerns, but some areas of concern remain, as follows: first, the inclusion of mining and landfills, on which the committee on the environment decided to table the amendments at first reading, namely the inclusion, within the scope of the directive, of all types of preparation or processing of dangerous substances at these sites, not just chemical or thermal processing, as envisaged by the commission, and, secondly, the clarification that we are only talking about active installations. we are aware that the commission has very recently launched a proposal for a specific directive on the management of waste from mining activities, the details of which will have to be decided with parliament at the appropriate time, but until then there is still a legislative deficit which, in view of the recent accidents which have alarmed public opinion, we cannot tolerate. i do not, however, exclude the possibility that, in the conciliation procedure, the development of the text of this new mining directive may facilitate the search for agreement on this point. question number two: the training of staff. here again, in agreement with the commission, we have proposed measures for the provision of emergency management training for all staff, including those in subcontracting companies. it is indeed appropriate to provide for appropriate measures not only for the handling of dangerous substances but also for the management of emergency situations, in order to contain potential damage as much as possible and to ensure the safety of workers to the maximum. i do not think it is necessary, as rapporteur, to include the list of training measures in the notification provided for in article 6 of the directive, which is why i reiterate the vote against amendment no 3 which i already voted against at first reading. the third point is spatial planning. the council has already taken into account parliament's concern to lay the foundations for the definition, at european level, of the methodological criteria necessary to assess the compatibility between the sites concerned and the areas at risk, including through financial support from the union. however, in view of the wide diversity of rules, territorial situations, competences and responsibilities which characterise this aspect of safety, i.e. location from an urban point of view, i believe that it is necessary to refer to the principle of subsidiarity and to leave it to the member states to decide on the minimum distances: that is why i have asked for a split vote on amendment no 6, voting in favour of only the first part of the amendment. the committee believes that the graphic display of areas surrounding installations at risk of accidents is an effective and understandable means for all concerned citizens, who have a right to greater clarity. the rapporteur has therefore adopted the wording of the european commission in the amended proposal for a directive. finally, the committee on the environment has proposed again the differentiation of potassium nitrate with new thresholds, in order to avoid farmers using a form of potassium nitrate which would not be classified as a fuel falling within the scope of the directive. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, these are the main points. it is clear that we are moving towards a conciliation procedure: the council was not able to reach agreement on a compromise package and, to be honest, the honourable member did not seem particularly interested in reaching such an agreement with parliament. however, i remain confident that a constructive debate can lead to a solution that maximises the safety of these plants. i would like to thank all my colleagues on the committee on the environment and the services of the european commission, who have been particularly helpful and cooperative.

- the next item is the report (a5-0171/2003) by mr lisi, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on a community action plan for the conservation and sustainable exploitation of fisheries resources in the mediterranean within the framework of the common fisheries policy (com (2002) 535 - c5-0623/2002 - 2002/2281 (ini)).
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we have welcomed with great interest the commission's communication on the union's action plan for fisheries in the mediterranean. this communication responds to a request that has been repeatedly raised and is entirely legitimate, both because of the importance of the mediterranean fisheries economy in the european context and because of the specific nature of fishing activities in this region. the regulation on fisheries in the mediterranean in force since 1626 has so far survived only a series of derogations which, while they have helped to save what can be saved, as in the case of special fisheries, have also highlighted the inadequacy of the union's approach to the mediterranean question. we all know that the application of the principles of the common fisheries policy in the mediterranean in any one way is counterproductive, and sometimes even harmful, if we consider the socioeconomic consequences of such application. i therefore welcome the commission's efforts to impose the specific character of the mediterranean and the sustainability of fisheries as new criteria for the future action plan. the positive aspects of the communication are considerable, for example: the delegation of coastal fishing to the member states, the involvement of fishermen's associations, the dialogue with third countries, the first consideration of the phenomenon of sport fishing. however, it seems to the rapporteur and to our committee that, after a proper analysis of the sector and its specific features, carried out by the commission with regard to solutions, the classic instruments of the cfp, of the common policy, are being used too easily, without any particular effort of imagination. in the mediterranean, we need innovative and coherent action, which proceeds in stages and is not afraid to adjust the approach whenever the need arises. i would now like to draw your attention briefly to a few points in my report: first, the union's systemic and multilateral approach must be a reality and not just a wish. the involvement of fishermen's associations must also mean promoting the experience gained at local level for responsible fisheries management, experience that demonstrates the effectiveness of selective gear, the effectiveness of alternative measures to fishing effort management, such as temporary closure; rigid and automatic transposition of cfp management mechanisms, such as minimum sizes or tacs, risks frustrating the efforts of fishermen and may prove counterproductive; in addition, the early introduction of inadequate technical measures risks rendering sterile the multilateral dialogue which the commission intends to engage with third countries in the mediterranean area for the sustainable management of the whole basin. what we are asking is that negotiations with the countries which, like us, fish in the mediterranean sea, be started as soon as possible, so that we can present the results of these talks at the next interministerial conference on mediterranean fisheries, which will be held in venice in november. a second point is to emphasize the key role of research in supporting an effective fisheries policy. we know that the specific nature of the mediterranean has always been a problem in this respect, but we must insist on scientific research which can be applied to the action plan. it is in this sense that we propose a mediterranean research model based on local data collection networks. there is also the structural impact of the action plan, which we believe is being underestimated by the commission. we are particularly disappointed with the part devoted to this aspect. we in the committee propose that you consider innovative support measures, for example in this case, in particular the measure extending the de minimis rule to the fisheries sector. it should not be forgotten that in the mediterranean, fishing is 80% artisanal, highly dependent on the territory, whose socioeconomic balance is often close to subsistence. finally, mr president, there is the reasoning on the environment proposed by the commission: the commission's proposal is not a good one, but it is a good one. in a region where fishing is strictly coastal, the key to sustainable sustainability is in any case the integrated management of coastal areas, on which the commission does not place enough emphasis. president. - ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the members of the committee on fisheries for their very useful suggestions, which have finally allowed us to reach unanimous agreement on this report.
mr president, the community action plan for fisheries in the mediterranean, presented by the commission, is an important first step towards the sustainable management of the sector. but these are good intentions which, although not all of them fully agreeable, should be implemented with a certain degree of urgency. some of the points made in the report by mr lisi, which i welcome, are particularly important. the commission rightly believes that one of the essential elements to be borne in mind in the context of a sustainable approach to fishing in the mediterranean basin is the specific nature of the mediterranean itself. that's right! i would remind you that in the mediterranean the main areas of reproduction and re-population of many - not all - fish species are concentrated in coastal areas. i can therefore only welcome, on behalf of the uen group, the european commission's proposal to delegate the management of coastal fisheries to the member states. i would also point out that another characteristic of the mediterranean sea - a relatively small and warm sea compared with the northern seas - is that it is difficult to create fish stocks of a particular species. it is for this reason - and here i am dissociating myself from the commission's proposal - that i believe the fisheries system in the mediterranean is not suited to the effective application of tacs and quotas. the commission's analysis is supportive of the strengthening and improvement of scientific research in the mediterranean, as well as the involvement of the categories in the strategic choices of the fisheries sector: the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would like to point out, however, the excellent proposal to admit the fisheries organisations to the eventual and desirable mediterranean consultative council. in conclusion, and while remaining within the specific context of the mediterranean, i would like to emphasise a very important and vital aspect for the economy of the sector, an aspect that is certainly valid for italy: the commission's proposal for a regulation on the common organization of the market in fishery products, which is to be adopted by the council on 1 january, is a step in the right direction.

the rapporteur. mr president, we are facing a reform these days and we will therefore be voting on it on wednesday, which, given the interest it has aroused and the debate it has generated, is certainly one of the crucial steps of this legislature and one of the crucial steps in opening up the markets and in implementing the internal market in a european way. we are now going to the second reading, having overcome a number of difficulties we have had in the past with the translations and with the amendments. we have had a long discussion, both directly and indirectly, with the commission. i thank commissioner bolkestein and all his staff for tackling this matter at the outset. we then tackled it together in many circumstances, outside this house, outside parliament but within the institutions, to reach a conclusion that was the best possible. i thank all those who have been useful by their interest, by their contribution, by the amendments they felt they should have tabled. it is a major and important reform which comes to the end of its parliamentary term after a period lasting almost the whole of this legislature. simplification, adaptation to technological and social developments, completion of the internal market were and are the imperatives that have moved this parliament. the dialectic, the comparison, the different political position and the different national interests stimulated and guided the conclusions. the value of goods, services and works in the eu is estimated at some €1.4 trillion a year, which shows that this legislation is at the heart of the eu economy. and we are writing general and fundamental rules in which the national rules of detail will move. general rules which must contain principles which are useful to all and not to a few, useful to the community and not to the lobby of a party; the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the rules for tendering cannot and must not differ according to the amount: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the future of the internal market. the thresholds currently allow only about one eighth of the amount i have mentioned to be used in european competitions. the rest escapes national or regional regulation. i therefore agree that the thresholds should be abolished. however, since this was not possible, a criterion was proposed, which already existed indirectly, according to which the guiding principles of the legislation must always be respected, even by the autonomous territorial legislation. it is necessary that the procedures available are up to date and that the use of ever more rapidly evolving technologies is allowed and codified. contracting entities will thus benefit from the proposals made, using electronic systems not only for the management of calls for tender and the receipt of tenders but also for the actual auction. it is, of course, called for the latter to be limited to the purchase of codified and standardised materials. the aim is to enhance and change the freedom of organisation of the firm by leaving open the possibility of subcontracting for that part of the work which, if identified, can be entrusted to firms for which the main contractor is responsible. in order not to complicate participation in the tender, the partner should be identified after the entrustment. the complex problem - and this has been a very controversial point - of designing and executing in a single context, which is appreciated and desirable for particular categories of procurement, cannot be a rigid rule. the separation between services and work is as obvious and natural as their unification can be, if properly justified. respect for this principle also strengthens qualitative competition, which would otherwise run the risk of being crushed in an exclusively economic and technological environment, which is also the sole property of the undertaking and therefore not always favourable to the contractor. the rapporteur's proposals are based on this principle. it is important to bear in mind that we are dealing with a subject which has a strong and exclusive economic value and as such cannot and should not contain rules and principles which are the subject of specific legislation, such as specific social and environmental requirements. environmental and social matters have specifically defined and definable routes and are therefore made mandatory in other forms and in other areas. however, certain principles are provided for and proposed within the standard, with particular reference to the respect of the needs of disadvantaged groups and the legislation on safety at work. the environment - the great disease of our time - is also the subject of extensive attention. furthermore, any exaggeration in this area is not desirable. the award of the most economically advantageous price cannot be done without a weighting criterion clearly defined in the call for tenders, since otherwise there would be a discretion in the subsequent allocation of the parameters which in the past has created so many legal problems throughout the community. the confidentiality of information which, depending on the procedures chosen, is provided to the contracting authority by the parties concerned will be protected and guaranteed by precise rules. there are controversial views on in-house procurement: the commission's proposal to reserve to an undertaking of which the contracting authority is a member, even if it is an autonomous legal entity, the right to award contracts without a call for tenders, is strongly opposed by the representatives of the categories of producers, and the rapporteur agrees with this view. it was proposed to extend the grounds for exclusion in the event of convictions for further serious offences against a competing undertaking for bankruptcy, unfair behaviour, failure to respect collective labour agreements, drug dealing. finally, it was proposed to set up an independent agency to ensure control mechanisms for procurement with the member states. while not prejudging the possibility of bringing legal proceedings, it is hoped that this agency will be able to verify the procedures followed and may also cancel an award which is found to be non-compliant. in conclusion, mr president, the content of the rules under discussion, because of their economic importance and the employment, social, environmental and economic implications they entail, can be described without a shadow of a doubt as fundamental to the organization of modern society. different political positions, differing views on political and/or bureaucratic grounds mean that a broadly shared path is not foreseeable. the rejection and referral to committee, or the conciliation as the final act of legislation is certainly not easy, but it is foreseeable and desirable. all this is for the good of the union and in the interest of an internal market which must be increasingly consolidated and transparent. the vote tomorrow will decide the democratic course which we must all follow.

of money: if investors are not found, it is also because for many of these projects the utility, socioeconomic viability and - we add - environmental sustainability were not ensured. we must return to the spirit of the delors plan and to two strong ideas in the commission's white paper on transport, which unfortunately we all seem to forget at times: the investments must not only serve to fill the territory with infrastructure but also to promote economic and social cohesion. we must abandon the idea that economic growth must necessarily be accompanied by transport growth, otherwise we will soon be in a permanent traffic jam. what is the point of spending 6 billion euros on the messina bridge to save half an hour of travel time, if thousands of sicilians have no drinking water and it takes them three hours to travel 100 km by train? what is the point of investing 15 years of work for the turin-lyon line in a 54 km tunnel, drilling through a mountain full of asbestos, when the modernisation and upgrading of the existing line would allow it to absorb twice the freight traffic in five years? we would like to discuss not pharaonic and perhaps unrealizable projects, but investments that promote innovation, renewable energy and the regeneration of the territory, for which the participation and acceptance of the citizens living in that territory is considered a value interesting turn of phrase, which refers - we believe - to the need to bring to europe an idea that is very fashionable in italy, namely total deregulation. we will oppose this export attempt, which is particularly risky in times of enlargement, because it is strictly functional to the policy of 'all infrastructure' and derives from an outdated concept of the environment as a commodity to be used and sold. italy is second only to spain in terms of environmental law violations. your government, mr president, has changed the waste laws to make controls more difficult, even though 11 million tonnes of waste are lost in italy every year and the turnover of the eco-mafia is estimated at around 2.5 billion euro; has so relaxed the rules on environmental impact assessment that it has become a purely formal procedure; has given its blessing to the indiscriminate hunting culture in the parks by the regions; this year, it has allocated eur 56 million for protected areas, which is less than the cost of building a 1 km tunnel motorway. the commission is preparing the indiscriminate decriminalisation of environmental offences, and this is all without regard to the community legal framework. we believe that there is a "case italy" on this issue as well as on the media. president prodi, in a field where the union has real powers and international responsibilities, we fear that the cumbersome infringement procedure is no longer sufficient and that, by maintaining an attitude of too much tolerance and attention to formal detail rather than substance, there is a serious risk of contributing to the hollowing out of community environmental legislation. president berlusconi, on foreign policy we would like you to take advantage of all of us of your excellent relations with plan for the court of justice adopted in may 2002. and besides, you have an excellent relationship with president putin. we would really like you to make this friendship, once again, useful to all of initiative, to convene a regional conference for the caucasus where we can address all, all the ongoing conflicts. and then, mr president, we believe that we would be proud, with you, if you could help to convince president putin to ratify the kyoto protocol. a final word on the european constitution. we will support the italian presidency's call for a short intergovernmental conference so as not to undermine the otherwise poorly achieved results of the convention, but, mr president, please keep nuclear out of the constitution and, mr vice-president, help us keep nuclear out of the dangerous energy source, which exists today in the constitution. the rapporteur. mr president, we are about to come up with a report, an initiative of the commission which this parliament has welcomed with great enthusiasm and which seems to us to be one of the most important points of the work done by the committee on regional policy in recent years: the european union is committed to a single european sky, with efficiency, safety and cost-effectiveness as its objectives. it is clear that the single sky is a reality of behaviour and rules, not a literary metaphor: rules and synergies that must be defined, applied and respected. the commission proposal, mr president, has had the merit and the courage - we acknowledge the commissioner, mrs de palacio - to raise this issue with rigor and urgency, even in the indication of deadlines. one year ago parliament had the merit of accepting the commission's challenge at a particular moment, after 9/11, at a time when discussing safety in the skies entailed an added value of sensitivity, reasoning and attention. parliament has accepted this challenge and has supported this draft with a broad and convincing consensus, which was approved at first reading and which has been entrusted to a few simple rules which we hope will be reaffirmed and applied. the most basic rule is that there must be harmony and synergy between all the institutions, bodies and agencies which are called upon to achieve the objectives of the single sky - efficiency, safety and cost-saving - and therefore, above all, attention, punctuality and the definition of a clear relationship between eurocontrol - the agency which has been responsible for the technical know-how of managing the european skies - and the commission, the european union. in this sense we have managed to reach a very precise point of balance, which gives the commission the function, the responsibility for the management, the political governance of this single european sky and asks eurocontrol to make its expertise, its experience and its
