the rapporteur. i am pleased to present to the house the recommendation for second reading on the regulation on assistance and compensation to air passengers in the event of denied boarding, long delays and cancellations. i think it is useful to sum up briefly the developments which have taken place since this proposal was presented last year. the first reading was approved in this house last year and had already highlighted the weaknesses of the commission's initial proposal. the 39 amendments adopted by parliament were mainly aimed at making the legislation more consistent with the real needs of passengers and more practical for airlines. the council's common position, while substantially altering the form of the regulation, has since incorporated a number of concerns raised by parliament: i would like to thank the commissioner for his report, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report, which is a very good report, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report, which is a very good report, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. since the perhaps most thorny issue - the total amount of compensation - has, we can say, been resolved to the satisfaction of almost all colleagues at this point, i shall only mention the remaining open questions which are the subject of this second recommendation. the first concerns tour operators and their right of recourse. the result of the vote in the committee on transport was not, in my view, entirely satisfactory, and now we have a recommendation which is partly contradictory on the tour operators issue. in fact, in the opinion of the speakers, there is a need for minor changes in the definition of tour operators and the reciprocity of the right of recourse - amendments nos 5 and 16 - but overall the council's position has, from this point of view, well focused the problem, since it has placed the overall and general responsibility on the carrier operating the service. it is for this reason that i do not agree with amendments nos 1 and 9, nor with the second part of amendment no 17, which was the subject of a split vote. the second theme is the mileage bands. the first reading of the parliament adopted a single distance criterion, namely the division into three kilometre bands for delays, compensation and the placement of passengers in a lower or higher class. the council, on the other hand, adopted three different criteria in its common position and also introduced a new one, that of the intra- or extra-european union; however, from this point of view, there is no clear justification for this addition. this creates a disparity which does not help the clarity of the legislative text and certainly does not help the passenger to understand exactly what his rights are. that is why we propose that the three different council proposals be brought together again under a single criterion: the commission has also proposed that the maximum length of the three-mile band be increased to three kilometres for all cases. then there is the issue of cancellations. the council's proposal, the result of a laborious compromise, does not, in my view, provide the necessary clarity and risks making communication with passengers very difficult. i have taken the liberty of proposing a single compromise amendment in this field to define clearly when passengers are entitled to assistance, especially in relation to cancellation, and to define a single deadline - five days before the scheduled departure - beyond which passengers may be entitled to financial compensation. i ask my colleagues to follow this position which is precisely trying to make it clearer and more communicated to passengers and also to the airlines what we are talking about. as regards delays, immediate assistance should be guaranteed in the event of long delays, so information, assistance, refreshments, possibly accommodation, while we believe that re-routing and reimbursement of the ticket - fully justified for cancellations and for denied boarding - would, in the event of delays, represent an incredible complication and would trigger a chain of delays that would paralyse air traffic. finally, an amendment was tabled on entry into force, which i think should be accepted because it is common sense: we give the companies time to get equipped, and 12 months is the proposal we make. in conclusion, apart from a few other small comments on amendments which are not of substance, i believe that at this point, if we succeed in approving this proposal, there may be a somewhat more constructive attitude on the part of the council, which gives me confidence that we can close this dossier soon, in the interests of passengers but also of the airline industry.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report we are discussing today is fully in line with the european policy on equal opportunities, which, as we know, is based on two main pillars: specific actions for women and gender mainstreaming, i.e. the introduction of the gender perspective at all stages and levels of public policies by all actors involved in decision-making processes. gender budgeting is the application of the principle of gender mainstreaming in budgetary procedures. as we all know, the budget is not a neutral instrument, but reflects the distribution of power in society. in defining revenue and expenditure policies, public budgetary authorities at all levels make policy choices. the budget is not a mere economic instrument but a key instrument with which political authority defines the model of socioeconomic development and the criteria for redistribution within society; it decides the priorities of intervention in relation to the policies and needs of its citizens, producing different impacts and effects on them depending on whether they are women or men. the way public budgets are normally constructed ignores the diversity of roles and responsibilities between women and men. in most cases, the indicators and data used do not distinguish by gender, presenting themselves as a neutral economic instrument: the public budget, in fact, reflects and reproduces the socioeconomic inequalities already present in a community. analysing fiscal policies according to their differentiated gender impact and redefining them accordingly is a way of ensuring that public budgets respond to the needs of equity and economy. public spending is not only efficient but also fair when it is able to promote development and to exploit the full potential of all parts of society. it is therefore a matter of adopting an economic and social philosophy according to which, even within an open and globalised market economy, economic and social development are inseparable and mutually nourishing. an economy cannot be competitive, dynamic and healthy over time unless, behind the production, trade and financial processes, there is a stable, cohesive and just society, where human rights, resources and capacities are adequately developed. the strengthening, modernisation and reorganisation of public interventions, and therefore also of budgetary policies, for social development is in reality an intangible investment in capacity, empowerment, the creation of resources and opportunities which is absolutely indispensable for economies which want to be dynamic and competitive as they are based on knowledge, as the european council set out to do in lisbon. if this is the first time that this parliament has discussed gender budgeting, it is not a new concept. the platform for action drawn up in beijing on the occasion of the fourth united nations world conference on women makes explicit reference to this; a working group of experts has been set up within the directorate-general for human rights of the council of europe; the commission itself, following the conference organized by the belgian presidency, set up an expert group. but there are also many experiences in western countries, starting with australia, which adopted this instrument in 1984, as well as many developing countries, and in recent years, interesting experiences within the european union, both at national and local level. what are the specific objectives of this report? firstly, to raise awareness among the public, political and economic actors at all levels; to raise awareness of the gender budgeting approach strategy at the level of the union institutions, member states; calls on the commission, which has already expressed its support, to produce an information brochure on gender budgeting for widespread dissemination; involve, at all levels, the actors working in the field in participating in the construction of the budget; but above all, to indicate a framework for action for the implementation of gender budgeting, which provides for democratic participation from below and the involvement of organised actors, from non-governmental organisations to women's associations. i conclude, madam president, with this reference: where these experiences are already taking place, especially at local level, they have also broken the indifference and detachment which we now see at all levels between citizens and public authorities. it is a great instrument of participation, as well as of justice.

commission. - mr president, i shall take these questions one by one. i think mr rübig is right when he says that the stakes in these negotiations are important for small and mediumsized enterprises. this is a fancy way of saying that it is not just the big multinationals who have an interest in balanced progress in the multilateral trading system. geographical indications are a complex subject. i would like to recall briefly the union's negotiating objectives in this area. first, with regard to wines and spirits, we want a binding register to be established at the wto. we also want to extend a number of existing schemes for the protection of geographical indications for wines and spirits to other agricultural and food products. finally, we want to recover, as seems natural, a number of geographical indications, which we have listed under the auspices of franz fischler, which are important for our farmers, and which are still being usurped in other parts of the planet. mrs mcnally recalled the socialist group's position on investment. i will also say a word in reply to mrs lucas. how do we reconcile our desire for multilateral agreement on a number of investment principles to be developed at the wto with our developmental aspirations? firstly, we believe that investment is an important factor in development, that a number of simple and basic rules on transparency, predictability of investment schemes, for example, are an important contribution to investment; secondly, we are prepared to take into account a number of concerns of the developing countries in this negotiation, such as those which they have sometimes expressed and which are that such rules would reduce their political sovereignty. we are prepared to answer this question by presenting a draft which contains a number of general rules which could be adopted by developing countries which wish to do so without imposing any obligation on those which do not wish to do so. this is one way of taking into account a number of objections. i would remind mrs mcnally and mrs lucas that the developing countries are divided on this issue, some are in favour of it and some are against it, as is the case on a number of other issues. there is no north front on all issues or south front on other issues in the world trade organisation. on this point, i simply remind mrs lucas that these four subjects - investment, trade facilitation, transparency in public procurement and competition - are part of the negotiating programme, as adopted in doha, with the understanding that we must agree on the negotiating modalities, as is also the case for other subjects, agricultural issues or industrial tariffs, for example. mr olsson is right: agriculture is also not a subject which, within the wto, pits an uncompetitive and protectionist north against a competitive and liberalising south. it is enough to compare the position of brazil with that of india, or that of africa with that of indonesia or thailand to realize immediately that this is not the case. in reply to mrs frahm, i would say that our philosophy is quite clear in this discussion. firstly, agricultural trade cannot be trivialised in the way we advocate for tyres, socks, shirts or cars. the specific nature of agricultural production means that we europeans are not in favour of complete liberalisation of agricultural markets for a number of reasons. we therefore want to maintain public intervention in agriculture. the terms of these public interventions, however, need to be adapted to correct some of the disadvantages they present for agricultural policies in third world countries. we did this in 1992, in 1999 and in 2003, and franz fischler, who is here with me tonight, deserves to be honoured for the various efforts he has made on these occasions. in each case we have adapted our common agricultural policy to international trade, particularly in favour of developing countries. we're going to continue on this path. we have made negotiating commitments to further reduce our domestic support in terms of trade-damaging effects, to increase our market access, to reduce our export support. we will do this as a matter of priority for the benefit of developing countries. this is the basis of the union's negotiating position. i would like to make one final point in reply to mrs frahm. there is indeed a problem of articulation between respect for fundamental rights and the rules of international trade, just as there is between the rules of international trade and international environmental agreements or between the rules of trade and public health concerns. in the field of public health, this arbitration has just been carried out at the world trade organisation in favour of access to generic medicines. the negotiations, the programme of which was adopted in doha, include negotiations on the link between environmental and trade rules. on the other hand, there is no negotiation on the relationship between the fundamental rights of workers, and in particular the five basic conventions of the world labour organisation, and the rules of international trade, because we have not succeeded in making our point of view prevail. this was part of our negotiating objectives in doha. we have come up against a wall of the united states of america and the developing countries. they didn 't wish it; they do not want that and so far the union's position, however valid it may be - and i have always defended it vigorously because i think it is the right position - has not prevailed against the joint position of the developing countries and the united states. it is a balance of power which we have not yet been able to reverse in our favour.

commission. - i have listened to all these questions, mr president, and in listening to them i am afraid that the members of the european parliament are giving the lie to those who say that agriculture is the only subject on the table in cancun. i would remind you that this is not the case because there are about 19 others. on a more political level, i would point out that it is not necessarily in the union's interest to pretend that agriculture is the only subject on the table in cancun. it is not the area in which we have the most offensive interests, although we do have some - i said a word about geographical indications. i therefore hope that those of you who are concerned about the interests of the union in this negotiation will not contribute to this general presentation that says that agriculture will be the only subject at cancun. i shall nevertheless answer the questions that have been put. mr cunha is right: since the situation in the developing countries is very different, we must adopt a different approach depending on the country we are dealing with. this process must take place within the multilateral system, although it is not always very convenient to get brazil to admit that india does not have the same position as it, and vice versa, even if brazil tells us that it is in favour of full liberalisation, when we know very well that this is not the indian position. these arrangements must therefore be found within the world trade organisation. we must also involve the rest of our agricultural trade policy, which, as you know, is based on asymmetrical bilateral agreements, knowing that we are offering more openness to developing countries than we are asking for. i am thinking of the system of generalised preferences or the 'everything but arms' system, under which we have, unilaterally, in a way, made provisions for the developing countries. as regards the questions by mr o'neachtain, mr bernié and mrs maes on the relationship between the common agricultural policy, its developments and the international negotiations at the world trade organisation, my answer will be clear. on this point, the position of franz fischler, my own, the commission's and the union's is simple: we first decide on the reforms of the common agricultural policy that we consider necessary and, once we have taken these decisions, depending on what the other parties propose, we agree to put into the marble of the world trade organisation the disciplines that correspond to those we have adopted between ourselves. in short, the hen is the common agricultural policy and the egg is international trade negotiations. in so far as we are building, if i may say, our position, we are different from the americans who negotiate internationally, make commitments and then draw the consequences at the level of their own agricultural support system. therefore, our agricultural mandate is, by definition, limited by the current state of reforms of the common agricultural policy. the situation has always been perfectly clear on this point, it is seen and known by everyone. take sugar, for example. the sugar market has not yet been reformed; the commission is working on it and a proposal is expected in the coming weeks. the same is true of cotton, tobacco and olive oil. but at this stage the european union cannot engage in these negotiations, which would involve, as far as sugar is concerned, a change in the common organization of the market which we have not yet decided. in short, the situation is perfectly clear on this point. experience shows that we know how, when necessary and usually for our own reasons, to decide on reforms which give us a certain margin of manoeuvre in negotiations. as regards the agreement between the united states and the european union, or more precisely the interim framework agreement which we negotiated this summer, i reply to mr de clercq that we acted at the request of the other members of the world trade organisation. they have pressed us, the two big elephants who devote about 1% of our national wealth to supporting the agricultural sector, to agree, believing that as long as the united states and europe are on different positions, it will be difficult to move the negotiation forward. we have responded to their request. it is in fact an intermediate step which would allow us to negotiate halfway. in that case, we would have to complete the other half of the journey. we know that some countries, japan on the one hand, brazil and australia on the other, feel that the balance we have achieved is not exactly what they would like - and this is not surprising. i would like to conclude by replying to max van den berg and mrs maes, who referred to the agreement on access to generic medicines for the poorest countries. the agreement itself was the result of discussions and unanimous agreement at the world trade organisation, including two-thirds of the wto's developing country members. i am sufficiently familiar with the modalities of international negotiations to know that it is indeed the countries around the wto table that make the decisions and not others who make them for them. the interest of the developing countries, around the negotiating table at the wto, the who, the fao and the international labour organisation, is expressed by the representatives of the governments of these countries and, since they are satisfied with a decision which they have been asking for years and which they have obtained, this means for me that the negotiations are closed. i know that some non-governmental organization thinks that developing countries should have negotiated harder. rest assured, there are also, on the other side, some pharmaceutical industry organization that thinks we should have negotiated harder. this is the very principle of compromise and i cannot put myself in the place of developing countries to say what is good or not good for them. it is a political decision that has been taken and, therefore, it is this compromise that will guide our action in the years to come. however, as i said earlier, only part of the problem of access to generic medicines in the poorest countries is solved in this way: the problem of international patent law. she's 10% of the problem. we have to solve the whole part that does not depend on the patent problem: the problems of financing, production, availability, which means that 90% of the way is still to be done. this path must be taken together with other international organisations, in particular those set up to finance the fight against a number of the diseases concerned. it's a matter of development aid, it's a matter of national governance. i don't overestimate the 10% of the way that has been traveled. i have always considered, as you know, because we have been saying to you very often for three years, that we had to do this to show the way for the rest. the way is open and this is a situation of hope which we have not known about this subject for a long time, unfortunately.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. as mrs frassoni rightly points out, the supply of water resources in spain would increase with the implementation of the spanish water management plan. the commission does not currently have detailed information or studies on the impact of such additional water supply on production in the european union and on agricultural prices. we can therefore only estimate. the commission estimates that the increase in water resources will have very little effect on the volume of agricultural products supported by community agricultural funds. for most irrigated crops, community support is already subject to a ceiling based either on the area covered, as in the case of maize or rice, or on guaranteed national ceilings, as in the case of cotton, olive oil and processed fruit and vegetables. if the area under cultivation exceeds the eligible reference area, the payments shall be reduced proportionately. the possible increases in yields or an increase in irrigated areas resulting from the spanish water management plan therefore had no impact on the total amount of payments. the implementation of the plan could also not affect milk production because of the quota system. the only sector in which production could increase is the 'fresh fruit and vegetables' sector. the sector is already very market-oriented and an increase in production would only be possible if there was a corresponding market potential. in addition, irrigation could improve the quality and competitiveness of fresh fruit and vegetables. if the invisible balance of mediterranean agriculture were affected by the spanish plans, such a development would not be supported by the community, because increases in production do not automatically entail an increase in community support.
the problem, commissioner, to which we have tried to draw your attention is that, as you yourself have said, there are still no precise estimates of what the effect of the national water plan will actually be on prices. since we do not know what the price will be for water, we obviously do not know what effect this will have on prices. i therefore ask you to pay particular attention to this aspect, because according to the latest information we have received, in addition to the increase in the supply of water in relation to the national hydrological plan, a number of desalination plants are being planned which will further increase - according to some estimates, by up to 400 cubic metres per year - the capacity for producing water in this area of spain. we feel that the commission has a special responsibility from the agricultural point of view to pay particular attention to these elements, and you yourself confirm to me that the commission is not yet in a position to do so.

the requirement for unanimity and has further strengthened the primacy of the council in key areas of the union's competences. while we acknowledge the quality of your work, we believe that the way in mr president, ladies and gentlemen, information technology is the backbone of the future development of every nation in the world, and its fundamental pillar is technology, hardware, and science, software. every technological innovation is currently protected and patented; on the contrary, the development of software gives rise to a copyright that protects its intellectual property. to make it clear, let's draw a parallel with the world of music. the electronic computer is an instrument with which music is played, composed not of notes but of codes and commands which, alternating with the rhythm and the sequence devised and developed by the developer, give rise to different actions and results. what would happen to music if one day you could patent the scales, the chords, the trills and everything that makes the world's symphonic landscape full and exciting? the same fate would befall computer science, where patents would protect every little command, those sequences of codes and algorithms, effectively turning the market into a jungle of limitations. if existing patents were to be validated, all software development would be limited, circumscribed and increasingly curbed, as this would force all small and mediumsized enterprises and the programmers themselves to acquire or license, effectively putting them out of the market. the intellectual property of a picture or a book is not protected by patenting its subject or subject matter, but by guaranteeing its dissemination within the framework of the laws protecting copyright, thus stimulating other minds to produce works of ingenuity, similar but not copies, improving where possible the original work or reinterpreting it according to different and more interesting schemes. a growing market, open to new horizons of fervent inventions and fantasy, such as the european one, cannot afford to impose additional rules, in effect putting new brakes on the development of the european nations. it is our firm conviction that the mccarthy report cannot be accepted because its support would seriously jeopardize the development and technological growth which can only be generated by a people with a free mind and spirit.
mr president, i thank the rapporteur and the commission for the work they have done and the difficulty of it. the radical bonino list meps will vote in favour of the amendments aimed at restricting the scope for patentability of software and will vote against the overall proposal if the core of these amendments is not accepted. why would you do that? perhaps because we are against the need for european harmonization? no, of course not. we agree with the commissioner and the rapporteur in taking note of a situation where the european patent office has, in fact, accepted thousands of software patents. in the face of such a flagrant violation of the spirit and the letter of the european patent convention, what was necessary, what would be necessary, what is necessary, is to clarify and confirm the non-patentability of software. the distinction between software patentability as such and software patentability as part of a technological invention is a subtle one, and one that we risk making a mess of, whereas the solution, in my view, is there and it's very clear: if software is an integral part of an invention, it is the invention that is patentable and patented, not the software. but it is already possible to do this through the laws that govern technological inventions that call themselves such. software is excluded from patentability for a very specific reason: for the same reason that mathematical formulas are excluded, for the same reason that theorems are excluded, for the same reason that musical formulas or symphonies are excluded, which belong to the field of ideas, the organization of ideas, the transformation of ideas. we know that the same functionality that a piece of software can perform can be translated into an infinite number of different types of code, by an infinite number of different programmers, with different programming languages. this is what makes patents on software dangerous, especially if they last for 20 years, a geological age for software development. independent programmers and programmers in general would now be allowed to use features patented in 1983, when we were in the prehistory of software and computers. that's the danger. i think it would not have been necessary for us to venture into complex formulas on the distinction between software patenting as such and software as part of technological inventions. it was enough to continue to make technological inventions patentable and to enforce the rule that software is not patentable, which in any case allows protection through copyright. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive. i also believe that we cannot proceed to adopt the proposal here because otherwise the member states will do it themselves. we try to do the best we can here. i also believe that the involvement of hundreds of thousands of people who have individually spoken on this issue should be seen as a democratic contribution and not as a nuisance.

case or cases we may wish to bring against individuals. i hope that on examination it will be understood that i say this in a mood of explanation and transparency, not apology or evasiveness, and it is necessary simply because of the material we are dealing with. i realise that if there had been a historic background of trying to keep confidentiality to a minimum, and transparency to a maximum, then it would be easier for this house to understand that, when it is critically essential that we use confidential procedures, it is done for absolutely the best reasons. i hope that, amongst other products of activity-based management and budgeting and the transparency that mr virrankoski spoke about, we will see a further evolution of the readiness of the commission to make maximum disclosure whilst trying to safeguard the integrity of necessary procedures. the report will be available under annex iii of the framework agreement procedure when it is ready. it is being finalised literally now, so that it can be available in the proper form at the time promised. as regards the consolidation of political responsibility i do not yet envisage the full implementation of the architecture that mr casaca desires, though i have a lot of sympathy for it. that architecture consists in the establishment of a full financial control unit, as it were, in the office of every commissioner. but i consider that we have made substantial progress towards achieving that, on the one hand in the general ambit of the financial regulation, but more specifically in the reforms adopted by the commission, in some cases as recently as july 2003. those guarantee an absolute requirement for reporting on management conduct and financial operation in a dg at least twice a year, specifically to the responsible commissioner, so that commissioners will in future continue to be au fait with the practical operational management of the directorate-general, as well as bearing their straightforward and obvious political responsibilities. it will not diminish political responsibility, portfolio responsibility or policy engagement: it is likely to add to those. commissioner schreyer and i sent a letter to all dgs in july 2003. the response we got from the dgs - with very thorough analysis seeking to detect any practices remotely related to what we have observed in eurostat - was rigorous and encouragingly thorough. i know that mr casaca, with his interest in these matters, and probably mr mulder, will want to examine that. that will be very welcome. mr virrankoski obviously shows great understanding and i know his background really gives him an authority in this area. i would simply say to him that i agree with his forecast for future structures and the practices that he anticipates, and express confidence that they will come to pass. culture in an organisation of human beings is substantially a product not of ethnic or national origin or regional origin or language. culture is a product of the systems and structures in which people work. by making massive reforms that radically change systems and structures, we foster the kind of culture of transparency and accountability which is fundamental to the successful operation of activity-based management and of the activity-based budgeting which reinforces that process. to mr ferber i would say: it is a matter of record that my promise at the outset of the commission - and i am not trying to denounce or go back on any catchphrases about the best in the world, etc. - was that we would strive to achieve, through radical modernising reform, a well managed, high-performance, service-orientated, independent european commission in the service of the peoples of the european union. i do not think that was modest, and yet we are accomplishing it. to use his phrase, i do not imagine that the sky is as blue as he says i have painted it. we acknowledge in our frequent progress reports the shortcomings, the target dates that we have missed, as well as the ones that we have bettered. we acknowledge where further development needs to take place. it was, after all, this commission which - as soon as we had prima facie evidence that gave us legal security in undertaking certain actions - suspended contracts, opened disciplinary proceedings, established the strongest, biggest ever inquiry task force in the history of the commission, increased the staffing of the internal audit examination of contracts from 9 to 24 persons and has had those reports coming in absolutely on schedule. this is not evidence of a slothful or lax commission, but neither does it mean that we imagine that the sky is permanently blue, nor do these glasses have any rose tint. i am impatient for further change. i want to see total implementation. that ambition is shared universally by my colleagues and we could not have made the progress we have unless we had had massive cooperation from staff assuming these obligations in addition to their normal workload and if we had not had the full-hearted commitment of every single member of the college of commissioners. therefore, i do not try to pretend that we have done more than we have. i simply ask for a factual examination of what has been achieved. for instance, automatic mandatory mobility for senior management and for people in money-handling, contract-handling posts will in itself provide a safeguard against a repetition of the double accounting that we have detected in eurostat. more than any other measure, but in addition, reforms of structures and systems of audit control and management control that give us - insofar as any human organisation handling money can get it - real, strong safeguards against any form of repetition of what we have detected and are acting upon now. as far as the response to parliament and the council is concerned, i respect it. i come from a parliamentary tradition where an elected house of commons obtained its strength by having the vote on the budget. therefore i fundamentally respect and want to endorse that democratic procedure. i do not plead for us to depart from that. i do not make an argument for being insulated against the representations and judgment of parliament or of the council which represents the taxpayers. i do not ask for that for one second. i simply say that it is a practical reality that, without autonomy, it is difficult to exercise responsibility, and when we have autonomy our responsibility must be fully accountable. however, if we do not have the resources or the people whose presence, qualities and qualifications we can totally justify, then it is very difficult to see how the commission can undertake the tasks it has now, let alone the ones that are to come as a consequence of this glorious enlargement, but which nevertheless we recognise to be additional obligations which we must discharge with efficiency and honesty.

commission. mr president, as i said to the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs on 9 september 2003, and in accordance with the messages i received from members of parliament on that occasion, the commission is pursuing its negotiations with the american authorities which receive passenger name record data transferred from the european union with a view to obtaining improved undertakings on four major issues. first, i will touch upon purpose limitation. so far, the united states has refused to limit its use of passenger name record data to the fight against terrorism. the americans also want to cover other serious domestic criminal offences. so far, they have not been prepared to further narrow these down. second, as far as the scope of the data required is concerned, the united states requires 39 different pnr elements, which it is hard to regard as necessary for or proportionate to the purpose. the commission is seeking a reduction in the list of 39 data elements from the united states. thirdly, the data storage periods are still far too long. mrs boogerd-quaak has stressed that they last six to seven years. fourth, american undertakings are insufficiently legally-binding, since the available extra-judicial redress mechanisms are not fully independent. therefore we must insist that rights are, to the greatest possible extent, legally-binding and thus actionable before american courts. currently, we are working with the target date of christmas 2003, the date that i set when i last spoke to the libe committee. ideally, an adequacy decision should be well on track by that time. an adequacy decision will only be possible, however, if the united states is ready to improve significantly its undertakings. i must be frank with the house and say that i am not confident that we shall be able to secure the necessary significant improvements in order for the commission to be able to make an adequacy finding. however, progress in the united states' commitments is in any case necessary for any kind of solution, whatever its legal form - be it an adequacy finding or, if supported by the european parliament, a bilateral international agreement. the most recent step in our negotiations with the united states was the meeting which i held yesterday with under secretary asa hutchinson of the us department of homeland security - he is the number two person in that department. that was a useful meeting in which we discussed all the main issues and agreed to put our officials to work to make further efforts to find a solution in the coming weeks. when i am in washington in mid-october i expect to meet with senior homeland security officials, including, hopefully, secretary tom ridge. i emphasised to mr hutchinson yesterday the urgency of finding a solution – and of course i also referred to the serious concern with which pnr transfers are viewed in this parliament. i find it difficult to accept any remark that the commission is tolerating the situation and not doing its job as guardian of the treaties. as far as the data protection directive is concerned, applying the law is a job for the member states and their data protection authorities. the commission's immediate role is to ensure that it is the member states that respect the directive, not the airlines. but the problem, in any case, is not one that we can solve via purely intra-european means. we have a conflict of laws with the united states and that is the heart of the matter. in my talks with the united states authorities, i hope to be firm. but being entirely inflexible on the european side will not necessarily obtain more flexibility from our counterparts. regarding passenger consent, which was mentioned by some members as a possible way out - at least in the short term - this would not, in our view, constitute a legally-secure, longer-term solution. first, making consent unambiguous would prove very burdensome in practice. second, the result would be a transfer of data that – despite being legal in the eu – would still lack any significant protection on the american side. therefore, securing the best possible undertakings from the united states on the way in which they will treat the data collected from eu citizens is much to be preferred. the oral question submitted by mrs boogerd-quaak also refers to what should happen if an adequacy finding cannot be reached by the end of the year. she proposes to stop the data transfers that are not in accordance with the principles of non-discrimination, prior informed consent and an efficient appeals procedure, and to begin immediate negotiations on an international agreement with the united states. these measures reflect to some extent the options for possible courses of action that i outlined in my meeting with the libe committee earlier this month. however, as i stressed then, we should be very prudent not to shoot ourselves in the foot. enforcement action may be superficially attractive, but it is not clear that its consequences would be those that we seek. therefore, let us cross that bridge when we come to it. political judgments will have to be exercised at the right moment. it is clear that the course we shall follow will fully involve the parliament and the council. i am sure we can all agree on the need to unite to combat terrorism. but we equally agree on the need to avoid security concerns becoming an excuse for dismantling our civil rights and liberties. i should like to assure the house that the commission will continue to devote its unstinting efforts to finding an agreed solution with the united states on this important but also very delicate issue. the solution needs to be found as a matter of urgency, and must respect the law on both sides of the atlantic.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have heard some key dates in this affair. the first is certainly on 5 march 2003, when the united states asked airlines operating between the united states and europe to make available all passenger data: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the data are not only available to the airlines but also to the airlines. the second date is march 15th of this year. only a week later, in a timely fashion worthy of the best cause, this parliament passed the resolution calling for the application of the 1995 directive and the 1989 regulation on the protection of privacy. the third date is september 23rd, today: six months after the adoption of this resolution, it seems that almost nothing has changed. the commission's calls for action are not being heeded overseas. it begs the question: are the americans deaf or is the commission unable to find the right words? and so, even today, those who go to america are asked, in addition to the usual generalities, about the religion practiced, the food tastes, the places of the last holidays and the relatives near and far. of course, it's certainly too much! and it is right that the commission should speak out, that this parliament should call for a more determined commitment, perhaps through an international treaty, as the resolution proposes. however, i think it is also worth remembering another date: i was in the hospital on september 11, 2001. we all remember that it was then that the application of strict controls began. in the face of this shocking memory, i think we can still find a small dose of patience and understand that perhaps, alongside a definitely annoying form of indiscretion towards the person, there is still too much fear. i mean, as the commissioner said, perhaps a little flexibility could help the dialogue.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the current situation of illegality is obvious. the direct, unfiltered access of the us authorities to the personal data of european passengers is without legal basis and contrary to article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights; is contrary to community provisions on the protection of personal data; is contrary to the community regulation on electronic reservation systems. the european commission is partly responsible for this illegal situation, because the us legislation which required the collection of this data dates back to november 2001, was updated in may 2002, and the system only came into force in march 2003. in the meantime, the commission failed to inform parliament, negotiated with the united states at the level of officials and finally reached a joint declaration on 18 february 2003 which in fact allowed the us authorities indiscriminate access to the personal data of european citizens, collected for other purposes by airlines, and even suggested to the national supervisory authorities that they should not take any action against airlines that accepted us requests. only the firm reaction of the european parliament and the supervisory authorities themselves finally led the commission to recognise that the adequate protection required by article 25 of the directive for the transfer of data collected in the union does not exist. i would like to point out, however, that in the case of italy, the ban on access by the supervisory authority to data collected by alitalia did not lead to any negative reaction or sanctions by the us authorities. the commission must therefore make a stronger effort to reach a genuine international agreement with the united states in the short term, which would regulate the matter on the basis of fundamental principles: respect for the principle of reciprocity, according to which if the union guarantees us citizens the same rights as its own citizens, the us must do the same for european citizens; respect for the principle of proportionality; the principle of informed consent of the persons concerned with the right to have recourse to an independent authority or court. in the meantime, until a satisfactory agreement is reached, legality is restored and access to data that breaches community rules is prohibited. in the future, we must also ensure that a centralised system is set up at european level for the computerized collection of data on air travel reservations, with appropriate filters for the transmission to third parties of the only data which it is legitimate to communicate, in compliance with the fundamental rights of european citizens which we, parliament and the commission, have an obligation to protect, including in the face of terrorism.
mr president, commissioner, flexibility is great for negotiations, but it is terrible for law enforcement. article 2 of regulation no 22/99 prohibits the disclosure of personal information about a passenger to third parties who are not parties to the transaction without his or her consent. commissioner, you said that the responsibility for compliance with the legislation lies with the member states. that is true of the directive, but it is not true of the regulation. you have full powers to intervene, to enforce the law, under article 11 which states: the commission, acting on a complaint or on its own initiative, shall initiate proceedings to bring to an end any infringement of the provisions of this regulation. we want to ask for a counterproductive respect for the law? i believe, first of all, that when a law exists, it must be respected and that any prerequisite for reform - even if it is a reform of an international treaty - is respect for the form. commissioner, you would gain more power in international negotiations if the commission - as it has the power, as well as the power of the member states - immediately enforced compliance with the law. the deadline is not one of our own making, but it is - and in my view must be - that of article 232 of the treaty, which provides for two months from our request to act, otherwise we have two months to bring an action before the court of justice.

mr president, the convention has done an important job, handing europe the text of a constitution which will make an effective contribution to building our future. this work must be defended by detractors and opponents, but it must be further improved. it is not true that there is no scope for doing so. i therefore share and support the proactive view of president prodi, who sees the value of the text but also sees the limitations and risks that may result from it. i am not going to go into detail here. i am not referring to inadequate content and social rights, which are the result of the actual and present balance of power. it is no coincidence, for example, that the constituent assembly, which wrote the splendid italian constitution after the war, had the communist umberto terracini as its president, while today our convention is presided over by the very respectable but very moderate mr giscard d'estaing. i am therefore referring to strictly institutional matters: firstly, a full-time president of the council, who is in office for a long time, instead of being in rotation, ends up overlapping the president of the commission and coming into conflict with him, causing paralysis and crises in the institutions. secondly, unanimity should be abolished in all matters, since the right of veto can block any innovative process at any time. thirdly, the foreign policy must be unique and must be accompanied by a european military force which, by surpassing nato, will enable us to play a role which is not only autonomous but also balancing the unipolar and imperial domination which is present and looming in the world today.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr commissioner, these days we are watching our heads of state and government parade one by one before the united nations gallery. whoever does not march is europe. i think this image is enough to avoid making big speeches and, above all, to say what is not in this convention. in the end, this convention is the expression of a laborious institutional tinkering, difficult to explain, even more difficult to understand and, consequently, unpleasant. it is a complicated, complex and, i fear, not very functional job. there are undoubtedly improvements in the internal areas relating to european citizens or our lives - those which have been defined as 'collateral' areas - but the problem which this convention does not address and does not solve is that of defining the role, the responsibility, the means, the procedures for making europe not only what it already is - a great economic power - but what it should be, that is, a political co-actor and responsible for world affairs. we did not even try to answer that. the convention expresses the image of an introverted europe, an almost umbilical europe, which certainly cares about the welfare of its citizens but which gives itself no structures, procedures, commitments, nothing at all as regards its responsibilities which it also has beyond its borders. we are not even giving ourselves the means to respond to this need for europe, to this call for europe, to this demand for europe, which is so strong in so many parts of the world, starting with the near middle east and the southern shore of the mediterranean, to this need for european values, to be partners in a development that is substantially fairer, that is to say more based on human, civil and political rights. we condemn ourselves by this convention to be always and in any case - mr president, mr council representative, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome and fully agree with the contents of the report under discussion. we would certainly have liked the text proposed by the convention to be more progressive towards the process of integration, but we realize that the compromise reached is the only possible one and we must acknowledge this, sharing the approach given by president giscard d'estaing, who said at the opening of the convention: our unity is the reason for our existence. i believe that a text so agreed upon cannot easily be changed by the intergovernmental conference, except in a few marginal respects. the point on which we should concentrate our pressure on the intergovernmental conference is therefore one and the most important, namely the rules for the revision of the constitutional treaty. if we tie any amendment to the constitution to the unanimity of the 25 or 27 member states or, in the future, of a still greater number, we risk turning this great stage in europe's history into a stopover for its future and the end of its hopes.
mr president, i have two comments to make on the gil-robles/tsatsos report, which reflects the expectations but also the fears of this parliament. the first point concerns the identity of europe. i remember the words of a great liberal historian: because we can't not call ourselves christians. reference to christian roots could reinforce the secularism of a policy that continues to be threatened by the indifference and idolatry of power. but what we call for in order to unite must not divide europe. i am convinced that the reference to the human person and to peace, freedom and democracy, human rights and pluralism is the constitutional expression of the christian and democratic values which inspired the action of the founding fathers of the european community. the second point concerns the prospect of revising a compromise which the intergovernmental conference can improve without calling into question the institutional balance proposed by the convention. the report deplores the fact that the unanimity of the states continues to determine the process of revising the constitution, even in the long term. i think that the commission's view, as reiterated by commissioner barnier, that the igc should pave the way for more flexible revision procedures, which do not allow for the right of veto, at least as regards the non-fundamental provisions of the treaty, should be supported.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is necessary to make a start, after having congratulated the rapporteurs on their work. there was a long debate on whether it was necessary, appropriate and proper to introduce a reference to christian values or even to god in the context of the text under consideration and the text to be approved. i believe that, beyond the formal aspects - and i would not mind if there were a reference to christian values - and beyond what the verbal expressions may be, it is important to note that the text that has emerged, which is emerging in the course of its evolution, respects those values. i think the text shows a substantial respect for christian values: respect for human life and respect for human dignity are in fact reference points on which much work has been done in the convention. i think it is important to stress that, beyond the wording of the text, there is a reference to our history, to our life, which has been conditioned and shared by christian values. the steps taken to reach a convention, a constitution and new treaties have been useful in my view. i am not pessimistic, but i think that the work done, although slow, has been fruitful overall, although some progress can still be expected. i often think of what europe might have been like if the institutions that exist today had not existed, and i remember what our continent was essentially like 60 years ago. i must therefore say that what has been done - both in terms of the direct legitimization of citizens, the search for channels of consensus and the management of institutions and consensus - is to be considered positive overall. many argue that the citizens are still far away. perhaps these citizens should be more involved in the development of europe; it is perhaps up to us to recognize their rights and to ensure that, through an important source, namely the call for justified expenditure, effective and valid bureaucracy, there can be a link with civil society.
mr president, i would like to emphasize three points: the question of unanimity, the mention of god and christianity, the traditionally resident minorities. the work done by both the convention and the rapporteurs is certainly positive; i am therefore addressing the pessimists and those who always say no. i am saying that, compared to a complete constitution, we are obviously halfway there, but compared to nice, we have made steps forward which were and are giant steps. but this report also needs to be corrected, as president prodi has said in this house, and i share his view. the first point i would like to make is that of unanimity. in my view, requiring unanimity for even minor constitutional changes is surely closing the door to future developments. we are trying to be more forward-looking and more open, and in this respect i also share the spirit of amendment no 20, which i shall be voting in favour of. on the second question, namely the mention of god and christianity, i cannot understand the intransigent position of certain sections of this house, which is in fact contrary to the opinion of the vast majority of the population. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european parliament is given the opportunity to express its views on the matter. the third point concerns linguistic and cultural diversity and minority rights, which are included in amendment no 22 in recital h. i believe that the minorities which were included in the copenhagen criteria should also have a place in this report. i ask the italian presidency to make efforts to this end, before and during the igc, and to ensure that they are also mentioned in the convention.

mr president, i did not vote for the report, although i was in favour of the text adopted by the convention, in which i was a substitute, because this report excludes any reference to the christian roots of europe. in addition, there is an excessive propensity to limit the voting to unanimity, which is one of the values on which the european union was initially founded, even when it had another name. i believe that the unanimous vote is a bulwark in defence of the sovereignty of the states and in defence of that national interest which is so dear to the majority of italian political forces. i hope that the intergovernmental conference will substantially confirm the work of the convention, even against the wild attacks of president prodi, who is trying in every way to bring about its overthrow.
in writing. - (it) i am not satisfied with this resolution, which is too long and not easily understood by the uninitiated; the commission has also been ambiguous on a fundamental point, the revision procedure. it is not enough to deplore the continuation of the unanimity vote and the rejection of the european parliament's ratification power. parliament's demands should be made a central issue, since the only way to fill the gaps in the text of the convention is to ensure that a democratic method of ratification is in place to move forward. on this point, the rapporteurs and the majority of the parliament preferred to maintain a rigid and erroneous position: it is wrong to say that the revision procedure is part of the agreement concluded by the convention. this is practically the only point on which we are asking the intergovernmental conference to take a decision! why, then, did i decide to vote in favour of this resolution, which i do not like? because for the time being, it is necessary to send a clear message: the igc must not unilaterally reopen the essential points of the text adopted by the convention. that is what the resolution says. as from 4 october, if the igc decides to reopen the agreements, we will start fighting again about its content.
in writing. - (it) no one can deny the need for a european union with institutions that are more transparent and better defined in terms of their respective competences and roles and, therefore, less bureaucratic and more capable of intervening quickly, as needed, in a europe that would entrust the individual member states with matters of an exclusively internal nature to deal only with the major problems affecting society as a whole and our continent in particular, all of which are the objectives that form the basis of the text developed during the eighteen months of work of the european convention. we welcome the fact that the convention has established that europe must be a union of nation states, respectful of the languages, cultures and traditions of each of its components, and that from this union, strengthened by a constitutional treaty, must emerge a political, economic and social project capable of protecting our children, but also the rights of the children of others: a europe which, while defending democracy, freedom and peace for its peoples, is also able to promote freedom, peace and justice in other parts of the world. it is precisely in order to ensure that democracy is respected that we call on the intergovernmental conference to welcome the proposal for a commissioner with voting rights for each member state, recalling how the peace of westphalia introduced the concept of equality between states, beyond the number of inhabitants. in writing. - (it) we voted against a very complex draft constitution which is difficult to explain and understand: it is difficult to imagine how its different mechanisms, dialectics and balance of power will work in reality. a very complex institutional organization is by its very nature not secular except for the priests of the bureaucracy who control the reality of every day: the reality that is not controllable and cannot function. although there is no denying that progress has been made compared to the present situation, it is in the field of home affairs and related matters. but there are also regressions, such as the insertion of article 51 (1), the declaration annexed to the treaty, which confirms the status of religious bureaucracies. in fact, the union is being forced to engage in regular dialogue with the churches, thus violating the principle of secularism, the principle of separation between public institutions and religious organisations. this is a sanction for the power of the churches to interfere, which is likely to constitute an obscurantist obstacle to the right of european citizens to decide freely on ethical and scientific questions. the union is also prevented from examining or reconsidering the situation of the churches in the member states, thus ensuring the preservation of the privileges they enjoy thanks to the concordat signed with franco in spain, mussolini in italy, salazar in portugal and hitler in germany. mr president, i have the impression that too many speakers in this house refer to the roadmap without having read it and then, because of their ignorance of the document, draw an ambiguous lesson. the roadmap is a three-step plan. the premise of all this is the very title of the first phase ending terror and violence, normalizing palestinian life, building palestinian institutions and it aims to undertake an immediate and unconditional cessation of violence by the palestinians. this is the crucial point, without which everything else becomes ambiguous, uncertain or vaguely predicative. it is quite absurd to ask israel, in the absence of a palestinian cessation of terrorism, to take other or different initiatives from those it has taken so far. no european state would fail to respond to a series of terrorist attacks, particularly against defenseless civilians, by force and legal repression. i am not convinced by the calls to keep arafat where he is, because he is the legitimate representative of the palestinian people, when everyone recognizes that there are no democratic institutions within the palestinian community. arafat has failed camp david and he has failed abu mazen. i think it would be more serious on the european side to take a very strict attitude towards his behaviour, which is the precondition for a different approach.
mr president, listening to and participating in this debate, after fifty years and seven wars in the middle east, we feel that we are running the risk of each of us becoming a little master of democracy and the budget, capable of applying measures and prejudices which are only ours. it is true that we may not always have appreciated the role played by arafat, as we have almost never appreciated the role played by sharon, but we cannot forget that president arafat was democratically elected president of a people who have no country, no territory, no peace. it 's a sin to forget . a sin of presumption, a sin of reticence and a sin of superficiality. if we condemn with firmness and with absolute sincerity the terror against israel - and we condemn it with all our strength, with all our indignation - we must condemn with equal force and indignation the media lynching of a democratically elected president of a people. we ask the presidency not to confine itself to denouncing exile as an unacceptable outcome. the indecency of the incitement to murder, which was made by a minister in the israeli government and by an authoritative newspaper such as the jerusalem post, must be denounced. what can europe do? just put hamas on the blacklist? that's not enough. three things must be firmly established: we must demand an end to the blockade of the palestinian territories. we must demand the cessation of all settlement-related activities. we must demand the demolition of the security wall, which is de facto annexation and illegal under international law. europe must do its utmost, and one possibility is to send a force on the ground to make a decisive and concrete contribution to ensuring that mutual obligations are respected. the only alternative to peace is peace, but for that to be possible europe must do something.
madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr urso, commissioners, the first game played in cancún was a game of trade agreements. i believe that if the wto is to survive, this must remain the main theme of the negotiations. but essentially, the game was political, based on a paradox - repeatedly mentioned by commissioner lamy in his meetings with the european parliament delegation - that at the beginning almost all the discussions were about agriculture, which accounts for 20% of international trade. and it's true, it's a paradox that we've all contributed heavily to creating. the cancún summit was a propaganda game, and the heirs of metternich and talleyrand need hardly be told how important propaganda is in international politics. we europeans have offered our adversaries, if they were any, a formidable argument and propaganda on a silver platter to international public opinion. it was said that there were red lines concerning agriculture, the general abolition of the odious export subsidies and a ceiling on the green box subsidies, which, in theory, should not distort markets. it was said that rather than cross this red line, it was better that the negotiations should fail, as they did. the fact that an industrial power such as the european union is showing itself with these remorse, with these red lines, is one of the reasons why we are today mourning a failure that weighs on the european union much more than it does on, for example, the united states. and i won't have time to explain why, in my opinion, this is happening. the very fact that the commissioner for agriculture - and i am not sure about mr fischler - is here today, on an equal footing with commissioner lamy, to explain to us what has happened in cancún, is an anomaly, it is the european paradox on agricultural policy. of course, we say that european agricultural protectionism, after all, is not so different from that of the united states; in fact, perhaps with the reform of the european agricultural policy we have managed to overtake the united states. the japanese do worse with rice than we do. but we are thinking of europe's interests! the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. they were doing it for instrumental reasons, to cover the tariffs of close to 90 percent on indian textiles. that may be true, but how do we explain to these people that we want new rules for investment? we ask developing countries for rules on competition, on public procurement, and then we continue to subsidize the export of meat or rice or whatever. we could then have a long discussion, madam president, about everything but arms. we have postponed the final abolition of tariffs on rice, bananas and sugar until 2010. is that all we can offer the developing countries? the president interrupted the speaker.

- the next item is the report (a5-0292/2003) by mr lisi, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the reduction of emissions of volatile organic compounds due to the use of organic solvents in decorative paints and varnishes and in products for automotive retouching, and amending directive 1999/13/ec (com (2002) 750 - c5-0632/2002 - 2002/0301 (cod)).
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as the commissioner has already said, the proposal we are discussing today is a proposal for the reduction of organic solvents in paints and it is a proposal that is part of a broader environmental strategy, namely the attempt to meet national emission ceilings, in this case for voc emissions. this proposal can therefore be regarded as one of the necessary steps towards the overall improvement of the quality of the air we breathe, and we can only express our full support for it. it is precisely because we firmly believe in this objective - which, as the commissioner said, was brought so dramatically to our attention this summer - that we know that it is in our interest and in the interest of future generations to ensure effective environmental protection. for these reasons, from the very beginning of this legislative process, i have set my work as rapporteur on a very simple line of reasoning: the achievement of the objective of that directive is closely linked to the guarantee of the quality of the products covered by the directive, namely paints. the reasoning is very simple: there is a threshold below which the quality of these products available on the market is bound to fall inexorably, and if the quality - let us not forget that these are most often paints which are used as protective films, especially against atmospheric agents - falls below an acceptable threshold, we would have the opposite effect to what we want. in the medium and long term, there would be a proliferation of applications for these paints and therefore, inevitably, an increase in emissions. i have therefore tried to strike that balance between what is technically possible, without falling too far below an acceptable level of quality, and what must be done, for the reasons just mentioned. i shall now briefly review the main points of the directive. as regards the objective of the directive as such, there have been different reactions from colleagues, especially on the health of workers and on certain national laws to protect them. the commission has again made it clear this evening that the objective of the directive is environmental protection, without prejudice to or alteration of existing measures at national or community level to protect the health of workers, as is also stated in recital 14. some colleagues have tabled amendments in this direction in the plenary, but after the commission's clarifications, i would reiterate that we should reject this enlargement proposal by voting against the amendments, in particular amendments nos 2, 10, 16, 49, 54, 80 and 82. as regards amendment no 84, which helps us to define and clarify the aim of the directive, i am in favour of it. there is also a problem with labelling. personally, i agree with the commission's proposal to entrust a committee with the labelling requirements for the products concerned, especially because, in the light of the many efforts made by the industry to provide clear information to consumers, this committee can be enriched by the experience of existing good practice. i do not think it is useful to impose any further requirements, and that is why i am asking the house to vote against amendment no 20. as regards the so-called substitution principle, as provided for in amendment no 23, i do not think it applies in this context because the undertakings and the industrial system to which we are addressing need data and certainty - what we indicate in this directive - precisely in order to be able to invest in research and develop the formulas necessary to achieve the objectives. there are also many amendments concerning the thresholds, i.e. the percentages which the commission has proposed and which parliament, in the committee on the environment, has amended. i don't go through all of them. i think these are proposals which, by bringing us below the threshold of equilibrium i mentioned earlier, should be rejected. finally, i would like to mention other matters concerning minor derogations for historic vehicles and buildings, monuments and so on, which the commission has accepted and which i ask the house to approve, and some amendments concerning the definition of solvents and their boiling point, which i think will be the subject of further discussion this evening. finally, i would like to thank all the members for the very valuable contribution they have made to the committee.
the rapporteur. mr president, while the commissioner is taking note of this, i would like to say that i agree with what mrs corbey has said. that is exactly the meaning of the proposal in the list of votes proposed by the rapporteur: amendment no 11 and amendment no 13 are in contradiction. i would point out to mr corbey, however, that this is a mess made by our committee. i therefore ask that amendment no 11 be supported and approved and that amendment no 13 be voted against, precisely in order to establish a definition of 'diluents' which is consistent with the rest of the legislation.
