amended. these requirements related primarily to the verification of solvency, the auditing arrangements, the adequacy of the administrative and accounting procedures and the internal control mechanisms. in order to respect the procedural rights of complainants, in the second half of july 2003 my services wrote to all complainants, as well as to petitioners who had not lodged a formal complaint, explaining the results of this preliminary analysis and indicating the intention of the services to propose that the commission should close the case. my services are now completing their analysis of the responses received from complainants before preparing a proposal for a final decision on the case by the college of commissioners. in accordance with parliament's wish, we shall be seeking to take this decision as quickly as possible, before the end of october 2003. most of the comments received related to the past situation, before the introduction of the fsma 2000. as i have already explained to this parliament and to complainants, the objective of infringement proceedings under community law is to ensure or restore the compatibility of national law with community law, not to rule on the past compatibility or incompatibility of the prior regime. that is a task – i say this in particular to mr perry – for national courts to address. from the beginning of our investigations into this complex and sensitive file, we have repeatedly made it clear to complainants that any action for damages must be undertaken before national courts. indeed, i understand that, currently, such an action has been instigated by a group of complainants before uk courts. therefore, in accordance with the relevant case-law of the court of justice, the task of the commission is to examine the compatibility of the new regime with the requirements of the insurance directives. during our investigations, access to the file has been a hotly-debated subject. from my opening comments i trust members will recognise that, throughout the conduct of its enquiries, the commission has always sought to keep parliament fully informed to the greatest extent possible. as the report by the petitions committee recognises, the commission is bound by point 1.5 of annex iii to the framework agreement between parliament and the commission. this provides that information on infringement procedures remains confidential until a final commission decision is made. clearly, after a final decision, the commission will make documents available, subject to any remaining confidentiality constraints. assuming a decision is taken by the college of commissioners to close the case, the commission will, in response to a formal request from parliament, provide file access in accordance with the framework agreement subject to the respect of any confidentiality requirements imposed by the uk on documents which it has prepared. furthermore, general public access to the file will be granted in accordance with the terms of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001. lastly, i would like briefly to touch upon an issue which, in the light of the extensive contacts we have enjoyed with parliament, i had hoped would not be necessary. there are those who imply that, in the conduct of its enquiries, the commission has exposed itself to accusations of maladministration and unnecessary delay. let me be clear. despite the complexity and sensitivity of the case and the considerable volume of correspondence received, the commission has always sought to carry out its investigations as rapidly as possible, consistent with due process and thorough investigation, while subject to real constraints on resources. petition 318/2000 runs to seven lever-arch a4 files. the commission has carefully examined complaints and entered into substantial and sustained communication with complainants. two press releases were issued and sent to all complainants and petitioners. furthermore, as i have just said, in accordance with the procedural safeguards for complainants, the commission services have written to all complainants informing them of the results of the commission's preliminary analysis and seeking their comments. finally, an allegation of commission maladministration has recently been examined by mr diamandouros, the european ombudsman, and rejected by him. in particular, may i respectfully remind parliament that mr. diamandouros specifically considered allegations of commission maladministration regarding access to files and examination of the current regulatory regime, as opposed to the past, pre-fsma 2000 regime. in both cases mr diamandouros found no maladministration. i have spoken somewhat longer than i would have preferred but, given the importance of the case and the tragic stories that surround it, i wanted to be crystal clear in my statement to this parliament. in closing, let me again assure you, president, of the willingness of the commission to cooperate fully with parliament. this cooperation is, however, always subject to the legal constraints imposed on the commission. as on previous occasions, i would be very happy to try and answer any further questions you might have.

mr president, the relationship between the free market and the professions is not a simple and natural one - that is also clear from the words of commissioner monti - and you know that in my committee, together with mr lehne, mr zappalà and other colleagues, we have been working on a directive on professional qualifications for over a year and so we are well aware of the typification and the exceptional nature of the problem of the professions. the freelancer offers a service independently, which requires a very high level of knowledge, which is difficult to assess. for this reason, professional work is governed by an ethic which oversees the relationships between professionals and between professionals and the client, between the professional and society as a whole. the behaviour of the professional responds to an ethics which corresponds to precise duties, to the needs of the service which the professional himself determines, and therefore the ethics represents the premise with respect to the rules, as a way of interpreting and applying. an american sociologist, fredson, in his writings shows that the system of professions responds to the work ethic, which must find the right balance and here i agree with commissioner monti with respect to profit and the execution of orders, typical instead of the market and bureaucracy: so there is an exception. the maintenance of this delicate and difficult balance requires a special status for the selfemployed, not in his own interest but in the interest of the community. article 5 of the charter of rights provides for freedom of profession, that is to say the right to pursue a profession freely chosen and accepted. and professional freedom is different from freedom to do business. as the treaty states, the general interest mission of the professions can also justify restrictions, commissioner monti, on the competition rules. legislative provisions and ethical rules may therefore derogate from competition law in particular cases: in the case of professional rates, which may also be compulsory in comparison with those fixed by the state; in the case of the exercise of the profession in an integrated form; in the case of advertising, where the codes of ethics may exclude the possibility of expressing judgments about a colleague among the various professions; in the case of membership of social security institutions; the obligation to join pension funds, which is allowed; in the case of exclusivity in favour of certain regulated professions. in conclusion, mr president, rules which are necessary in the specific context of each profession to ensure the impartiality, competence, integrity and responsibility of the means of the profession itself are not considered to restrict competition. the activities of the professions must therefore ensure that the professional and his product, the service he provides, contribute to providing useful solutions to the challenges we are facing, in order to protect the general interest of the community. the standards which are established by the professional categories under their responsibility, in order to guarantee the quality of services, ensure that the standards themselves are observed in accordance with the canons of professionalism and professional ethics. in this sense i believe - and this is also clear from the words of commissioner monti - that in this way, and only because of the fragile balance between profit and ethics that we have to determine, there is a correct relationship between free markets, competition, rules and ethics in general.
mr president, commissioner, whenever liberalisation is called for, whenever it is called a necessity or when liberalisation is pursued, the question of specificity is put to those who propose liberalisation. when we talk about liberalizing a sector which provides a service to the public, we say that this sector has its own specific features which must be taken into account and that the market rules which should apply to other economic and industrial sectors cannot apply to this sector. the same applies to the professions: every profession has its own specificity. but the liberal professions, the liberal professions have the characteristic in europe, and even in some countries such as italy, of being the least free of all. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the fact that today in europe the free professions - the so-called free professions - are in fact based on closed corporations which exercise a collective monopoly by defending positions of income, creating obstacles for young people who want to take up those professions. i'll give you an example of the order of journalists. in italy, a french journalist, who claims to have extensive professional experience, recently came to italy his publishing house bought newspapers in italy and was appointed editor of one of these newspapers: the professional order of journalists rebelled and got that person, a frenchman, not to carry out the same activity in italy. the liberalisation of professional services, as called for by the italian antitrust authority, is necessary to help make many european industrial sectors more competitive, those that rely more on having competence and a competitive capacity on international markets. the october conference is welcome, provided that it is clear that the balance in europe today is achieved if the monopolistic, corporate power of the professional orders is overcome.

the rapporteur. mr president, the green paper presented by commissioner busquin, which parliament particularly welcomed, reiterated the strategic importance of space policy for the independence, security and economic growth of a europe that wants to remain at the forefront of scientific research and technological innovation. in recent months, a turning point has been reached with the constituent convention, which has recognised a specific role for space policy, thus providing a legal basis for community programmes and consolidating the strategy launched with the extraordinary success of the galileo project. however, we are aware that the commission has also given a concrete response to the unprecedented crisis which has hit the space sector, particularly launchers, affecting the activities of many industries and accentuating distortions on the world market. the space asset is crucial for the concentration of expertise, research and technologies that characterise the development of the knowledge economy. it is a resource that cannot be wasted and the commission and the esa council have shown themselves to be fully aware of this. the european parliament's report stresses the role of esa and the national agencies and welcomes the framework agreement, which the european community and esa have signed and which parliament had strongly urged. this framework agreement confirms esa's irreplaceable role in organising research and technological and industrial supply. this role needs to be clarified in the presence of a european space programme which also redefines the commission's responsibilities in relation to public demand and new initiatives requiring political representativeness and specific institutional competence. the european union's role as a major player on the international scene, involving all the countries of the union, does not exclude the need for international cooperation: the european union is also committed to the development of a european space policy, a cooperation which concerns primarily the united states - think of the international space station - but which also covers other countries, from russia to japan to china itself. however, we must be aware that the quality of international agreements - especially when it comes to space - depends on the quality of scientific, industrial and even financial contributions. europe's ambitions must be supported by public resources, as is the case throughout the world, and by a more active organisation of common policies, from agriculture to telecommunications, from the environment to transport. private initiative needs to be encouraged, as is the case with galileo, but it should be noted that the goal of doubling the space budget in ten years would not close the gap with the united states, but would still be halfway there. space science has played a pioneering role. the quality of human resources and basic research therefore deserve greater attention. the future of european space policy depends on this attention. for these reasons, we believe that the next research framework programme should devote more financial resources to the space sector, and in this context guarantee a share for small and mediumsized enterprises, which are becoming the indispensable support for new innovative enterprises. the last consideration concerns the convention's orientation towards an armaments agency open to all member states, under the structured cooperation method. this approach can contribute to the implementation of the industrial and technological asset. it is not a question - and this must be made clear - of militarizing space, but rather of recognizing that we are discussing dual activities, both civilian and military, and together a strategy for european security which cannot be abandoned to the temptations of american unilateralism. to avoid misunderstandings, the report refers to the un resolution on preventing an arms race in space and to the convention itself, which aims to promote peace and contribute to the security and sustainable development of the earth. we are now awaiting the white paper, after having discussed the green paper, and this expectation is based on the positive assessment we have expressed so far, and it is, in our view, also the expectation of the world of science and of the world of european industry.

the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, last december the commission adopted a plan to bring about a major reform of the merger control system. the reform is the result of a review process which started in 2000 and which is based on a new draft regulation, which i hope the council will adopt soon so that it can enter into force in time for the next enlargement. the reform is designed to leave the merits of the current system intact. what we are proposing is a series of significant improvements to the current system, aimed above all at further improving the system in terms of transparency and consistency of merger control. at the same time, beyond the regulation, we are improving the commission's decision-making process, making our investigations of proposed mergers more accurate, more targeted and better supported by sound economic analysis, and taking full account of the rights of the parties to the concentration and of third parties; we are also aware that the court of first instance requires a high standard of proof from the commission. this has obvious consequences for the way we work. the merger control reform package consists of a proposal for a new community merger regulation and a draft notice containing guidelines on the assessment of horizontal mergers. in addition to the preparation of these documents, the last few months have seen the adoption of many measures concerning the staff and internal organisation of the directorate-general for competition, in particular the introduction of a new figure - the chief competition economist - and of arrangements such as peer review panels to have greater freshness of verification in the course of analyses. the proposal for a new merger regulation has three main features: first, clarification of the substantive criterion for assessing the possible effects of concentrations on competition; secondly, questions of jurisdiction, where we propose to streamline the system of referrals between the commission and the member states; thirdly and lastly, a number of procedural changes are proposed to give a little more flexibility in the timing of investigations and notifications of concentrations, and in aligning the powers of inquiry provided for in the merger regulation with those laid down in regulation no 1/2003 which, as you know, concerns the application of articles 81 and 82 of the treaty.
the rapporteur. mr president, mr commissioner, over the last three years the commission has embarked on a thorough review of the community antitrust system. as you have said, commissioner, the proposal for a new regulation on mergers between undertakings which we are examining today is one of the most important steps in this process. the regulation in question the previous one has become increasingly central to the competition policy of the european union, and has had important merits in offering merger companies a one-stop-shop perspective and predetermined timelines. however, the increasing integration of markets and the consequent increase in the number and importance of merger cases examined by the commission have brought the existing rules to a critical point, as evidenced by the recent judgments of the court of justice which rejected certain commission decisions, to which you, mr commissioner, also referred. hence the need to reform the existing rules, to which the commission has been quick to respond. the three crucial points - as you said, commissioner monti - in the commission proposal and also in the parliament's report concern the substantive criterion, the judicial aspects and the procedures. on the question of jurisdiction, the scope of the regulation and therefore the allocation of cases between the authorities of the member states, there is a need to solve the problem of multiple notifications, which will become even more burdensome for the companies involved after enlargement, which contrast multiple notifications with the one-stop-shop principle, which is what we all refer to. in this proposal the commission has abandoned both the possibility of intervening on thresholds, probably because of the complications this entailed, and the so-called "3+" principle, which was also present in the green paper and on which parliament had expressed itself in the berenguer fuster report, expressing a positive assessment. this positive assessment was reiterated by the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, which defined a criterion of automaticity in the possibility of referral to the commission even at the pre-notification stage, when dealing with a notification in several countries. parliament therefore reiterated the line already taken in the debate on the green paper. as regards the principle, the substantive criterion has so far proved effective; but there was a lot of discussion. some people proposed that we should move to substantial lessening of competition, a principle used in the united states and some other member states. i had reacted to the commission's proposal to add a paragraph to article 2 which should have defined the dominance criterion better. i was proposing a reformulation, but the economic committee decided at this point to propose that the commission should leave things as they are, thus giving a positive value to the criterion and its effectiveness, which has been demonstrated so far. as regards the procedural aspects, i should like to say a few words about the powers of inquiry. as a committee we have proposed that some of the provisions in the proposal for a regulation be reduced, because we believe that a criterion of proportionality makes it absolutely unnecessary to level the powers of investigation provided for in the case of cartels with those provided for in the case of mergers, because they are completely different cases. the merger is business as usual and so we feel there should be no presumption of infringement. we believe that parliament should be firm on this, all the more so since the commission is quite legitimately proposing powers for itself. we believe that parliament should have a more assertive position on this. two points to conclude: first, the role of the worker. the debate showed the proposal and concern of some colleagues, particularly socialists, to take account of the possible employment impact of mergers, even making eligibility conditional on the preservation of jobs. we believe that this clause cannot be inserted here because it risks being in conflict with the logic of the regulation, which is to ensure a competitive single market, precisely in order to increase employment. the regulation already contains some rules on the issue of participation and information of workers; other european legislation provides for other rules on this very point. i do not think it is necessary to include these elements here, and i would ask my colleagues, and in particular mr berenguer fuster and mr van den burg, to consider: the fact that these amendments are rejected cannot affect the vote on the whole of the measure. i am also voting in favour of mr schmidt's amendment.

commission. – mr president, honourable members, i address you today in the knowledge that a compromise package aimed at securing a first reading agreement is on the table. accurate monitoring of greenhouse gas emissions is vital to give us an overview of how effective eu policies are in reducing greenhouse gas emissions and what more needs to be done to meet our kyoto targets. this decision is an important further step in implementing the kyoto protocol and in ensuring that the community delivers on all its commitments under the protocol. let me extend my thanks to the rapporteur, mr sacconi, and his colleagues in the european parliament, who have worked hard to enable a first reading agreement to be reached on this decision. reaching agreement at first reading stage will enable this decision to enter into force quickly and be implemented by the member states and would be a further concrete demonstration of the community's commitment to addressing the problems of climate change. finally, of course, i warmly encourage members of the european parliament to support this possible deal.
the rapporteur. mr president, since 1992, the international community, or at least a large part of it, has been reacting and fighting against one of the greatest environmental and economic challenges facing humanity: climate change. we know that it is the most important issue in the world in the field of environmental sustainability and that it is having disastrous effects not only on the climate but also on ecosystems and living species. the union accepted the challenge in may 2002 by ratifying the kyoto protocol, thus demonstrating that the fight against climate change is one of its strategic priorities. by the decision to ratify the protocol, the member states agreed to fulfil the obligations of the protocol jointly. to ensure that the community as a whole can meet its legally binding international obligations, they have agreed to different emission limitation and reduction targets for each member state. member states therefore remain responsible for reporting annual emissions data. the proposal for a decision we are about to vote on therefore provides the framework for the community and its member states to ensure that their obligations in the field of reporting and accounting for emissions are met by improving the quality and accuracy of the information provided on policies and measures adopted, as well as on emissions and removals of all greenhouse gases, without forgetting the methodological aspects. based on the structure of the kyoto protocol and the guidelines of the un convention, the reporting obligations vary depending on whether the information is to be reported on an annual or a periodic basis. moreover, in the context of the convention and the kyoto protocol, two provisions are essential and necessary to fulfil the commitments made: first, the implementation and periodic updating of national programmes to limit or reduce gas emissions; second, transparent monitoring of actual and projected emissions. the vote tomorrow will oblige the member states to determine and report to the commission, by 15 january each year, the actual and provisional gas emissions data which will enable progress to be assessed and annual reports to be prepared by the community in accordance with its international obligations. the limited amendments made by the committee on the environment to the legislative proposal were aimed at making the mechanism even more binding and efficient, especially in the light of the latest discouraging data that greenhouse gas emissions in the european union are expected to increase for the second year in a row. as mrs wallström has already said, in the informal negotiations with the council and the commission, following the opinion of the committee on the environment, it was possible to reach an agreement on these amendments, which incorporated the substance of our amendments, including the most significant ones from a political point of view, such as those concerning the necessarily and compulsorily supplementary nature of the use of flexible mechanisms compared with the internal action plans that each state must set and implement in order to achieve its greenhouse gas reduction targets. that is why we are putting a package of agreed amendments to the vote in the house tomorrow. i hope that this parliament will really give a boost to the measure, allowing the states to move quickly to adapt to these rules. i think it is also a good political signal in the run-up to an important meeting in milan next december, at which we hope the wider international community will ratify the kyoto protocol.
the rapporteur. mr president, with today's debate and tomorrow's vote, the elearning programme is officially born. it is therefore time to congratulate those who have generated this programme. the mother of the programme is certainly the european commission, which, with its communication of may 2000, launched the first elearning pilot action, an action which, however, did not have its own budget line at that time. tomorrow, after two years of painstaking interinstitutional work, the first multiannual programme on e-learning will be voted on. we can thus understand that there was a father of this provision, as well as a mother. the role of the father is becoming increasingly difficult to assign, and here too it remains a question mark, but i would say that it should be divided in half between parliament and the council. the council's efforts, both under the greek presidency and, more finally, under the italian presidency, have enabled parliament to find a significant outlet for its demands and thus to allocate to the elearning programme an amount at least sufficient to start it. this multiannual programme, which is in addition to the other historical programmes such as socrates and leonardo, meets the requirements of the lisbon, stockholm and barcelona european councils. the main objectives are to combat fragmentation by means of the implementation of digital literacy methods, the promotion of virtual campuses, school twinning via the internet, the promotion and dissemination of good practice and cooperation between community programmes and action instruments promoted at national level. the budget for the programme has been increased to eur 44 million, thanks to what i can call intensive interinstitutional work. as regards the electronic twinning of european schools, in line with the objectives adopted in the previous resolution of the european parliament, i wanted to stress once again that teacher training remains a priority. i would like us to reflect once again on the fact that in 2003, on average, 90% of primary schools, 98% of secondary schools, 99% of vocational and technical schools in the member states were connected to the internet, but only 39% of teachers, 50% of secondary school teachers and 58% of vocational and technical school teachers actually used the internet as a teaching tool. so there is a great need for this programme. in reality, these averages conceal dramatic differences between member states: the average figure for denmark is about 70%, as opposed to greece's figure of less than 9%. these figures, which are already very clear, suggest two conclusions: the first concerns the use of the internet as a tool to facilitate learning. it is not just a question of the availability of infrastructure and school equipment but also a problem of teacher training, mentality and school organisation. the second conclusion concerns the use of technological resources. the aim can really be to exchange good practice between teachers from different member states, both at methodological and didactic level, for example through the activation of virtual classrooms. for these reasons, i have tried to emphasise in the report how the elearning programme will have to place greater emphasis on finding the most effective ways for teachers to integrate the use of the internet in their teaching and encourage the dissemination of good practice in this area. i would like to thank the commission and all those who have worked for the success of the work.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the jarzembowski report stresses the importance of the accelerated development of rail freight networks, with particular attention to cross-border problems. in this context, i would like to stress the unsustainable situation of the italian railway line between savona and the french border. it is an axis linking the west of the liguria region with the côte d'azur. this single track line - i stress, single track - constitutes a bottleneck for rail freight and passenger traffic, causing substantial damage to the economy of the area which is linked to tourism, olive growing and the production of flowers and delicacies. the single track also increases safety risks. the effects of this inadequacy of the railway system are felt on motorway traffic, with serious congestion and pollution problems in an area with a strong tourist vocation. there's been talk of doubling the line since the '50s, when i was still wearing shorts. since then, the reality has not changed and the increase in traffic volumes makes everything much more critical, at the limit of sustainability, due to the continuous delays that accumulate damaging also the adjacent french trunk. recent works have moved upstream some sections of the railway line, which is still single track and runs along the coast, and is subject to marine erosion. these interventions have made matters worse because they have created further bottlenecks. i conclude by expressing my hope that, as part of the relaunch of international networks in the european union, the problem will be solved as quickly as possible by 1 january 2006, the date set for the opening of rail networks to all types of freight services.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am speaking in order to acknowledge, as chairman of the committee on legal affairs, the work done by the vice-president, mr rothley. this proposal for a directive has been put forward with great stubbornness and intelligence by mr rothley, and i want to acknowledge that to him in this house. we are particularly grateful to him because this directive is the result of article 192, which i particularly like, since it is an indirect legislative initiative, which sees parliament as the protagonist and also reaffirms the right of initiative of parliament and the members of the european parliament. this leads, in such a sensitive area, to more effective european citizenship, because, as mr rothley said, it makes it easier to take out or sign a short-term policy for a temporary stay in another member state and short-term insurance for a vehicle purchased outside the member state of residence of the owner. the result is that it will be easier to buy a car in any country of the union where the conditions are most favourable. i believe that this is of interest to many european citizens, because of the single insurance market which commissioner bolkestein spoke about and which is thus being established, and that it is therefore a valuable and useful piece of information for the european community as a whole. the most sensitive point in the report - which has already been underlined, but i would like to reiterate - concerns the higher amounts of guarantee provided for by the member states. the commission had provided for an amount of eur 1 million per victim in the case of damage to persons and eur 500 000 per claim in the case of damage to property. we believe that the amounts of eur 5 million per claim for personal injury and eur 2 million for damage to property are more appropriate and flexible and can provide a meeting point. i would like to formally acknowledge this compromise to mr rothley, because he has taken account of the different situations existing in the insurance markets, once again to give priority to a single insurance market. on the other hand, he also met the legal costs. it was not appropriate at this stage to extend insurance cover to injuries suffered by pedestrians and cyclists as a result of an accident involving them, because the matter is even more delicate and i think it could be regulated by an ad hoc regulatory instrument. if, as commissioner bolkestein has acknowledged, the work of reconciling parliament and the commission has been good and useful, i hope that the council and the commission will accept our amendments and that such an important directive will help to bring european citizens closer together in a common citizenship. i hope very much that this will be the case, because the compromise reached represents a high point of balance, which i hope the commission will take into account.
mr president, commissioner, the internal market in insurance must be completed by removing the barriers which still exist in this sector. it is no coincidence that the european parliament has asked the commission to submit a proposal to update the rules on car insurance, in order to ensure that the right of union citizens to live, travel and work without problems in any member state of the union itself is a reality. the proposal for a fifth directive on car rcds will certainly have the effect of modernising and improving european rules in this area. first, it will be easier to take out a short-term policy for a temporary stay in another member state and short-term insurance for a vehicle purchased outside the member state of residence of the owner. consumers will thus be able to buy a car more easily in any eu country where they find the best conditions, and this will help to stimulate cross-border competition. the directive also aims to update the limits on the minimum levels of cover for motorists. it therefore allows insured persons to change insurance more quickly. another objective is to improve the protection of pedestrians involved in accidents. finally, the directive allows citizens to obtain from their current insurer a statement of claims in which they have been involved, in order to be able to negotiate a new contract with another insurer. as regards minimum levels of cover, it is essential to avoid that they are too high, beyond all reasonable necessity. if this were to happen, the cost would inevitably be passed on to consumers, with significant increases in insurance policy prices. the negative impact would be particularly evident in some countries, including italy, where premium increases are already giving rise to a particularly heated debate. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft budget for the financial year. i therefore give the proposal a positive opinion; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner barnier, ladies and gentlemen, this is a report that photographs a problem, exposes a risk and outlines some solutions. the problem is the lurs, the still too wide gap between commitments and payments in the field of the structural funds, but also in other fields. rals are a composite phenomenon: there are physiological and pathological adrs; it is the latter that must be acted upon. the risk is not only that the regions concerned will lose structural funds; the biggest risk is the loss of credibility of cohesion policy in the european union. we know - and we are convinced - that the union, and even more so the enlarged union, needs an effective, strengthened and modern cohesion policy. the solutions we have outlined and on which we seem to have a good understanding with commissioner barnier, who is always ready for dialogue and discussion with us, can be divided into two groups: the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation in the community. the first of these concerns the adjustment of the level of payments entered in the budget. of course, this availability of resources must be accompanied by a more functional partnership between the commission and governments, between governments and regions, and between regions and subregional and local authorities. it is also urgent to step up the work of accompanying the new member states, which is already being carried out by the european commission. as regards the medium-term solutions, it is appropriate that the commission should present its guidelines for the regulation for the next programming period as soon as possible, in order to redefine the objectives and the methods of future application in a clear and easily understandable way. to this end, we believe that the following is necessary: first, emphasis should be placed on the commission's strategic role, which should be centred on the definition of development priorities, the compliance of actions with those priorities and the monitoring of the effectiveness of implementation systems, while member states should be given responsibility for implementation and management; secondly, to ensure simplicity, clarity and precision, and it therefore seems essential, in the context of this simplification objective, to unify the funds and to entrust the management of this single fund to a single commission department; thirdly, to provide for programming to be defined in the framework of a partnership between the commission and the member state; fourthly, to give the monitoring committee a wider role so that decisions on the programme and programme changes can be taken by the monitoring committee; finally, the measures to encourage the implementation of the actions, such as the n+2 clause for automatic decommitment, but also the bonus reserve for positive performance, should be maintained. i would like to conclude by addressing the question of automatic disengagement. the next 31 december is near and there is a new deadline. we believe that the rule should be maintained for the next few years as well, since it has undoubtedly had an important deterrent function. and yet, as commissioner barnier is well aware, in many situations, regions and national governments have taken shortcuts to certify 100 per cent of spending and to avoid the loss of funds. we ask commissioner barnier to exercise the strictest vigilance on this matter and at the same time we urge him to prevent the resources released by the so-called 'side projects' from being spent for purposes other than regional and national programming. i'll end with an example. if the italian government - to speak of my home - receives transport funds to build transport infrastructure in the south of italy and then, after having freed up resources with the shore projects, gives that saving to infrastructure in the north, we have to intervene to prevent that from happening. i hope that parliament will give this report a very broad support, because that would give the guidelines contained in it a very important political value. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, despite repeated calls from many quarters for the defence of human rights to be limited to the abolition of the death penalty, in recent years we have seen not only an increase in capital sentences in some countries but also the hardening of the systems of execution by barbaric methods. in calling for at least a moratorium on the death penalty, the national alliance would like to recall, by way of example only and on the basis of the forcibly partial data provided by amnesty international for 2002, that in iran, saudi arabia and sudan alone there were 113, 48 and 40 executions respectively, not to mention the 1,060 executed in china. in this context, while we support the urgency of a moratorium on the death penalty, we must also call for the european union and the united nations to intervene in relation to those countries where penalties are applied which are not linked to secular systems but to fundamentalist cultures or traditions of whatever origin. it is also necessary that, while upholding the right to religious freedom for every individual, it should be firmly proclaimed that the application of sharia law, within a state or in part of a state, cannot be accepted by the member states of the european union. for this reason, the moratorium on the death penalty must also be accompanied by sanctions that europe must impose on those governments which, by not accepting the moratorium, continue to apply the death penalty by means of cruel methods such as stoning. one of the desirable sanctions could be the suspension of economic relations with these countries: i am not saying that we should not continue to help people wherever possible, but that we should stop trading - the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report i am about to present concerns the commission's proposal for a council directive on compensation to victims of crime. this initiative follows the green paper on compensation for victims of crime, with which the commission started to promote the debate on this subject in september 2001, which was the subject of a report i had the honour to draw up a year ago and of a resolution by this parliament. on several occasions, in the debates in this house on the subject of justice and the fight against crime, a european-level justice system has emerged which focuses almost exclusively - and i would say quite rightly - on punishment, punishment and repression. only in a secondary way does this system also deal with the rehabilitation and social reintegration of prisoners and, more generally, with the policy of preventing crime. the taillight of this list is unfortunately the victims of crime: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's citizens are not left behind. this is why the protection of victims must also be at the heart of the debate on justice. the most urgent problem to be solved is the existence of wide disparities between national compensation systems, of enormous differences in the way and extent of compensation in each individual member state. this cannot be considered compatible with the principles underlying the creation of a single area of freedom, justice and security. much progress has been made during the year. the european union has identified the possible objectives to be pursued, identified the difficulties linked to the different legal codes of the member states, assessed the type of needs of the victim of crime and established the common minimum measures applicable. but the most awaited and significant progress is the will now to adopt a binding legislative strategy, at community level, to actually fulfil the political objectives of tampere. this directive will make it possible to take a first step towards harmonising european criminal law in the treatment of victims of crime, by ensuring that they receive appropriate attention, recognition of the support they need and reparation for the damage suffered, even when the offender has not been identified, is missing or is insolvent, while fully respecting the principle of subsidiarity. the identification of common categories for the concepts of victim of crime, of the beneficiary of compensation where the victim has died and of common payment methods and formalities therefore constitutes the minimum legislative basis which the european union is duly called upon to provide, so that it no longer appears that the amount of compensation or the very possibility of obtaining it must depend on the place of residence or the place where the crime was committed. to this end, while agreeing in substance with everything proposed by the commission, it was decided to add, in comparison with the original text, a more explicit description of the type of damage to be compensated and the time allowed for compensation. the minimum amount of exclusion from compensation was specified; the commission has proposed that, in order to avoid linguistic difficulties, harmonised forms and, where appropriate, translations should be provided in a language which the victim can understand. the priority objective is to guarantee the fundamental principle of non-discrimination for all citizens and legal residents in the union and to limit, as far as possible, the consequences and suffering of those who, having suffered unjust harm, are again victims when they are denied support by inadequate or sometimes non-existent compensation systems. i would like to conclude, mr president, by thanking my colleagues who have contributed to the success of this work.

commission. mr president, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr hernández mollar, for his excellent report. the commission shares his view about the crucial importance of setting common minimum standards on procedural safeguards. this is vital to ensure the mutual trust which forms the basis of the measures set out in the mutual recognition programme of which the european arrest warrant was the first to reach political agreement. a common set of minimum standards on safeguards is necessary to ensure that the fundamental rights of european union citizens are respected in an equivalent way in the 25 member states. a proposal for a framework decision is planned by the commission as a follow-up measure to the green paper if the main ideas that we have put forward deserve the support of this parliament. a measure of this sort was envisaged at the tampere european council, hence the references to protecting the rights of individuals. this measure does not, in fact, go further than the already existing provisions – the european convention on human rights and the vienna convention on consular relations. it will highlight what is seen at eu level as essential for a fair trial and it will make mutual recognition measures operate more smoothly, since member states will be more willing to accept that other member states have proper safeguards in place. regarding the recommendation made by the rapporteur to include provisions governing other fundamental rights such as the right to bail, or rules on the admissibility of evidence, the commission explains in the green paper that these two very important areas will indeed be the subject of separate measures of their own in order to do them justice. the work on the right to bail, which also covers detention conditions, forms the subject matter of a measure in the mutual recognition programme and will be more appropriately dealt with as a single issue. i can even tell the honourable members of the house that the commission has presented a questionnaire to the member states on this specific issue. we have received the first answers and we will be presenting a first evaluation of these to the justice and home affairs council, which will meet tomorrow morning here in brussels. a communication on the subject is included in the commission's work programme for 2003. in the work programme for this year, there is also a green paper on the approximation, execution and recognition of criminal sanctions in the european union. this is designed to ensure equality of treatment for convicted persons throughout the european union so that, for example, those sentenced in a member state other than their own are not discriminated against by virtue of their foreign nationality. regarding fairness in handling evidence, this area is too vast to be covered in a green paper that already proposes several rights, as does the current one. the commission therefore decided to devote more time to this topic and conduct a specific study as soon as the first stage of the procedural safeguard work was complete. the commission has now started work on a study of safeguards on fairness in the gathering and handling of evidence. this will cover, inter alia, the right to silence, the right to hear witnesses, the problem of anonymous witnesses, the right to disclosure of exculpatory evidence, how the presumption of innocence is to be understood, whether there are circumstances where the burden of proof may be reversed, and many other aspects of the law of evidence. this is one of the most complex issues in penal law. regarding the ne bis in idem principle, an initiative tabled by the former greek presidency is currently being discussed in the appropriate council bodies and, once again, the justice and home affairs council will discuss this greek initiative tomorrow. finally, on the questions of the conditions of prisoners in the european union, the commission recently prepared and sent a questionnaire on this issue to the competent authorities of the member states. the replies to this questionnaire are now arriving and are a useful source of information which is being taken into account in the process of preparation of the two green papers mentioned on pre-trial detention and approximation, mutual recognition and enforcement of sanctions.

mr president, i believe that the motion for a resolution contained in the report by mr hernández mollar is an important addition to the commission's green paper on procedural guarantees, thanks also to the contribution of the numerous amendments from all the political groups. i would therefore like to thank president hernández mollar for the work he has done. as i said, it is an important enrichment, not only because the resolution contains a strong encouragement for the adoption of a framework decision on common minimum standards, and not only because it also contains the critical indication of the chapters still missing, as the commission itself acknowledges, for the construction of a comprehensive system of common minimum guarantees laying down the basic european rights to a fair criminal trial. the list of those rights should be extended to include issues relating to the admissibility and evaluation of evidence, the criteria for pretrial detention, the same conditions of detention, and the right to appeal, which is particularly important in matters of personal liberty. the main contribution of the motion for a resolution is to identify in detail the specific content of the rights already covered by the green paper: legal assistance and counselling, which must be free of charge for those who need it and provided by experienced professionals; ensuring adequate and complete interpretation for those who speak a different language; the right to consular assistance, to adequate protection for vulnerable persons, especially but not only minors. the proposal for a written statement of the rights of the person being investigated and the person being accused, to be submitted at the first contact with the authorities responsible, which must be detailed and drawn up in several languages, is also innovative and of particular interest. we are well aware that all member states are bound to respect the european convention on human rights and that the strasbourg court, with its elaborate case law, monitors compliance with it. but it's not enough. the irreducible diversity of legal systems, procedures and traditions themselves raises concerns which have a negative impact on the confidence which european citizens must be able to have in the judicial systems of the member states if, in an area without internal frontiers, the necessary cooperation based on the mutual recognition of judicial decisions of the different countries is to be developed. it is therefore necessary and urgent, in order to guarantee both the freedom and the security of citizens, that common minimum standards be introduced to set, at european level, the high standards of procedural guarantees which europe is proud to ensure to all those citizens and non-citizens who come into contact with its judicial systems. i therefore announce that my group will vote in favour of the hernández mollar report.

- the next item is the report (a5-0381/2003) by mr mussa, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a council recommendation on cancer screening (com (2003) 230 - c5-0322/2003 - 2003/0093 (cns)).
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank all the members of the committee who have made a valuable contribution to the drafting of this scientifically and socially relevant report. as i have already said on other occasions, i believe that public health must increasingly take a leading role in european policies, also in view of future enlargement. this recommendation is a first step towards the harmonisation and coordination of policies on cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment. unfortunately, cancer is the main scourge in industrialized countries, both for the patient and for the family and for the operators themselves. the socioeconomic impact is therefore enormous, not only in terms of the cost of treatment and the support given to patients, but also in terms of the emotional commitment that this entails. this situation is not only a human tragedy but also a continuing decline in the proportion of the healthy population which is europe's productive and cognitive backbone. the latest statistics show that the average age of onset of these diseases is decreasing: the younger the patient, the more aggressive the disease. therefore, the therapeutic potential is undeniably linked to the timeliness of its diagnosis; the late diagnosis of cancer also makes the use of aggressive, mutilating and psychologically, economically and socially impactful therapies indispensable. although member states are responsible for health policies through their national health systems, such an important preventive activity, both in the social and health fields, cannot be allowed to remain a national or regional reality, depending on the economic and cultural possibilities of each country. the social impact of this disease must be supported and coordinated at european level, to guarantee the right to equal treatment opportunities and thus to achieve a standard of outcome. the current capacity for radical treatment in oncology seems to be more linked to the possibility of prevention, based on epidemiological, etiopathogenetic knowledge and early diagnosis, than to surgical, radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy techniques. for example, the five-year survival rate for gastric cancer ranges from 95 percent for patients with intramuscular cancer to less than 10 percent for patients with advanced invasive cancer despite treatment. on the one hand, a correct and adequate screening must have the greatest ability to highlight even the smallest lesions sensitivity and a good ability to discriminate them from benign ones specificity; on the other hand, the diagnostic test must be non-invasive for the subject and in any event involve almost no risk of harm arising from the procedure itself, taking into account that, by definition, those procedures concern asymptomatic persons, who are only potentially ill. it is clear that new early diagnosis tools must be tested and validated by experience before they can be produced in the european field. finally, the excellence of good screening practice needs to be monitored through analyses of relevant data and mortality in all member states, which will hopefully be collected in a european database. it is essential to mobilise economic resources to increase diagnostic facilities, so that the workload imposed by screening does not compromise the quality of the examination or increase waiting times for the examination, worsening the quality of care for patients who are already suffering from cancer. it is therefore essential to focus europe's action on four main areas: first, health information and education for the european citizen; second, the implementation of the already validated screening; third, periodic quality controls of the screening; fourth, the study of the applicability of new methods for screening. this recommendation will enable europe to act in a united way against a common, cruel, socially destructive disease, namely neoplastic disease. the urgency of strategic action at european level against cancer is underlined by the alarming epidemiological figure that one in four europeans has or will have a malignant tumour in their lifetime. finally, it is advisable that therapeutic guidelines for disease should be added to screening at european level.
commission. – first, i should like to thank the rapporteur and the members of this house for their comments on this report. i can reassure you that cancer prevention still figures very high on my agenda. as some members have rightly stated to me in writing, after 15 years of continuous european community efforts and involvement, this represents a significant and visible success for the community in an important area of disease prevention and health promotion for european citizens. work on cancer, including screening and surveillance, will be taken forward by the commission. the cancer screening recommendation will be taken forward by member states' authorities and the commission, once it is adopted by the council. funding will be through ongoing projects within the previous 'europe against cancer' programme and through the new public health programme. for 2003, a number of cancer-related projects have been identified for funding. under the current contracts, a fourth edition of the european guidelines for quality assurance in mammography screening and the first comprehensive edition of european guidelines for best practice in cervical cancer screening will be finalised in 2004. the commission has already enhanced the prevention of diseases, including cancer, in the new health programmes draft work programme for 2004. the draft specifically provides for a reference to cancer under the first and third strand objectives. this will enable cancer surveillance applications to be fully considered. project proposals on the status of best practice in the member states, as well as in acceding countries, would also be covered. in the light of the views expressed today, the commission intends to review the situation of cancer prevention even further with regard to the public health programmes work programme of 2004. we will then have to decide how to best underpin the commission's role in cancer prevention, while implementing the council recommendation on cancer screening.as the matter is especially important for acceding countries too, we are considering a meeting between experts from these countries and cancer screening experts, in order to ensure that the achievements of the cancer networks benefit the new member states as well. the points raised in the report and during the debate today have demonstrated clearly the importance of the issue. in the report of the committee on environment, health and consumer protection, 33 amendments are proposed. a further amendment was tabled for the plenary session. the commission can in principle support 11 amendments, namely amendments 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 11, 14, 15, 19, and 22. in addition, we partially support four amendments, amendments 1, 29, 30 and 32. in addition to general improvements in the wording of the text, the acceptable amendments concern, for example, improving compliance and equal access for european citizens, as well as enhancing the role of the commission in following up the implementation of the council recommendation. the commission cannot, however, support the remaining 19 amendments. amendment 25 cannot be supported, as all rules and regulations on data protection in the member states must be in accordance with directive 95/46/ec. exceptions, for instance for medical registries, must be in accordance with article 8 of the directive. thus the amendment would simply reiterate the 'acquis communitaire'. in addition, amendments 5, 13 and 34 cannot be supported. they refer to tests that have not been successfully evaluated in randomised controlled trials. finally, amendment 33 cannot be accepted. even though it makes the necessary distinction between evidence-based tests and new tests currently under evaluation or new variations of recommended tests, these new tests are already sufficiently covered by articles 6(c) and (d). to mention a few specific ones would immediately raise the question as to why only those tests have been singled out.

- the next item is the report (a5-0391/2003) by mr blokland, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council regulation on shipments of waste (com (2003) 379 - c5-0365/2003 - 2003/0139 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, i am pleased to say that the commission can accept 26 amendments fully and a further 23 amendments in principle or in part. certain amendments to article 13 on objections to waste for recovery pursue national solutions rather than solutions at community level, and these amendments are particularly aimed at addressing the issues of so-called standard dumping in relation to waste destined for recovery by allowing a number of further justifications for objecting to shipments destined for recovery. as we all know, the problem relates to the fact that waste for recovery travels almost freely within the single market and, at the same time, waste treatment that respects higher standards is often more costly than conventional waste treatment. i agree with the rapporteur that we can allow competition on costs but not on environmental standards. however, we are legally obliged through the treaty to safeguard the environment while also respecting the rules of the internal market. a solution can therefore be best found at community level and should be based on three main elements. firstly, the establishment of standards at eu level through the extension of the ipc directive; secondly, the establishment of guidelines regarding sham recovery and thirdly, clearer distinctions between the different recovery and disposal operations. i agree with those who say that it is not easy to see a solution until this long-term solution is found or established, but we in the commission definitely recognise the problem and the need to discuss a possible solution in the meantime, and this will be part of the process from now on. another issue of concern to the commission is the proposed banning of the interim treatment operations. amendments 13, 14, 34 and 41 propose banning shipments of waste for interim treatment operations and define recovery and disposal operations as only covering final treatment and not interim operations. the commission believes that an outright ban would both lack environmental justification and would conflict with the treaty. further, the commission believes that it is essential that the horizontal definitions of recovery and disposal operations as established in the waste framework directive are adhered to within this regulation. establishing different definitions would be both inconsistent and unnecessarily complicated. this issue of consistency with existing legislation also arises in other amendments. certain amendments to article 13 aim to establish criteria to classify a treatment as recovery and address the issue of sham recovery. in fact, such criteria could be among several deemed relevant for the distinction between recovery and disposal in general, which is a horizontal issue which should be settled in the context of the waste framework directive rather than in the specific context of this regulation. even though the commission might not entirely disagree with the substance of the proposed clarifications, there is a strong argument for consistency in the lists in the annexes and if changes are required they should, as a first step, be introduced at their point of origin. another element regarding annex v, namely that of giving priority to the eu hazardous list above the basel non-hazardous list in relation to the so-called basel ban on exports of hazardous waste from oecd to non-oecd countries, can be supported – amendments 69 and 70. let me just make a brief comment on the question of the double legal basis. as the explanatory memorandum establishes, the primary objective of the regulation is protection of the environment. that main objective has been maintained in the new proposal and the legal basis is in article 175 of the ec treaty: environment. however, as regards the provisions of titles iv, v and vi on exports out of, imports into and transit through the community to and from third countries, it can be argued that these are rules which pursue an overall and general environmental objective, as well as rules on international trade. environmental rules, therefore, also apply to the trade regime and are linked to it. therefore, the legal basis as regards the specific provisions in these three titles is article 133 of the ec treaty. amendment 95 proposes to allow tacit consent in relation to shipments of hazardous waste for recovery. as is also stressed in the explanatory memorandum, this is not acceptable to the commission. firstly, we have to apply the precautionary approach to shipments of hazardous waste within the community and, secondly, we have to respect the basel convention's requirements in this respect. the basel convention is very clear and leaves no room for interpretation. written consent for shipments of hazardous waste must be applied. the commission supports the amendments which pursue the same goal as the commission proposal, namely the promotion of eu standards and certain internationally-agreed guidelines in the country of destination outside the community. the guidelines added to the list – the ilo guidelines on ship-breaking and the oecd guidelines on personal computers – can also be accepted. lastly, with regard to impact assessment, there is none. however, the system of notification and information is a well-established one. there is no specific impact assessment.

- the next item is the report (a5-0365/2003) by mr lisi, on the joint text approved by the conciliation committee for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 96/82/ec on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances (pe-cons 3665/2003 - c5-0435/2003 - 2001/0257 ((cod)).
the rapporteur. mr president, madam commissioner, i will begin by briefly referring to the legislative process of this measure. the dramatic incidents that have affected the chemical industry in recent years, but especially the people living around these sites and the surrounding environment, have been drawing the attention of the european union. places such as bay a mare, aznacollar, but especially toulouse and enschede have become synonymous with human and environmental tragedies that we cannot leave without a clear response. it is in this delicate context that the commission has presented to parliament and the council its proposal to amend directive 96/82 of december 1996 on the control of the risks of accidents caused by dangerous substances. this proposal was the result of a thorough scientific work and we welcome the commission's willingness to address the weaknesses of the previous directive in a constructive spirit which has enabled us all to send a clear message to both the chemical industry and the people. we will do everything possible to ensure that appropriate control measures are adopted and respected in future. at the first reading i explained, together with other colleagues, the reasons for the need for this strong signal from the european parliament and we took a joint approach, which we confirm today, that the accidents which have occurred so far should hopefully not happen again, with a guarantee of protection for the citizens and workers of these plants and strong protection of the surrounding environment. the council, as you know, reached a common position which essentially echoed many of the concerns of parliament. it is true that after this second reading there were still some areas of doubt, but i believe that the compromise we have reached together and which we are submitting to parliament for ratification has clarified them. i shall briefly mention the following points which the conciliation has resolved by compromise: the first concerns mining activities. the compromise we have reached is aimed at ensuring complementarity between the directive in question and the directive on waste from mining activities, which is currently undergoing its first reading in this parliament. the scope of the seveso directive is thus extended to include installations for the disposal of waste used in connection with the processing of minerals. as regards staff training, in this area we have insisted from the outset on the importance of proper training of staff in the prevention and management of any accidents. this concept was reaffirmed in conciliation and parliament has now obtained that adequate training is provided not only for the staff of the sites concerned but also for the staff of the subcontracting companies working on these sites. as regards a third aspect, risk mapping, parliament had repeatedly called for the inclusion of illustrative maps to inform the citizens concerned of the area and extent of the risks, considering that this was nevertheless a simple and clear means of communication that would allow all those concerned to be informed of the potential risks in the event of accidents. a conciliation agreement has been reached whereby these maps or illustrations - and thus equivalent tools - are integrated into the safety reports and made available to the public. the second to last point was the one on potassium nitrate. the specifications and new thresholds for potassium nitrate proposed by parliament were approved by the council in conciliation. this amendment will help us to avoid farmers who use a form of potassium nitrate which is not classifiable as a fuel being incorrectly included among those who must be subject to the safety measures provided for in this directive. the last point concerns the spatial planning database. the compromise reached with the council on a database of risks and accident scenarios bank to assess the compatibility of industrial sites with certain sensitive areas calls for the commission to draw up, within three years, the guidelines necessary for the establishment of such a database, while safeguarding the necessary subsidiarity in the face of the diversity of situations. i would like to conclude, mr president, by thanking the commission and my colleagues. i believe that we have reached a satisfactory agreement together, which takes account of all the requirements that have been expressed, especially the main objective that i mentioned at the beginning, namely to send a clear message to our fellow citizens. in conclusion, mr president, i would like to make one technical point. in annex i, part i, in particular points 5 and 6, there are definitions which could lead to misunderstandings. please note that the english version is the authoritative version.

mr blokland, mr president, this report calls for the free movement of waste in europe - urban waste, industrial waste - and i voted in favour of this report. i would like to see the pensioners of europe considered as deserving of at least the same freedom of movement as that granted to urban and industrial waste. you know, mr president, that a person who is entitled to a social security benefit, such as a blind person, a deaf-mute person or a citizen who needs constant care, if he moves around europe outside his own country, loses the right to receive a pension on these grounds of disability. i would therefore prefer that the directive in question should deal not only with the movement of waste but also with the movement of retired citizens.
mr president, with this report, mrs gutiérrez-cortines, a spaniard, is calling for the protection of the soil - through mapping and legislation - so that it remains capable of producing good agricultural products. i am very pleased about this, but when i read about soil protection, i naturally asked the rapporteur, i asked europe, whether it is not time to make a commitment so that our leaders, too, instead of having their heads in the clouds and their feet on the ground, walk firmly with their feet on the ground. too often, in fact, they think of the stars and the sky and not of the daily needs of all citizens. let me conclude, mr president, by saying that we need more presidents like you, because we need presidents like you in all the countries of europe, not just in france.
mr blokland's report, mr president, deals with the circulation of waste in europe, urban and extra-urban waste. i voted in favour because this is certainly progress for europe, but i would like mr blokland and europe to also be more concerned about the free movement of citizens, particularly pensioners, and particularly pensioners with disabilities, because unfortunately, at present, under regulation 1408, pensioners who have social and health care pensions - such as deaf-mutes, blind people, people in need of care - lose the right to receive their social security pension if they move around europe. i would like to see the same freedom of movement for european citizens as that which this directive provides for municipal and industrial waste.

the rapporteur. mr president, this report deals with three communications from the european commission: the first is entitled 'enlarged europe' 'neighbourhood: a new framework for relations with our eastern and southern neighbours'. the second is the communication entitled: 'prepare the ground for a new proximity instrument'. the third is: 'to give a new impetus to eu action with mediterranean partners in the field of human rights and democratisation'. this new policy, from the parliament's point of view, must involve the 25 countries of the 'next venture' union, that is, those whose full integration into the union has already been decided, albeit at different times, for different reasons, and the neighbours to the east and south. it is a coherent proposal for a complex geopolitical area, from russia to morocco, which can be described as a pan-european and mediterranean region because of its history, its cultural relations and its geographical proximity. it is in this context that parliament proposes that the south-east dimension be integrated into this policy as soon as possible, that is to say the countries of the caucasus, and that we look a little further, that is to say also at other countries of the middle east dimension, which cannot be included in this strategy today. the report focuses on the policies to be implemented, considering that these policies are needed today, for the present, to build, first of all, a common security dimension, if we do not give the concept of security only a military value. we are very pleased that the first item in the new security strategy presented by the high representative for european security was the relationship with our neighbours, because our security is their security and we must build it together. at the same time, there is a wealth of relations to be built, which will lead us to share mutually beneficial policies with the countries concerned, based on a political and institutional dialogue with the appropriate instruments. the report therefore makes a clear distinction between this strategy and that of future enlargement, confirming without any ambiguity the commitment to conclude negotiations with romania and bulgaria in 2007, to assess by 2004 the opening of possible negotiations with turkey and the prospect of accession for all the balkan countries. we do not hide in the report that there are other countries, for example ukraine and moldova, which make no secret of the fact that they aspire to be members of the union. although this is not the strategy that will decide their entry, we say that participation in such a strategy can only bring this perspective closer and certainly not further away. the report also delves into the specific features of such a vast, diverse and complex area. we have just spoken about russia and the document expresses the awareness that relations with russia cannot be reduced to a simple neighbourhood relationship. but you will find a paragraph, which was voted on by the committee on foreign affairs at an unsuspected time, which highlights the problems of democracy and the tragedy in chechnya as the present obstacle to a normalisation of our relations. finally, the action plans give the commission a flexible instrument to establish multilateral, regional and bilateral relations with these countries, just as the cross-border instrument will serve not to build walls at the new frontiers but to have an understanding, an exaltation of the local dimension. the report also deals with the institutional question. the european union is not a political union, but a political union, and we are not going to be able to do that. we also call for human rights policy to be fully incorporated into this strategy. we believe, however, that there is still no european doctrine on this subject, although the commission's communication makes some interesting proposals and is a step forward.
