we have heard from the rapporteur and the commissioner that we are faced with a new generation of schengen information system, which is very different from the previous one and therefore has a different meaning and a new responsibility towards the citizens of europe. sis i was set up as a compensatory measure to allow the free movement of persons, but in recent years its perception has changed towards being a useful tool also in the context of police cooperation. in short, sis ii and sis i data can now become a useful tool for purposes other than those originally intended. the enlargement of the european union also requires the development of a second generation information system by 2006. therefore, the council framework decision on the european arrest warrant and the surrender procedures between member states still provides for the use of sis, and therefore the need for its timely updating. on this basis, the council should promote a public debate on the nature of sis and the policy objectives to be achieved with sis ii, to ensure that the development of this new system is carried out in a transparent and democratic manner. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the future of the eu's information society. an agency headed by a board of directors composed of representatives of the european institutions and the member states; it is also an agency funded by the eu budget and therefore subject to parliament's control. a rapid and final location decision by the central sis is therefore required. in addition, a study is needed on the possibility of combining the different databases that exist today or those that will be launched in the coming months and years - the sis, europol, vis, eurojust and so on - on the basis of a single technical platform, to create a comprehensive and integrated information system throughout the european union. in this context, particular attention should be paid to the impact such a system could have on privacy, human rights and the risks inherent in the inclusion of biometric data. the citizens will therefore need to be well informed to avoid unpleasant surprises. finally, a theme which might seem a little out of place, namely the immigration emergency. it is clear to all that the illegal entry of illegal aliens into the free movement area of the union calls for an unforeseen role for the sis ii: the commission has also been asked to provide information on the implementation of the schengen information system.

agreement. since that debate six months ago, the commission has proposed further reinforcement of the eu's human rights dialogue with the vietnamese government, in the light of the eu's experience mr president, ladies and gentlemen, my speech is about the maccormick report on european governance and - as the rapporteur rightly said - a europe united in diversity. the commission communication which underpinned this debate, to which commissioner fischer referred first, proposes tripartite contracts and conventions binding the community, the states and regional and local authorities. it proposes that community rules be adapted to situations characterised by major environmental and demographic diversity and to the different union policies, from transport policy to regional and territorial policies and so on. it is an important choice, but it should be noted that it will be the beginning of an experimental phase in which we will have to take stock of the lessons to be learned, which will be partly procedural but which, as has already been noted, may also concern the better management of the community's regional policies. we know that these are conventions which are bound by an obligation to be compatible with the treaties governing the life of the european union and to make adjustments which must not create obstacles to the functioning of the internal market. in essence, the principle to which the commission refers in this communication, which is correctly reflected in the maccormick report, is that of flexibility. this principle implies respect for the different constitutional systems of the member states, but it recognises that in some states there are constitutional systems which attribute to the regions and local authorities responsibilities of extraordinary importance which should not be undermined, although, in these cases too, it is necessary that the increased demand for democratic participation does not create situations of inequality which could also run counter to the guidelines set out in the constituent convention. the tripartite agreements cannot however derogate from the provisions of secondary law applicable to the whole of the european union, because, as i said earlier, this is the only way to remain consistent with the guidelines of the constituent convention. the aim is to improve the implementation of community policy. it is therefore important that the tripartite conventions and contracts set clear objectives motivated by the need to take account of the diversity existing in the territory of the union, although, on the basis of this experience, it will also be possible to revise a policy for the management of community policies that goes beyond the problem of diversity and that deals more thoroughly with the more general problem of democracy without, however, compromising - i believe this should be emphasized - the uniform application of community law throughout the european area.

mr president, i agree with the rapporteur, mr klaus-heiner lehne: the whole issue of the directive on the sale of alcohol seems like a never-ending story. starting in january 1989 with the commission's first proposal, an ambitious proposal which aimed to create an internal market for corporate control, the apa directive seems to have been, throughout its history, a kind of obstacle race, alternating between maximalist proposals unacceptable to some member states and the council of ministers and minimalist compromises unacceptable to others. i would remind you of this obstacle course when the european parliament rejected a joint proposal from the conciliation committee on 4 july 2001. but i also remember the commission's very interesting proposal of october 2002, drawn up after collecting the suggestions of a group of high-level experts. this proposal, in addition to maintaining the passivity rule in article 9, sought to achieve the objectives set by the european parliament and the experts consulted, the neutralisation of certain pre-bid defensive measures and the proportionality between risk capital and voting rights, while the more dangerous instruments such as trusts and multiple votes were unfortunately excluded from the neutralisation. another obstacle course has begun, one which we thought the presidency's insight in june 2002 offered a way out: the commission has also proposed that the member states and listed companies respectively be given the option of choosing between the model directive with a passivity rule and the neutralisation of the defensive measures type a companies or the maintenance of the defensive measures type b companies , all of which is complemented by an obligation of maximum transparency of the scheme to which a company is subject. in order to put all operators on an equal footing, it is envisaged that type a company may decide not to be scaled up by a type b company. the solution has many advantages: it indicates the ideal solution type a, the benchmark and creates reciprocity. the neutralization of defensive measures is also a first uniform rule of european company law: article 11, which allows for options, is essentially a derogation from the ordinary system. these options may be waived once the market has created the conditions by rewarding the type a company. it's not just that. under the current system, listed companies subject to regulations which do not provide for passivity rules and neutralizations can opt for litigation, which they would not be able to do without the directive. furthermore, the maximum transparency of company structures and internal rules, provided for both by article 10 of the proposed directive and by the parallel proposal for a directive on the transparency of listed companies, also under discussion at the moment in the parliament and the council, means that companies which fully accept articles 9 and 11, the stars, are the true clearly identifiable european companies. this will enable the market to reward them. institutional investors should explain to their clients why they are investing in a non-litigation type b company rather than a litigation type a company. finally, the compromise, by providing for partial pre-emptive opa, allows many countries not to change their legislation substantially without risking, at the same time, exposing companies to unfair competition from companies in other countries.
mr president, i think it is fair to say, in agreement with the views expressed by commissioner bolkestein, that once again an opportunity has been missed to modernise the capital market, first of all by means of rules which can ensure that european companies are more liable to litigation and, through this, more effective protection for shareholders. this means: i think that to call this a directive on takeovers - as mr huhne has said before - is an exaggeration. the point here is to recognize that there are different regulations and to ensure that the various countries maintain protectionist legislation in respect of their own companies, their own national samples, whether public or private. i think we need to take a much longer step: the european council in strasbourg on 14 and 15 december adopted a resolution on the situation in the european union. the rules, as proposed by the council, remove very few of the obstacles to the litigation of companies that exist under the laws of certain states, with the result that hostile escalations - which are the norm in an evolved financial market, where capital moves where it is believed that there are margins of efficiency to be recovered, in the interests of companies and workers in those companies and other companies, in the interests of consumers of products, goods or services - unfortunately become impossible. there is also a risk that this crystallization of the present situation will lead to retrograde steps. in italy, where legislation - the draghi law - is very open and efficient in this respect, there are already calls for a step backwards, arguing that in europe they do not go as far, opening up the litigation of companies. it is to be hoped that this measure - which is not, i repeat, a directive on takeovers - if it is approved tomorrow by parliament, will create real competition between legal systems and make those systems where takeovers are penalized and hindered pay through the so-called 'football vote' of international investors. there are very few positive elements: the recognition of the protection of minority rights and the sunset clause, i.e. the idea that the debate on the subject can be reopened. perhaps that is why this measure, which is not a european law on the opa, is worth adopting. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that employment in europe, the interests of workers and the unemployed, are also protected by efficient capital markets. we do not have that today, nor do i think this directive will create the necessary conditions.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the directive on takeover bids is a legislative act essential to the construction of a genuine internal market in corporate control: the commission has also proposed a legislative act which will give a decisive boost to the sound movement of capital in europe. virtuous circulation means more productivity, more growth, more competitiveness and - i say this to my colleagues on the left - more employment. after 14 years we are finally close to the finish line and i regret that the commission does not take the positive aspects of the current compromise. in recent months there has been a lot of cooperation between the council and the european parliament, and that is a positive result in itself. god knows what europe needs today, positive results! it is certainly a compromise, the only compromise possible today. we would have liked more, especially in my country, which has a very advanced and open legislation. we would have liked a directive which would have created a real common playing field with the passivity rule and the complete neutralization of defensive measures. we tried, but it was not possible because of the opposition of certain member states, which are now perhaps hiding behind so-called social amendments. the compromise we are voting on tomorrow reflects the state of european capitalism, which is still a mixture of family capitalism and mainstream capitalism. the rights of workers are well protected. hence the opt-in/opt-out system with respect to the level-playing field. but there is a commitment to try again in a few years' time, with the appropriate sunset clause, when the time may be right because the financial markets will have rewarded companies that have chosen to be litigated. it is therefore enough to remove article 11a, to make a few minor adjustments and a new directive will be ready for the future. with this directive and the others we are adopting under the financial services action plan, litigant companies, their governance and their budgets will be transparent. and we need transparency, given the recent cases like enron, cirio and parmalat. the choice of litigation will be facilitated by the fact that the litigating company may not be 'opare' by a non-litigating company. we have set the benchmark and we have protected it, which is better than a directive with only transparency procedures, as in the united states. all in all, we can be proud of it.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to join the unanimous chorus of those who consider this directive to be important and fundamental - perhaps the most important - that has come to pass in the current legislature. i would therefore like to stress, as chairman of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, the great balance shown by mr manders in proposing amendments which go in the right direction on a subject on which exaggerations or underestimations are equally negative, as one can well understand. the directive is complex and the impact, positive or negative, that it can have on the environment and the whole production system depends on the wisdom of our balance. a directive that goes beyond what is reasonable would, in practice, risk imposing on undertakings heavy and unbearable obligations and costs, perhaps pushing them to relocate to other countries where these rules do not exist and would do so reluctantly in order to compete on the international market. i too would like to stress that the principle - not trivial but important - that 'the polluter pays', that is, that those who cause damage must restore damaged goods, is fundamental in a society that wants to guarantee a good quality of life in the future. it is also important to establish the subject matter of protection and, therefore, the resulting liability: who is responsible, for how long and to what extent. i believe that the council's common position in itself makes a positive contribution in this respect, and we must be associated with it. thus, the principle of 'wisdom and balance' which i constantly repeat and which has been the leitmotif of our whole discussion has led to the identification of protected sites, the definition of responsibility and the exclusion from responsibility of those who have complied with the authorisations and legal rules. i would simply like to add to the proposals of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights, together with mrs niebler - who has done a very good job as a shadow rapporteur, as she has shown in her speech this evening - an amendment which i particularly welcome and which is aimed at clarifying the definition of 'operator', which, as it is now formulated, does not exclude the involvement of banks and other financial institutions in the context of liability for environmental damage caused by financial entities. i understand that the commission does not agree with this point, which i would like to see dealt with in greater detail, so that it can consider more carefully whether it is appropriate to arrive at a definition which does not cover all the cases which may actually arise in this area and which could lead to a claim for compensation for such damage to a financial intermediary. i think that is a fair request and i would recommend support for this directive. in conclusion, i believe that the position of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights has been linked to a common position; i hope that it will be able to gather a broad consensus in the house during the vote.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the position of the committee on legal affairs, summed up in the recommendation of mr toine manders, whom i thank for the important work he has done, is a correct one. it does not change the substance of the council's approach, but it does clarify some of its fundamental principles, so as to bring the directive more into line with the union. in view of the impact of the rules on industrial activities, it is considered necessary to eliminate asymmetries between the countries of the union in order to avoid distortions of competition and of the competitiveness of undertakings. however, certain principles need to be clearly reaffirmed: the concept of 'operator' should not be extended to persons exercising control over activities. the identification of only potential damage is contrary to the principles of legal certainty and could therefore lead to a lengthy litigation which cannot be dealt with by the available technical and scientific instruments. operators responsible for the damage should be able to take the necessary measures directly and inform the competent authorities in a timely manner. the intervention of the authority, both as regards preventive measures and measures to remedy damage, should be limited to cases where the operator is unwilling and unable to intervene, as it is not acceptable that the authority itself be left with the unquestioned discretion to take the measures in question directly. it is therefore clear that such intervention is necessary only in the case of 'orphan' or 'public' sites, that is to say, in cases where the operator does not provide. these provisions need to be clarified in order not to leave too much discretion to the different member states. in the text of the common position, exceptions relating to damage caused by an emission, activity or event which is permitted by the applicable rules and regulations or by the authorisations granted to the operator, or which is considered to be harmful according to the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time of emission and the performance of the activities, may constitute a discretionary derogation of individual member states. as regards the award of costs in the event of multiple perpetrators, the council left it to each member state to provide for both a strict liability and a proportional liability, depending on the national legislation in force. the imposition of financial liability in the form of a lump sum, in addition to being clearly contrary to the 'polluter pays' principle, would certainly make it more difficult, if not impossible, for operators in the productive sectors to quantify insurance cover and other financial guarantees. the allocation of responsibilities and related costs must therefore be carried out only in accordance with the criteria of fairness and reasonableness, and it must be provided that each operator provides for the part of the reorganization corresponding to its share of responsibility.

the rapporteur. mr president, after this report on the legislative package on medicines, which has made the veins and the pulses tremble, as we have seen, my report is like drinking a roman chamomile for relaxing purposes. i am very pleased and would therefore like to thank both the council and the commission, but also all the shadow rapporteurs, in particular mrs roth-behrendt, who is unfortunately not here because she is affected and has apologised for her absence, and of course all those colleagues who have helped to improve this directive. the directive, as adopted, finally puts order into a very confusing and controversial field. on the one hand, it specifies the areas to which the directive applies and excludes the use of plant products as provided for by other directives; on the other hand, it specifies certain quality and good manufacturing practice characteristics in the interests of consumer health and consumer protection. while the value of traditional herbal therapies should be recognised, it should not be forgotten that improper use can lead to the development of undesirable, sometimes serious, side effects. so far, for example, the food and drug administration has recorded about 2900 cases of toxic effects, including, pay attention, 104 deaths mostly from ephedra abuse, but also serious side effects from other products that are used daily, such as st. john's wort, ginkgo biloba and even ginseng. this is why it was important to adopt a directive aimed at protecting the health of consumers, requiring high quality and safety standards on the one hand, but also requiring labels and package leaflets to contain strictly scientific, simple and clear information for the public on the potential toxicity of medicinal herbs and their interaction with food, drink and other medicines taken at the same time. as you know, traditional medicinal herbs are those used for at least 30 years, 15 of which have been in the community. however, at the request of a single country and this has been a reason for improvement of the directive and on the basis of a reasoned opinion of the technical and scientific committee for plant medicinal products of the emea, the 15 year period of use can be significantly reduced. another positive aspect, mr president, is the establishment of a committee on medicinal herbs within the emea. parliament has clearly indicated that this committee should be distinguished from the committee for the evaluation of medicinal products. it will be responsible for classification, preparation of a list of traditional medicinal herbs, updating of the list, preparation of appropriate monographs, and evaluation of dossiers in case of disputes at national level. the commission has also proposed and approved two amendments at second reading. in particular, a first amendment inserted in the recitals is intended to clarify further, if necessary, the scope of this directive, by specifying that it concerns only traditional medicinal products of plant origin, while the use of plants or herbs for food is regulated by specific existing european legislation concerning foodstuffs. the second amendment is just a clarification: it's about putting the word traditional when we talk about herbal products. both amendments were subsequently approved by the council, as is apparent from the communication to the committee on the environment of 8 december 2003. finally, this directive establishes a harmonised legislative framework for all the countries of the european union, facilitating the free movement of traditional medicinal herbs within the community. it also ensures the highest level of protection of public health on the basis of the required documentation on quality, efficacy and safety.
mr president, our group in this house is strongly in favour of a statute for members of the european parliament. we have always been convinced that it is necessary to create a statute guaranteeing equal political and financial dignity to the representatives of the peoples of europe. to this end, we have always followed and proactively encouraged all the steps leading up to the current proposal under discussion in the council. i would like to make it equally clear that we are opposed to any delaying manoeuvre. the group of the european united left calls for the adoption of these statutes as soon as possible. the principle of equality between members of the european parliament seems to us to be a necessary element of justice and clarity for our citizens. of course, as with all compromise proposals, we are not entirely satisfied with the proposal under consideration, but we will not fail to make our constructive contribution, open to dialogue between all the parliamentary groups. the most important point of disagreement is the age of retirement. the current proposal is to grant pension rights to members at the age of 63, while the group of the european united left thinks that this age should be lowered to 60. this proposal is not intended to protect the privileges of members: we do it because we believe that all european citizens should retire at the age of 60 at the latest. with my colleagues i have always fought pension reforms based on raising the age of retirement, which i consider unfair. we believe that there are financial resources to enable all european citizens, including members of parliament who are citizens like everyone else, to retire at the age of 60. as regards the principle of the single salary, we are convinced that it represents a principle of democracy and equal treatment. why should an estonian mep be paid much less than a german? at the same time, however, we realise that in certain member states of the european union, there could be situations where an mep receives a salary several times higher than that of his president of the republic. that is why we must show political flexibility. perhaps we could bring the remuneration of members of parliament closer together by taking into account the monthly salaries of the highest state officials in this or that country, but the principle of a single, uniform salary is a principle which we cannot abandon. finally, on the reimbursement of travel expenses for members of the european parliament, we would remind you that the bureau of the european parliament has drawn up a proposal which the majority of my group is calling for to be put into practice at the same time as the entry into force of the statute.

would like to thank in particular mr imbeni and the rapporteur, mr costa, and the council for the efforts made during all this time to find a solution to the problem, discussing it with the council in order to reach an agreement. i want to say very clearly, and for the avoidance of doubt, that the commission supports this commitment. i know that the austrian authorities and members of parliament consider this to be insufficient, and i understand that they may be particularly sensitive, since it is true that we are talking about transit through austria. but i would like to state once again, ladies and gentlemen, that this commitment improves the conditions of traffic through austria, for the simple reason that protocol no 9 of the act of accession of austria to the european union provides, in article 11 (5) that, at the end of a series of extensions - all of which have already been fulfilled - the whole of the community acquis will apply. the last of these extensions has already been adopted and expires on the 31st of this month. if this compromise is not adopted, then the principles of free movement would mean that all the trucks that travel in the rest of the european union would be travelling through austria. we are all aware of the particular sensitivity of this issue and that is why we have all made an effort to achieve this. i would like to stress once again that i understand that the authorities and the parliamentarians, and quite possibly also the austrian citizens - since this is a matter which affects austria as a whole with great concern - would have wished for even greater protection, but i believe that this transitional arrangement does, in spite of everything, maintain a privileged position - let us be clear - in the interests of protecting the environment in austria. we are in fact banning the most polluting lorries from passing through that country, lorries which can and will nevertheless continue to circulate in the rest of the european union. that is to say, we are diverting the most polluting trucks to other routes and allowing only the cleanest trucks to pass through austria. i think that this is an element of european solidarity which, although it may seem to you to be insufficient, i insist that it is a very important step, because we are still maintaining the points system, which, in addition to suppressing the traffic of the most polluting trucks, limits the traffic of trucks with an intermediate level of pollution, so that only the most modern and most efficient trucks can circulate freely in austria. and so, i repeat, all the trucks that are more polluting or less efficient will be driving in the rest of the european union. it is crucial that parliament votes today, as the current system expires on 31 december. however, operators will no longer have eco-points as from 1 january 2004 and therefore a decision should be taken on the immediate application of the future provisional points system and on allowing the movement of lorries in transit through austria in a clear and decisive manner, with those limitations which i would like to stress again. i know very well that this is not the solution; that the solution must be found through the urgent adoption of the euro-vignette system. today we have adopted the tele-toll system, which includes the technical elements that will facilitate the introduction of a euro-ticket system, and if we can all agree and show flexibility, we could adopt the euro-ticket system in the next three or four months, with this same parliament and this same commission, during the irish presidency. the commission will make every effort to achieve this objective, and i hope that mr cocilovo and this parliament will continue to work as they have done so far to achieve it.
mr president, commissioner, i think that what mr hatzidakis said, also on behalf of the rapporteur, explained the technical content of this difficult conciliation very well, and i think that the words of the commissioner, which i share, illustrated the political content of this very complex, very complicated decision, which is difficult to call by any other name. we, taking on board the difficulties we have understood, even if we cannot justify the austrian population, decide to grant a further privilege because that is what it is about, as the commissioner said, by extending it to a particularly sensitive area such as the alpine to the whole of the austrian territory, thus doubling the privilege, and instead of limiting it to 2004 and then possibly seeing what to do in 2005-06, we extend it automatically to 2006. this is the subject of the agreement which we are now prepared to support, well aware that it is being forced. but we also believe that for the sake of the very idea of a european community, it is right that this sacrifice should be made. other arguments are therefore out of place. overall, a compromise is reached, which is excellent and the best compromise possible because it ensures a balance between the right to mobility and respect for the environment, because it has a gradual approach, because it punishes the so-called non-virtuous behaviour of those who do not renew the car fleet and rewards those who have this virtuous behaviour, because it enhances the specificity and the delicacy of an area. if anyone wants to call themselves out of this compromise, they are free to do so, but they would certainly make a mistake: this is the best choice that could have been made and should therefore be supported.
